instruction: Implement a user profile edit feature where users can update their display name, email, and avatar. The form should validate email format, prevent duplicate emails, show loading states during upload, and handle avatar image compression client-side before sending to the API. The existing UserEditForm component is a controlled form but has no file upload capability.
reasoning: This requires integrating file upload into an existing controlled form without breaking its validation flow. Avatar compression must happen before state updates to avoid UI lag. Email uniqueness validation needs debouncing to prevent excessive API calls. The implementation must preserve existing form behavior while adding new capabilities across frontend and backend layers.
answer: Add file input with onChange handler that uses client-side compression (e.g., browser-image-compression). Implement debounced email validation that calls GET /api/users/check-email?email=... after 500ms. Update form state to include avatarPreview (blob URL) and avatarFile (File object). On submit, send FormData with avatar file and JSON fields. Backend: add multer middleware for avatar upload, validate file type/size, resize with sharp, save to storage, update user record. Add loading states: isUploading for avatar, isCheckingEmail for validation. Clean up blob URLs on unmount. Handle race conditions by canceling pending validation requests when email changes.

instruction: Add pagination to the product listing page. The current implementation fetches all products at once and renders them in a grid. Requirements: 20 items per page, URL-based pagination (?page=2), preserve filter state across page changes, show loading skeleton during transitions, handle direct URL navigation to specific pages.
reasoning: URL-based pagination requires syncing router state with component state while preserving filters. The naive approach of just adding offset/limit breaks when users navigate directly to page URLs with filters. Loading skeletons must replace the grid without causing layout shift. Filter state must be serialized into URL params and restored on mount.
answer: Create usePagination hook that reads page from URL search params, defaults to 1. Modify API call to include page and limit params. Serialize filters into URL: ?category=shoes&page=2&sort=price. Use router.push with shallow: true to avoid full page reload. Implement skeleton loader that matches grid dimensions. On mount, parse URL params to restore filters and page. Add error boundary for invalid page numbers (redirect to page 1). Backend: add LIMIT/OFFSET to query, return total count for pagination UI. Handle edge case where page exceeds total pages by redirecting to last page.

instruction: Implement optimistic updates for a todo list where users can toggle completion status. The current implementation waits for API response before updating UI, causing perceived lag. Requirements: immediately update UI, revert on API failure, show error toast, prevent duplicate rapid toggles on same item.
reasoning: Optimistic updates require tracking the previous state to enable rollback. Rapid toggling creates race conditions where multiple requests are in flight. The solution needs request deduplication and proper state reconciliation when responses arrive out of order. Error handling must distinguish between network failures and validation errors.
answer: Store optimistic updates in a Map<todoId, {previousState, requestCount}>. On toggle: increment requestCount, immediately update local state, send API request with request ID. On response: decrement requestCount, if error and requestCount === 0 then rollback to previousState and show toast. Use AbortController to cancel pending requests when same todo is toggled again. Backend should return current server state on conflict (409) so client can reconcile. Add visual indicator (spinner) when requestCount > 0. Handle offline scenario by queuing updates in localStorage.

instruction: Refactor the authentication flow to support refresh tokens. Currently, the app stores JWT in localStorage and redirects to login on 401. Requirements: implement automatic token refresh, prevent multiple concurrent refresh requests, handle refresh token expiration, maintain user session across tab closures.
reasoning: Token refresh creates a race condition when multiple API calls fail simultaneously. The naive approach sends multiple refresh requests. Need request queuing during refresh. Refresh token storage requires security considerations (httpOnly cookie vs localStorage). Session persistence needs careful handling of token lifecycle.
answer: Create auth interceptor that queues failed requests during refresh. Store refresh token in httpOnly cookie (set by backend). On 401: check if refresh in progress, if yes queue request, if no initiate refresh. Refresh endpoint: POST /auth/refresh returns new access token. On refresh success: retry all queued requests. On refresh failure (401): clear tokens, redirect to login. Add token expiration check before API calls (decode JWT exp claim). Implement sliding window: refresh token when access token expires in <5 minutes. Handle concurrent tabs with BroadcastChannel to sync auth state. Add retry logic with exponential backoff for refresh failures.

instruction: Add real-time notifications using WebSockets. The app currently polls /api/notifications every 30 seconds. Requirements: establish WebSocket connection on login, handle reconnection on disconnect, queue messages when offline, show connection status indicator, gracefully degrade to polling if WebSocket fails.
reasoning: WebSocket implementation requires handling connection lifecycle, reconnection logic, and fallback strategies. Message queuing during disconnection needs persistent storage. Connection status affects UI components across the app. Fallback to polling must be transparent to consumers. Need to handle server-initiated disconnections and authentication on reconnect.
answer: Create WebSocket service singleton with connect/disconnect/send methods. On connect: authenticate with JWT, subscribe to user channel. Implement exponential backoff reconnection (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, max 30s). Queue unsent messages in IndexedDB. Emit connection state events (connecting, connected, disconnected). Create useWebSocket hook for components. Add connection status badge in header. Fallback logic: after 3 failed connection attempts, switch to polling mode. On successful reconnect: sync missed notifications by fetching since last received timestamp. Handle server heartbeat (ping/pong). Clean up subscriptions on unmount.

instruction: Implement a multi-step form wizard for user onboarding. Steps: personal info, preferences, payment method, confirmation. Requirements: persist progress across page refreshes, allow navigation between completed steps, validate each step before proceeding, show progress indicator, handle payment method tokenization without storing sensitive data.
reasoning: Multi-step forms require careful state management across steps. Persistence strategy affects security (don't store sensitive data). Step validation must prevent skipping ahead. Payment tokenization needs to happen client-side before submission. Navigation between steps requires tracking completion status and allowing edits.
answer: Store form state in sessionStorage keyed by step (not sensitive data). Create FormWizard component with steps array, currentStep, completedSteps state. Each step component receives onNext/onBack handlers. Validation: run schema validation on current step before allowing next. Payment step: use Stripe.js to tokenize card, store only token ID. Progress indicator shows completed/current/pending states. Allow clicking completed steps to edit. On final submit: send all step data with payment token. Backend validates each step's data. Handle browser back button by syncing with router state. Clear sessionStorage on successful completion or after 24 hours.

instruction: Add server-side rendering (SSR) to the product detail page for SEO. The page currently uses client-side rendering with React Router. Requirements: render initial HTML on server, hydrate on client, handle data fetching on both server and client, preserve existing client-side navigation, maintain meta tags for social sharing.
reasoning: SSR requires data fetching to work in both server and browser contexts. Hydration mismatches occur when server and client render differently. Meta tags need server-side injection. Client-side navigation must still work after initial SSR. Need to handle authentication state differences between server and client.
answer: Migrate to Next.js or add React Router's StaticRouter for server rendering. Create data loader function that works in both contexts (check typeof window). Server: fetch data, render to string, inject into HTML template with window.__INITIAL_DATA__. Client: hydrate with initial data, skip refetch if data exists. Add react-helmet for meta tags (title, description, og:image). Handle auth: server renders public view, client upgrades to authenticated view after hydration. Use Suspense boundaries for loading states. Implement streaming SSR for faster TTFB. Add error boundaries for hydration mismatches. Cache rendered pages with ISR (incremental static regeneration) for frequently accessed products.

instruction: Implement infinite scroll for the activity feed. Current implementation loads all activities at once causing performance issues. Requirements: load 20 items initially, load more when scrolling near bottom, show loading indicator, handle new items appearing at top while user is scrolled down, maintain scroll position during loads.
reasoning: Infinite scroll requires intersection observer for scroll detection, not scroll events (performance). New items at top while scrolled down causes content shift. Need to track viewport position and adjust scroll after insertions. Loading state must not cause layout shift. Consider accessibility: screen readers need loading announcements.
answer: Use IntersectionObserver on sentinel element at bottom. When intersecting: fetch next page, append to list. For new items at top: use position: sticky notification banner 'X new items' that user clicks to scroll to top (prevents content shift). Implement virtualization with react-window for large lists (>100 items). Loading indicator: skeleton loader matching item height. Store scroll position in state, restore after data updates. Add ARIA live region for loading announcements. Handle edge case: user scrolls to bottom, new page loads but is empty (end of feed). Implement pull-to-refresh on mobile for new items. Backend: cursor-based pagination (not offset) for stable results with real-time updates.

instruction: Add role-based access control (RBAC) to the admin dashboard. Currently, all logged-in users can access admin routes. Requirements: define roles (admin, moderator, viewer), restrict route access, hide unauthorized UI elements, validate permissions on backend, handle role changes during active session.
reasoning: RBAC requires both frontend and backend enforcement. Frontend restrictions are UX only; backend is security. Role checks need to be declarative to avoid repetition. Dynamic role changes require real-time updates. Need to handle partial permissions (can view but not edit). Route guards must redirect gracefully.
answer: Define permissions matrix: {admin: ['*'], moderator: ['read:users', 'write:posts'], viewer: ['read:*']}. Create ProtectedRoute component that checks user.permissions.includes(requiredPermission). Create usePermission hook for conditional rendering. Backend: middleware validates JWT includes required permission for each route. On role change: backend revokes old token, issues new one. Frontend: listen for 403 responses, refetch user profile, update permissions. Add PermissionGuard component for UI elements. Handle edge case: user has permission to view page but not all sections (show partial UI with disabled actions). Log unauthorized access attempts for security monitoring.

instruction: Implement a search feature with autocomplete, filters, and result highlighting. Requirements: debounce search input, show suggestions after 2 characters, support filtering by category and date range, highlight matching terms in results, handle keyboard navigation, show recent searches from localStorage.
reasoning: Search autocomplete requires careful debouncing to avoid excessive API calls. Keyboard navigation needs focus management and ARIA attributes. Result highlighting must escape HTML to prevent XSS. Recent searches need privacy considerations (clear on logout). Filter state must sync with search query. Need to handle search result caching to avoid refetching identical queries.
answer: Create SearchBar component with debounced input (300ms). On input: fetch suggestions from /api/search/suggest?q=...&limit=5. Render dropdown with keyboard navigation (up/down arrows, enter to select, escape to close). Use ARIA: role='combobox', aria-expanded, aria-activedescendant. Highlight matches: escape HTML, wrap matches in <mark> tags. Store recent searches in localStorage (max 10, LRU eviction). Filter UI: category dropdown, date range picker. Sync filters to URL params for shareable searches. Backend: full-text search with highlighting, return match positions. Cache results in Map<query, results> with TTL. Handle empty results: show 'no results' with suggestion to refine search.

instruction: Add drag-and-drop reordering to a kanban board. Columns: To Do, In Progress, Done. Requirements: drag cards within and between columns, persist order to backend, show drop zones, handle touch devices, prevent dragging unauthorized cards, animate transitions.
reasoning: Drag-and-drop requires tracking drag state across components. Touch support needs separate implementation from mouse events. Order persistence must handle race conditions when multiple users reorder simultaneously. Drop zones need visual feedback. Animations must not interfere with drag logic. Authorization: users can only move cards they own or have permission for.
answer: Use react-beautiful-dnd or dnd-kit library for accessibility and touch support. Each column is a droppable area, cards are draggables. On drag start: store dragged card ID in context. Show drop zones with dashed borders. On drop: calculate new order (index in array), send PATCH /api/boards/:id/reorder with {cardId, fromColumn, toColumn, newIndex}. Backend: validate user has permission to move card, update order atomically. Optimistic update: reorder immediately, rollback on error. Animate with CSS transitions (transform, opacity). Handle concurrent edits: backend returns 409 if order changed, client refetches. Add keyboard shortcuts (space to pick up, arrows to move, enter to drop) for accessibility.

instruction: Implement a dark mode toggle that persists across sessions. Requirements: toggle between light/dark themes, respect system preference by default, allow manual override, prevent flash of wrong theme on page load, update all UI components to support both themes.
reasoning: Theme persistence requires storage strategy (localStorage vs cookie). Flash of wrong theme occurs when theme is applied after initial render. System preference detection uses prefers-color-scheme media query. Manual override must take precedence over system preference. Need CSS variables for theme colors to avoid prop drilling. All components must use theme tokens, not hardcoded colors.
answer: Create ThemeProvider context with theme state (light/dark/system). On mount: check localStorage for manual preference, else use system preference via matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)'). Inject inline script in <head> that reads localStorage and sets data-theme attribute on <html> before React hydrates (prevents flash). Create CSS variables: --bg-primary, --text-primary, etc. in :root and [data-theme='dark']. All components use var(--bg-primary). Toggle component: cycles through light/dark/system. On change: update localStorage, update data-theme attribute. Listen for system preference changes, update if user preference is 'system'. Handle SSR: inject theme script server-side.

instruction: Add CSV export functionality to the transactions table. Requirements: export filtered results (not all data), handle large datasets (>10k rows) without freezing UI, include proper headers, format dates and currency correctly, show progress indicator, allow cancellation.
reasoning: Large CSV exports can freeze the browser if done synchronously. Need to stream data and use web workers for processing. Filtered export requires sending current filters to backend. Date/currency formatting must match user's locale. Progress tracking requires backend to report export progress. Cancellation needs AbortController. File download must work across browsers.
answer: Backend: create streaming endpoint GET /api/transactions/export?filters=... that returns CSV with Transfer-Encoding: chunked. Use cursor-based database query to avoid loading all rows into memory. Format data server-side (dates as YYYY-MM-DD, currency with 2 decimals). Frontend: show modal with progress bar, cancel button. Use fetch with ReadableStream to download chunks. Update progress based on Content-Length header or custom X-Export-Progress header. On completion: create Blob, generate download link, trigger download. Use web worker for client-side CSV parsing if needed. Handle cancellation: AbortController cancels fetch. Add rate limiting to prevent abuse. Log export events for audit trail.

instruction: Implement a comment system with nested replies. Requirements: support unlimited nesting depth, show reply counts, allow editing/deleting own comments, show edit history, handle real-time updates when new comments are posted, paginate long comment threads.
reasoning: Nested comments require recursive rendering and careful state management. Unlimited depth can cause layout issues (need indentation limit). Edit history needs versioning. Real-time updates must insert new comments without losing user's scroll position. Pagination strategy: load top-level comments, expand replies on demand. Deleting comments with replies needs strategy (soft delete vs cascade).
answer: Data structure: comments table with parent_id for nesting. API: GET /api/posts/:id/comments returns flattened array with parent_id. Frontend: build tree structure, render recursively with Comment component. Limit visual indentation to 5 levels (deeper replies show at same indent). Show 'X replies' button to expand/collapse. Edit: inline editor, save creates new version in comment_versions table. Delete: soft delete (mark as deleted, show '[deleted]' if has replies, remove if no replies). Real-time: WebSocket event 'comment:new' inserts comment into tree, increments parent's reply count. Pagination: load 20 top-level comments initially, 'Load more' button. Replies: load on expand (10 at a time). Use virtualization for threads with 100+ comments.

instruction: Add file upload with progress tracking to the document management system. Requirements: support multiple files, show upload progress for each file, allow cancellation, validate file types and sizes client-side, handle upload failures with retry, prevent duplicate uploads of same file.
reasoning: Multiple concurrent uploads need individual progress tracking. Client-side validation prevents wasted bandwidth. Duplicate detection requires file fingerprinting (name + size + modified date). Cancellation needs XMLHttpRequest abort (fetch doesn't support upload cancellation). Retry logic must handle partial uploads. Progress UI needs to handle many files without overwhelming the interface.
answer: Create FileUpload component with file input (multiple), file list with progress bars. On file select: validate type (whitelist: pdf, doc, docx, xls, xlsx), size (max 50MB each). Generate file ID: hash(name + size + lastModified). Check localStorage for in-progress uploads, skip duplicates. Use XMLHttpRequest for upload (supports progress events and abort). Show progress bar per file, overall progress summary. On failure: show retry button, store failed files in state. On cancel: xhr.abort(), remove from list. Backend: validate files again, store in S3/cloud storage, save metadata to database. Return file IDs and URLs. Handle quota: show warning when approaching storage limit. Use resumable uploads (tus protocol) for large files (>100MB).

instruction: Implement a shopping cart that syncs across devices. Requirements: add/remove items, update quantities, persist cart for logged-in users, merge guest cart with user cart on login, show cart count in header, handle out-of-stock items, calculate totals with tax and shipping.
reasoning: Cart sync requires merging strategies when guest cart conflicts with user cart. Out-of-stock items need graceful handling (show warning, don't remove). Price changes between add-to-cart and checkout need validation. Tax calculation depends on shipping address (not known until checkout). Cart count in header needs global state. Guest cart persistence uses localStorage, user cart uses database.
answer: Create CartContext with items array, addItem, removeItem, updateQuantity methods. Guest users: store cart in localStorage. Logged-in users: sync with backend (POST /api/cart/sync on changes). On login: merge guest cart with user cart (backend: if item exists in both, use higher quantity). Header cart count: read from CartContext, show badge. On add-to-cart: check stock availability, show error if out of stock. On cart page: revalidate stock and prices (items may have changed). Show warnings for out-of-stock items with 'Remove' option. Calculate subtotal client-side, fetch tax/shipping from backend when address is provided. Handle price changes: show 'Price changed from $X to $Y' warning. Persist user cart across devices via backend sync on every page load.

instruction: Add keyboard shortcuts to the application. Requirements: global shortcuts (cmd+k for search, ? for help), context-specific shortcuts (j/k for navigation in list view), show shortcut hints in UI, allow users to customize shortcuts, prevent conflicts with browser shortcuts.
reasoning: Keyboard shortcuts need event listeners at appropriate levels (global vs component). Shortcut conflicts with browser defaults require careful selection. Customizable shortcuts need storage and conflict detection. Context-specific shortcuts must only activate when component is focused. Need to handle modifier keys correctly across platforms (cmd vs ctrl).
answer: Create useKeyboardShortcut hook that registers shortcuts with KeyboardEventManager. Global shortcuts: attach to document, check event.target to avoid input conflicts (don't trigger when typing). Context shortcuts: attach to component, remove on unmount. Shortcut format: 'mod+k' (mod = cmd on Mac, ctrl elsewhere). Create ShortcutProvider context to manage all shortcuts. Show shortcut hints: add keyboard icon next to buttons, show full shortcut on hover. Help modal: list all shortcuts grouped by context. Customization: store user shortcuts in localStorage, validate no conflicts before saving. Prevent browser conflicts: avoid shortcuts like cmd+t, cmd+w. Handle key sequences (e.g., 'g i' for go to inbox) with timeout. Add analytics to track shortcut usage.

instruction: Implement a notification center with read/unread tracking. Requirements: show notification bell with unread count, dropdown with notification list, mark as read on click, mark all as read button, categorize notifications (mentions, replies, system), show relative timestamps, handle pagination for old notifications.
reasoning: Notification tracking requires distinguishing read vs unread state. Unread count must update in real-time. Relative timestamps need periodic updates (every minute). Pagination must preserve read state. Categories need filtering. Mark as read should be idempotent (don't error if already read). Need to handle notification deletion (user deletes post that was mentioned in notification).
answer: Backend: notifications table with user_id, type, data (JSON), read_at timestamp, created_at. API: GET /api/notifications?unreadOnly=true&category=mentions&cursor=... Frontend: NotificationBell component shows count badge (hide if 0). Dropdown: list notifications grouped by date (Today, Yesterday, Earlier). Click notification: mark as read (PATCH /api/notifications/:id/read), navigate to relevant page. 'Mark all as read' button: PATCH /api/notifications/read-all. Relative timestamps: use timeago library, update every minute with setInterval. Pagination: infinite scroll with cursor-based pagination. Real-time: WebSocket event 'notification:new' adds to list, increments count. Handle deleted content: show 'This content is no longer available' message. Add notification preferences: allow users to disable certain types.

instruction: Add internationalization (i18n) to the application. Requirements: support English, Spanish, French, German, detect user's browser language, allow manual language selection, handle RTL languages, translate all UI text including error messages, format dates and numbers according to locale.
reasoning: I18n requires extracting all hardcoded strings into translation files. Language detection needs fallback chain (user preference > browser > default). RTL support requires CSS logical properties. Date/number formatting must use Intl API. Translation keys need organization (by feature/page). Missing translations need fallback to default language. Dynamic content (user-generated) should not be translated.
answer: Use react-i18next or react-intl. Extract strings: replace 'Submit' with t('common.submit'). Create translation files: en.json, es.json, fr.json, de.json organized by namespace (common, auth, dashboard). Language detection: check localStorage, then navigator.language, default to 'en'. Language switcher: dropdown in header, save preference to localStorage and user profile. RTL support: add dir attribute to <html>, use CSS logical properties (margin-inline-start instead of margin-left). Format dates: Intl.DateTimeFormat with locale. Format numbers: Intl.NumberFormat. Handle pluralization: use ICU message syntax. Translate error messages: backend returns error codes, frontend maps to translated messages. Add pseudo-localization mode for testing (transforms strings to identify untranslated text). Lazy load translation files to reduce initial bundle size.

instruction: Implement a data table with sorting, filtering, and column resizing. Requirements: sort by clicking column headers (toggle asc/desc/none), filter by text search across all columns, resize columns by dragging edges, persist table preferences (sort, column widths) per user, handle large datasets (10k+ rows) with virtualization.
reasoning: Table state management needs to handle multiple interacting features (sort + filter + resize). Column resizing requires mouse event tracking and width constraints. Persistence needs to be table-specific (different tables have different preferences). Large datasets require virtualization to avoid rendering all rows. Sort and filter must work together (filter first, then sort).
answer: Create DataTable component with columns config, data, onSort, onFilter props. Sorting: store sortConfig {column, direction} in state, sort data array (use stable sort). Click header: cycle through asc -> desc -> none. Show sort indicator (▲/▼). Filtering: debounce text input (300ms), filter data array by checking all columns. Column resize: add drag handle on column edge, track mousedown/mousemove/mouseup, update column width (min 50px, max 500px). Store preferences: save to localStorage keyed by table ID and user ID. Virtualization: use react-window or react-virtualized, render only visible rows + buffer. Calculate row height, total height, scroll offset. Handle variable row heights with measured sizes. Add keyboard navigation: arrow keys to move between cells, enter to edit (if editable). Export table state to URL params for shareable views.

instruction: Add two-factor authentication (2FA) to the login flow. Requirements: support TOTP (authenticator apps) and SMS, allow users to enable/disable 2FA, require 2FA on login if enabled, provide backup codes for account recovery, remember trusted devices for 30 days.
reasoning: 2FA implementation requires secure secret generation and storage. TOTP needs QR code generation for authenticator app setup. SMS requires integration with SMS provider and handling delivery failures. Backup codes need secure storage and one-time use. Trusted devices require device fingerprinting and token management. Login flow becomes multi-step with state management.
answer: Backend: add 2fa_secret (encrypted), 2fa_enabled, backup_codes (hashed) to users table. Enable 2FA flow: generate TOTP secret (speakeasy library), return QR code (qrcode library) and secret key for manual entry. User scans QR, enters verification code to confirm. Save secret encrypted with user's password hash. Generate 10 backup codes (crypto.randomBytes), hash with bcrypt, store in database. Login flow: after password verification, check if 2FA enabled. If yes: return 2FA required response, show code input form. Verify TOTP code (allow 1 time step window for clock drift) or backup code (mark as used). SMS 2FA: integrate Twilio, send code on login, verify within 5 minutes. Trusted devices: generate device token, store in trusted_devices table with expires_at (30 days), set as httpOnly cookie. On login: check for valid device token, skip 2FA if present. Allow users to view/revoke trusted devices.

instruction: Implement a markdown editor with live preview. Requirements: split-pane editor and preview, support GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM), syntax highlighting for code blocks, auto-save drafts, show word count, allow image upload via drag-and-drop, sanitize HTML to prevent XSS.
reasoning: Markdown parsing needs to handle GFM extensions (tables, strikethrough, task lists). Live preview requires debounced parsing to avoid lag. Syntax highlighting needs language detection. Image upload requires converting drag-and-drop to file upload and inserting markdown image syntax. XSS prevention requires sanitizing HTML output. Auto-save needs debouncing and conflict detection.
answer: Use CodeMirror or Monaco editor for the editor pane with markdown syntax highlighting. Use marked or remark for markdown parsing with GFM plugins. Split pane: use react-split-pane, allow resizing. Live preview: debounce parsing (500ms), render sanitized HTML. Syntax highlighting: use highlight.js or prism.js, auto-detect language. Image upload: on drop event, upload file to /api/uploads, insert ![alt](url) at cursor position. Sanitize HTML: use DOMPurify to remove script tags and event handlers. Auto-save: debounce (2 seconds), save to localStorage with timestamp, show 'Draft saved' indicator. Word count: parse markdown, count words (exclude markdown syntax). Add toolbar with formatting buttons (bold, italic, link, image) that insert markdown syntax. Handle large documents: virtualize preview rendering for 1000+ lines.

instruction: Add a booking system for appointment scheduling. Requirements: show available time slots based on provider's schedule, handle time zones, prevent double bookings, send confirmation emails, allow cancellation with reason, show calendar view of bookings.
reasoning: Time zone handling requires storing times in UTC and displaying in user's local time. Availability calculation must account for existing bookings, working hours, and holidays. Double booking prevention requires database-level constraints (not just application logic). Email notifications need queuing for reliability. Cancellation logic depends on business rules (e.g., 24-hour notice). Calendar view needs to fetch and display bookings efficiently.
answer: Backend: bookings table with provider_id, start_time (UTC), end_time (UTC), status, user_id. Availability endpoint: GET /api/providers/:id/availability?date=2024-01-15 returns array of available slots. Calculate by: get provider's working hours for that day, subtract existing bookings, subtract holidays, return 30-min slots. Prevent double booking: use database transaction with SELECT FOR UPDATE, or unique constraint on (provider_id, start_time). Time zones: store UTC, convert to user's time zone for display (use date-fns-tz or moment-timezone). Booking flow: user selects slot, submit creates booking with status 'pending', send confirmation email (use SendGrid/AWS SES), update status to 'confirmed'. Cancellation: check cancellation policy (e.g., can cancel if >24h before), update status to 'cancelled', send cancellation email, free up slot. Calendar view: fetch bookings for date range, use FullCalendar or react-big-calendar component. Handle recurring appointments with recurrence rules (RRULE).

instruction: Implement a form builder that allows users to create custom forms. Requirements: drag-and-drop form elements (text input, select, checkbox, date picker), configure field properties (label, required, validation rules), preview form, save form definitions, render saved forms dynamically, collect and store form submissions.
reasoning: Form builder requires a flexible schema to represent form structure. Drag-and-drop needs to handle reordering and nesting. Field configuration needs a property panel that updates based on selected field. Dynamic form rendering requires mapping schema to components. Validation rules need to be serializable and executable. Form submissions need flexible storage (JSON field or separate table per form).
answer: Schema: forms table with id, title, fields (JSON array). Each field: {id, type, label, required, validation: {minLength, maxLength, pattern}, options (for select)}. Form builder UI: left panel with field types (draggable), center canvas (droppable), right panel for selected field properties. Use dnd-kit for drag-and-drop. Field properties panel: render inputs based on field type (e.g., show 'Options' textarea for select fields). Save form: POST /api/forms with schema. Dynamic form renderer: map field.type to component (TextInput, Select, Checkbox, DatePicker). Apply validation rules using react-hook-form or formik with yup validation schema built from form definition. Form submissions: submissions table with form_id, data (JSON), submitted_at. Submission UI: show list of submissions, allow export to CSV. Add form versioning: save new version on each edit, keep submission history tied to specific version. Implement conditional logic: show/hide fields based on other field values.

instruction: Add error tracking and monitoring to the application. Requirements: capture JavaScript errors with stack traces, track API error rates, monitor performance metrics (page load time, API response time), set up alerts for error spikes, provide dashboard to view errors and performance data.
reasoning: Error tracking requires global error handlers for both sync and async errors. Performance metrics need to be collected without impacting user experience. API error tracking requires intercepting all HTTP requests. Alert thresholds need to account for traffic volume (percentage vs absolute count). Error grouping is critical to avoid alert fatigue (same error reported 1000 times). Need to capture context (user ID, URL, browser) for debugging.
answer: Integrate Sentry or build custom solution. JavaScript errors: window.onerror for sync errors, window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection') for promise rejections. Capture: error message, stack trace, component stack (React error boundaries), user context, URL, browser info. API errors: axios/fetch interceptor logs 4xx/5xx responses with request URL, method, status, response time. Performance: use Performance API (performance.timing, performance.getEntriesByType('navigation')). Track: page load time, time to first byte, largest contentful paint. Send metrics to backend in batches (navigator.sendBeacon for reliability). Backend: store errors in errors table with fingerprint (hash of stack trace to group similar errors). Track error count over time windows (5 min, 1 hour). Alerting: send email/Slack when error rate exceeds threshold (e.g., >5% of requests fail in 5 min). Dashboard: show error list grouped by fingerprint, error timeline, performance charts. Add source maps for readable stack traces in production.

instruction: Implement a collaborative document editor where multiple users can edit simultaneously. Requirements: show other users' cursors in real-time, handle concurrent edits without conflicts, show user avatars of active editors, persist document changes, handle network disconnections gracefully.
reasoning: Real-time collaboration requires operational transformation (OT) or conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) to handle concurrent edits. Cursor positions need to be broadcast and rendered. Network disconnections require offline editing with sync on reconnect. User presence needs heartbeat mechanism. Document persistence must handle version conflicts. This is a complex distributed systems problem.
answer: Use Yjs or Automerge (CRDT libraries) for conflict-free merging. Each user has a Yjs document instance that syncs via WebSocket. Edits are represented as operations that can be merged regardless of order. Cursor positions: each user broadcasts cursor position via WebSocket, render as colored cursor with user name tooltip. User presence: send heartbeat every 5 seconds, mark user as inactive after 15 seconds of no heartbeat. Show user avatars in header. Persistence: save document state to database every 30 seconds or after 10 edits (whichever comes first). Use Yjs's built-in persistence adapters for IndexedDB (offline) and database (server). Handle disconnection: Yjs continues working offline, syncs changes on reconnect. Show connection status indicator. Load document: fetch latest state from database, apply to Yjs document. Version history: save snapshots every 100 edits, allow reverting to previous versions. Add awareness protocol to share user info (name, avatar color) with other clients.

instruction: Add a permission system for a project management tool. Requirements: projects have members with roles (owner, admin, member, guest), different roles have different permissions (e.g., only admin can delete project, only member+ can create tasks), allow inviting users by email, handle pending invitations, transfer project ownership.
reasoning: Permission system requires a clear permission matrix and consistent enforcement. Role hierarchy needs to be enforced (owner > admin > member > guest). Invitations need to handle existing vs new users. Ownership transfer requires careful validation (can't transfer to guest, new owner must accept). Permission checks need to be both frontend (UX) and backend (security). Need to handle role changes during active session.
answer: Backend: project_members table with project_id, user_id, role. Define permission matrix: {owner: ['*'], admin: ['edit_project', 'manage_members', 'create_task', 'edit_task', 'delete_task'], member: ['create_task', 'edit_own_task', 'delete_own_task'], guest: ['view_project', 'view_tasks']}. Middleware: checkPermission(requiredPermission) validates user's role includes permission. Frontend: usePermission hook checks permissions, conditionally render UI elements. Invitation flow: POST /api/projects/:id/invitations with email, role. If user exists: create project_member with role, send email notification. If user doesn't exist: create invitation record, send email with signup link. On signup: check for pending invitations, auto-add to projects. Ownership transfer: POST /api/projects/:id/transfer with newOwnerId. Validate: current user is owner, new owner is admin or member. Send confirmation email to new owner. On accept: swap roles (old owner becomes admin, new owner becomes owner). Audit log: record all permission changes with timestamp and actor.

instruction: Implement a caching strategy for the application. Requirements: cache API responses to reduce server load, invalidate cache when data changes, handle cache expiration, show stale data while fetching fresh data, allow manual cache refresh, measure cache hit rates.
reasoning: Caching requires choosing what to cache (not all data is cacheable). Cache invalidation is the hardest part - need to know when data changes. Stale-while-revalidate pattern improves perceived performance. Cache keys need to include relevant parameters (user ID, filters). Cache storage: memory for session, IndexedDB for persistence. Need to avoid caching sensitive data. Cache hit rate measurement requires logging.
answer: Implement multi-layer caching: 1) HTTP cache: set Cache-Control headers for public data (max-age=300 for product listings). 2) Application cache: use react-query or SWR for API response caching with stale-while-revalidate. Configure: staleTime (data considered fresh), cacheTime (how long to keep unused cache), refetchOnWindowFocus. 3) Manual cache: IndexedDB for large datasets (e.g., product catalog). Cache invalidation: when mutation occurs, invalidate related queries (e.g., after creating task, invalidate tasks list). Use query keys that include all relevant params: ['tasks', {projectId, status}]. Stale-while-revalidate: show cached data immediately, fetch fresh data in background, update UI when ready. Manual refresh: 'Refresh' button calls queryClient.invalidateQueries. Cache metrics: track cache hits/misses, send to analytics. Sensitive data: don't cache auth tokens, personal info. Service worker: cache static assets with workbox, use cache-first strategy for images, network-first for API calls.

instruction: Add a workflow automation feature. Requirements: users define triggers (e.g., 'when task is created') and actions (e.g., 'send email to assignee'), support multiple actions per trigger, show execution history, allow enabling/disabling workflows, handle execution failures with retry logic.
reasoning: Workflow automation requires an event-driven architecture. Triggers need to be registered and matched against events. Actions need to be executed asynchronously to avoid blocking user operations. Execution history needs to track success/failure and provide debugging info. Failure handling requires retry logic with exponential backoff. Workflows need to be evaluated in a specific order and support conditions (if/else).
answer: Backend: workflows table with user_id, trigger_type, trigger_conditions (JSON), actions (JSON array), enabled. Trigger types: task_created, task_updated, task_completed, comment_added, etc. Actions: send_email, create_task, update_task, send_webhook, etc. Event system: when relevant event occurs (e.g., task creation), publish event to message queue (Redis/RabbitMQ). Workflow executor: consume events, find matching workflows (trigger_type matches, conditions met), execute actions. Action execution: use job queue (Bull/BullMQ) for async execution with retry (3 attempts, exponential backoff). Execution history: workflow_executions table with workflow_id, event_data, status, started_at, completed_at, error. Show in UI: list of executions with status, expandable to show details. Conditions: support simple conditions (field equals value) and compound conditions (AND/OR). UI: workflow builder with trigger selector, condition builder, action configurator. Test mode: allow manual trigger to test workflow. Rate limiting: prevent infinite loops (workflow creates task that triggers same workflow).

instruction: Implement a multi-tenant SaaS application. Requirements: each tenant has isolated data, tenants access app via subdomain (tenant1.app.com), share application code but allow tenant-specific customization (logo, colors), handle tenant signup and onboarding, implement tenant-level usage limits and billing.
reasoning: Multi-tenancy requires data isolation strategy (separate databases vs shared database with tenant_id). Subdomain routing needs to extract tenant from hostname. Customization requires tenant-specific configuration that doesn't affect other tenants. Usage limits need tracking and enforcement. Billing integration needs to handle subscription lifecycle. Need to prevent cross-tenant data access (security critical).
answer: Data isolation: use shared database with tenant_id column on all tables (simpler than separate databases). Add tenant_id to every query via middleware that extracts tenant from subdomain. Subdomain routing: middleware extracts subdomain from req.hostname, looks up tenant in tenants table, attaches tenant to request context. All subsequent queries include WHERE tenant_id = :tenantId. Customization: tenants table with custom_domain, logo_url, primary_color. Load tenant config on request, inject into response (HTML template for SSR, API response for SPA). Tenant signup: POST /api/tenants with company name, admin email. Create tenant record, create admin user, send welcome email with login link. Onboarding: guide through setup wizard (invite team members, configure settings). Usage limits: track metrics (users, storage, API calls) in usage_metrics table. Check limits on relevant operations (e.g., before creating user, check if under user limit). Billing: integrate Stripe, create customer on signup, subscribe to plan. Webhook handles subscription events (payment succeeded, subscription cancelled). Show usage dashboard and upgrade prompts when approaching limits. Security: row-level security in database, never trust client-provided tenant_id.

instruction: Implement a rate limiting system for API endpoints. Requirements: limit requests per user/IP, different limits for different endpoints (e.g., 100 req/min for search, 10 req/min for signup), return proper HTTP 429 responses with retry-after header, allow whitelisting specific users/IPs, show rate limit status in response headers.
reasoning: Rate limiting requires choosing a strategy (fixed window, sliding window, token bucket). Distributed systems need shared state (Redis) to track limits across servers. Different endpoints need different configurations. Whitelisting requires bypass logic. Rate limit headers need to inform clients of remaining quota. Need to handle race conditions in concurrent requests. Sliding window is more accurate than fixed window but more complex.
answer: Use Redis for distributed rate limiting. Implement sliding window algorithm: for each request, increment counter with TTL equal to window duration. Key format: ratelimit:{endpoint}:{userId|IP}. Different endpoints have different configs stored in rate_limit_configs table: {endpoint, window_seconds, max_requests}. Middleware: extract user ID (from JWT) or IP (from req.ip), check rate limit before processing request. If limit exceeded: return 429 with Retry-After header (seconds until window resets). Add headers to all responses: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset. Whitelist: check whitelist table before applying limit. Sliding window implementation: use Redis sorted set with timestamp as score, remove old entries, count remaining. Alternative: use rate-limiter-flexible library which handles multiple algorithms. Add rate limit dashboard showing usage patterns. Handle burst traffic: allow burst up to 2x limit for short periods. Implement gradual backoff: after hitting limit, increase wait time exponentially.

instruction: Add a feature flag system to enable/disable features without deployment. Requirements: toggle features globally or per user segment, evaluate flags client-side and server-side, cache flag evaluations, support gradual rollouts (e.g., 10% of users), allow A/B testing with multiple variants, track feature usage metrics.
reasoning: Feature flags require a centralized configuration system that both frontend and backend can access. Client-side evaluation needs flag definitions synced from server. User segmentation requires consistent hashing to ensure same user always sees same variant. Gradual rollouts need deterministic assignment (not random each request). Caching prevents database lookups on every request. Need to handle flag dependencies and conflicts.
answer: Backend: feature_flags table with key, enabled, rollout_percentage, segments (JSON), variants (JSON array). API: GET /api/feature-flags returns all flags (cached in Redis, invalidated on update). Flag evaluation service: checkFlag(key, userId, context) returns boolean or variant. Segmentation: define segments by user attributes (e.g., premium users, beta testers). Gradual rollout: hash(userId + flagKey) % 100 < rollout_percentage ensures consistent assignment. A/B testing: variants array with weights, assign variant based on hash. Client-side: fetch flags on app load, store in context. useFeatureFlag hook returns flag value. Server-side: middleware evaluates flags, attaches to request context. Conditional rendering: {hasNewFeature && <NewFeature />}. Metrics: log flag evaluations with user ID, variant, timestamp. Track conversion rates per variant. Flag management UI: create/edit flags, target segments, set rollout percentage, view metrics. Audit log: track who changed flags and when. Fallback: if flag service is down, use default values. Cleanup: process to remove old flags after full rollout.

instruction: Implement a payment processing system with Stripe integration. Requirements: support one-time payments and subscriptions, handle payment failures with retry logic, manage customer records, send payment receipts, handle refunds, comply with PCI DSS (don't store card numbers), support multiple currencies.
reasoning: Payment processing requires careful security considerations - never handle raw card data. Stripe Elements handles card input securely. Subscription lifecycle is complex (trial, active, past due, cancelled). Webhooks are critical for handling async payment events. Idempotency keys prevent duplicate charges on retries. Currency handling needs conversion and formatting. Refund logic depends on business rules (full vs partial, time limits).
answer: Never store card numbers - use Stripe.js and Elements for card input. Create customer in Stripe on signup, store stripe_customer_id in users table. One-time payment: create PaymentIntent server-side, return client_secret, confirm on client with stripe.confirmCardPayment. Subscription: create Stripe subscription, handle status transitions via webhooks. Webhooks: POST /webhooks/stripe, verify signature, handle events: payment_intent.succeeded, invoice.payment_failed, customer.subscription.deleted. Payment failures: Stripe Smart Retries automatically retry failed payments. Dunning: after 3 failures, cancel subscription, send email. Idempotency: include idempotency_key header on all Stripe API calls to prevent duplicate charges. Receipts: enable Stripe automatic receipts or send custom emails on payment_intent.succeeded. Refunds: POST /api/refunds with payment_intent_id, amount. Validate: payment exists, not already refunded, within refund window. Create Stripe refund, update local records. Multi-currency: store prices in smallest unit (cents), use Stripe's currency formatting. Display with Intl.NumberFormat. Tax: integrate Stripe Tax or TaxJar for automatic tax calculation. Reporting: dashboard showing revenue, MRR, churn rate.

instruction: Add a real-time chat feature to the application. Requirements: support direct messages and group chats, show typing indicators, mark messages as read, support message editing and deletion, handle file attachments, show online status, persist message history, handle pagination for old messages.
reasoning: Real-time chat requires WebSocket connections and message broadcasting. Typing indicators need debouncing to avoid spam. Read receipts require tracking which users have seen which messages. Message editing needs version history. File attachments need upload and thumbnail generation. Online status requires presence detection with heartbeat. Pagination must preserve scroll position when loading older messages. Need to handle offline message delivery.
answer: Backend: conversations table (id, type: direct|group, participants), messages table (conversation_id, sender_id, content, attachments, created_at, edited_at). WebSocket server (Socket.io or ws): on connection, authenticate with JWT, join user to their conversation rooms. Send message: client emits 'message:send', server validates user is participant, saves to database, broadcasts to conversation room. Direct messages: create conversation on first message if doesn't exist. Group chats: create conversation with multiple participants. Typing indicator: debounce 'typing:start' event (emit after 500ms of no typing), auto-emit 'typing:stop' after 3 seconds. Read receipts: track message_reads (message_id, user_id, read_at). On conversation open: mark all messages as read, emit 'messages:read' to other participants. Message editing: allow edit within 5 minutes, save original to message_versions, emit 'message:edited'. Deletion: soft delete (mark as deleted, show 'Message deleted'), emit 'message:deleted'. File attachments: upload to S3, store URL in attachments JSON array, generate thumbnails for images. Online status: emit 'presence:update' on connect/disconnect, track in Redis with TTL (heartbeat every 30s). Message history: paginate with cursor (load 50 messages, load more on scroll up). Maintain scroll position by calculating height difference after prepending messages.

instruction: Implement a data migration system for database schema changes. Requirements: support forward and rollback migrations, track applied migrations, run migrations in transactions, handle large table migrations without downtime, support seeding initial data, integrate with CI/CD pipeline.
reasoning: Database migrations need to be versioned and ordered. Rollback support requires each migration to have an inverse. Large table migrations can lock tables and cause downtime - need online schema changes. Transaction support ensures atomicity but not all operations are transactional (e.g., CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in Postgres). Seeding needs to be idempotent. CI/CD integration requires non-interactive execution and proper error handling.
answer: Use a migration tool (Knex, TypeORM, Prisma) or build custom. Migration files: timestamped (20240115120000_create_users_table.js) to ensure order. Each migration has up() and down() methods. Migrations table: tracks which migrations have been applied (name, applied_at). Run migrations: read migration files, filter to unapplied, execute in order within transaction. Rollback: execute down() of last N migrations. Large table migrations: use pt-online-schema-change or gh-ost for MySQL, or CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY for Postgres. For adding columns: add nullable column, backfill in batches, add constraint. For renaming: add new column, copy data, update code, drop old column (multi-step over multiple deployments). Seeding: seed files that insert initial data (admin user, default settings). Make idempotent: check if data exists before inserting. CI/CD: run migrations in deployment script before starting new servers. Use separate database user with migration permissions. Backup: take database snapshot before running migrations in production. Dry run: show SQL without executing. Handle failures: if migration fails, transaction rolls back, log error, alert team. Never modify applied migrations (create new migration instead).

instruction: Add a content moderation system for user-generated content. Requirements: automatically detect inappropriate content (text and images), allow manual review queue, support appeals process, track moderation actions, allow custom moderation rules per community, integrate with external moderation services.
reasoning: Content moderation requires both automated and manual processes. Automated detection has false positives/negatives - need human review. Review queue needs prioritization (reported content first). Appeals process requires tracking original decision and reviewer. Custom rules per community need flexible rule engine. External services (Perspective API, AWS Rekognition) have rate limits and costs. Need to balance automation with accuracy.
answer: Backend: content_reports table (content_id, reporter_id, reason, status), moderation_actions table (content_id, moderator_id, action, reason, created_at). Automated moderation: on content creation, send to moderation services. Text: Perspective API returns toxicity scores, flag if >0.8. Images: AWS Rekognition detects unsafe content, flag if confidence >0.9. Flagged content: status = 'flagged', add to review queue. Manual review: moderators see queue sorted by priority (reported > auto-flagged, older first). Review UI shows content, flags, user history. Actions: approve (status = 'approved'), reject (status = 'rejected', delete content, warn user), escalate (to senior moderator). Appeals: users can appeal rejected content, creates appeal record, re-enters queue for different moderator. Custom rules: communities table with moderation_rules (JSON). Rule engine evaluates rules: if content contains banned_words, auto-reject. Track actions: log all moderation decisions with reason for audit and training. User penalties: track violations, auto-suspend after 3 strikes. Integrate with external services: queue moderation requests to handle rate limits, cache results. Fallback: if external service unavailable, queue for manual review. Metrics: track time to review, accuracy (appeals overturned), workload per moderator.

instruction: Implement a multi-language content management system. Requirements: store content in multiple languages, allow translators to work on translations, show translation progress, handle missing translations gracefully, support RTL languages, version content and translations together.
reasoning: Multi-language content requires a data model that links translations to source content. Translation workflow needs to track which translations are complete vs in progress. Missing translations need fallback strategy (show default language or placeholder). RTL support requires bidirectional text handling. Versioning ensures translations stay in sync with source content changes. Need to handle pluralization and gender-specific translations.
answer: Data model: content table (id, type, created_at), content_translations table (content_id, language_code, title, body, status: draft|review|published, translator_id, updated_at). When creating content: create base content record, create English translation (or default language). Translation workflow: translator sees list of content needing translation (filter by language, status). Translation UI: side-by-side view with source and target language. Mark sections as translated, save as draft, submit for review. Translation progress: calculate percentage of content translated per language, show in dashboard. Missing translations: fallback chain - requested language -> default language -> 'Translation not available'. RTL support: detect language direction, apply dir='rtl' to content, use CSS logical properties. Versioning: when source content updates, mark related translations as 'needs_update', show diff of changes. Translators can update translation and mark as current. Pluralization: use ICU message format for strings with variables (e.g., '{count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}}'). Translation memory: store previously translated phrases, suggest matches for new translations. Machine translation: integrate Google Translate API for initial draft, human reviews and edits. Language detection: auto-detect language of user-generated content.

instruction: Add a webhook system for integrating with external services. Requirements: allow users to configure webhook URLs, send webhook events on specific triggers (e.g., order created, user registered), retry failed deliveries with exponential backoff, provide webhook signing for security, show delivery history and logs, allow testing webhooks.
reasoning: Webhooks require reliable delivery with retry logic. Failed deliveries need exponential backoff to avoid overwhelming failing endpoints. Signing allows recipients to verify webhook authenticity. Delivery history helps with debugging. Testing feature allows users to verify their endpoint before going live. Need to handle webhook endpoint timeouts and slow responses. Payload format needs to be consistent and versioned.
answer: Backend: webhooks table (user_id, url, events (array), secret, active), webhook_deliveries table (webhook_id, event, payload, status, attempts, response_code, created_at). Configuration UI: users enter URL, select events to subscribe to, generate/view signing secret. Event triggers: when relevant event occurs (e.g., order creation), find subscribed webhooks, queue delivery job. Delivery: POST to webhook URL with JSON payload (event type, timestamp, data). Set timeout (10 seconds). Sign payload: create HMAC-SHA256 signature of payload using webhook secret, add X-Webhook-Signature header. Recipient verifies signature matches. Retry logic: if delivery fails (non-2xx response or timeout), retry with exponential backoff (1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 hours, 24 hours). After 5 attempts, mark as failed. Delivery history: show list of deliveries with status (delivered, failed, pending), expandable to show request/response details. Test webhook: send test event with sample payload, show response. Webhook management: pause/resume webhooks, delete webhooks. Rate limiting: limit deliveries per webhook to prevent abuse. Security: validate URL is HTTPS (production), allow HTTP for testing. Payload versioning: include version field, maintain backward compatibility.

instruction: Implement a background job queue for processing long-running tasks. Requirements: queue jobs for async processing (e.g., video encoding, report generation), track job status (queued, processing, completed, failed), handle job failures with retry logic, allow job prioritization, show job queue status dashboard, handle job dependencies.
reasoning: Background jobs prevent blocking user requests for long operations. Job queue needs persistence to survive server restarts. Status tracking allows users to check progress. Retry logic handles transient failures. Prioritization ensures important jobs run first. Dependencies allow chaining jobs (job B runs after job A completes). Need to handle job cancellation and timeout. Worker processes need to be scaled based on queue length.
answer: Use Bull (Redis-based) or similar job queue library. Job types: video_encoding, report_generation, email_send, data_export. Queue jobs: when user triggers long operation, create job with payload, return job ID immediately. Example: POST /api/videos/upload creates video_encoding job, returns {jobId: '...'} with status 'queued'. Job status API: GET /api/jobs/:id returns status, progress percentage, result (when complete). Frontend polls or uses WebSocket for real-time updates. Job processing: worker processes consume jobs from queue. Video encoding: use ffmpeg, update progress as each segment completes. Report generation: query data, generate PDF, upload to S3, return URL. Retry logic: configure retry attempts (3) and backoff (exponential). Mark job as failed after max retries. Prioritization: add priority field when creating job (high, normal, low). Bull processes high priority first. Dependencies: job B depends on job A - when A completes, automatically queue B. Use job.on('completed') event. Job cancellation: store job reference, call job.cancel(). Worker scaling: monitor queue length, auto-scale workers (e.g., Kubernetes HPA based on queue metrics). Dashboard: show queue length, active jobs, failed jobs, average processing time. Dead letter queue: jobs that fail max retries go to DLQ for manual inspection. Timeout: set job timeout (e.g., 30 minutes), mark as failed if exceeded.

instruction: Add a comprehensive audit logging system. Requirements: log all user actions (login, create, update, delete), log system events (deployment, configuration changes), make logs searchable and filterable, retain logs for compliance (e.g., 7 years), prevent log tampering, export logs for analysis.
reasoning: Audit logs are critical for security, compliance, and debugging. Need to capture who did what, when, from where. Logs must be immutable to prevent tampering. Search and filtering help find specific events quickly. Long retention requires efficient storage (compression, tiered storage). Sensitive data in logs needs masking. High-volume logging needs to not impact application performance.
answer: Backend: audit_logs table (id, user_id, action, resource_type, resource_id, details (JSON), ip_address, user_agent, created_at). Logging middleware: intercept requests, log relevant actions. Actions to log: authentication (login, logout, failed login), CRUD operations (create_user, update_order, delete_project), permission changes (grant_role, revoke_access), system events (deployment, config_change). Structured logging: use consistent format {action: 'user.login', userId: 123, ipAddress: '1.2.3.4', timestamp: '...'}, details: {method: 'password', success: true}. Sensitive data masking: redact passwords, credit card numbers, API keys. Search and filtering: full-text search on action and details, filter by user_id, action, resource_type, date range. Use Elasticsearch for fast searching at scale. Log retention: partition logs by month, compress old partitions, move to cold storage (S3 Glacier) after 1 year, delete after retention period. Immutability: use append-only table, no UPDATE/DELETE permissions. Add cryptographic hash chain (each log includes hash of previous log) to detect tampering. Export: allow exporting logs as CSV/JSON for date range and filters. Real-time streaming: use Kafka to stream logs to SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) system. Anomaly detection: alert on suspicious patterns (e.g., 100 failed logins in 1 minute). Dashboard: show recent activity, failed logins, permission changes.

instruction: Implement a notification preferences system. Requirements: allow users to configure which notifications they receive, support multiple channels (email, in-app, SMS, push), allow per-category preferences (mentions, replies, marketing), respect quiet hours, provide default preferences for new users, handle preference changes in real-time.
reasoning: Notification preferences require a flexible data model that maps users to notification types to channels. Quiet hours need timezone-aware logic. Default preferences need to be applied for new users without creating records for every preference. Real-time updates mean preference changes should take effect immediately. Need to handle preference inheritance (category-level vs specific notification type). Unsubscribe links in emails need to update preferences.
answer: Data model: notification_preferences table (user_id, notification_type, channel, enabled). Notification types: mention, reply, new_follower, marketing, system_update, etc. Channels: email, in_app, sms, push. Default preferences: define in code as defaults object {mention: {email: true, in_app: true}, marketing: {email: false, in_app: true}}. On user creation: don't insert preferences (use defaults). When checking preference: query database, if no record found, use default. Preferences UI: show all notification types with toggles for each channel. When user changes preference: insert/update record. Quiet hours: users set quiet_hours_start (e.g., '22:00'), quiet_hours_end (e.g., '08:00'), timezone. When sending notification: convert quiet hours to user's timezone, check if current time is in quiet hours, skip non-urgent notifications (queue for later). Real-time updates: when preference changes, invalidate cached preferences. Notification service checks preference before sending. Unsubscribe: email includes unsubscribe link with token (JWT with user_id and notification_type). Clicking link updates preference to disabled. Granularity: allow category-level preferences (disable all marketing) and specific preferences (disable marketing email but keep in-app). Migration: when adding new notification type, use default for existing users. Analytics: track notification delivery rates, open rates, unsubscribe rates per type.

instruction: Add a file versioning system for document management. Requirements: automatically create new version on each edit, allow viewing version history, compare versions side-by-side, restore previous versions, show who made each change, handle large files efficiently, support version comments.
reasoning: File versioning requires storing multiple versions without duplicating entire files (storage efficiency). Delta compression or content-addressable storage can help. Version comparison needs diff algorithms appropriate for file type (text diff, image diff). Restore needs to handle dependencies (e.g., restoring old version of document that references current version of image). Large files need chunking or streaming. Need to track metadata (who, when, why) for each version.
answer: Data model: documents table (id, name, current_version_id), document_versions table (id, document_id, version_number, file_path, size, checksum, user_id, comment, created_at). Storage strategy: for text files, use delta compression (store diffs between versions). For binary files, use content-addressable storage (store unique chunks, reference by hash). On file update: calculate checksum, check if chunk exists, store new chunks, create version record with references. Version history: GET /api/documents/:id/versions returns list with version_number, user, timestamp, comment, size. Version comparison: text files use diff library to show added/removed lines. Images use pixel-by-pixel comparison or side-by-side view. Binary files show metadata comparison (size, checksum). Restore version: copy version's file reference to current, create new version record pointing to old content (maintains history). Large files: stream file content, don't load entirely into memory. Use resumable uploads (tus protocol) for reliability. Version comments: prompt user for comment on save (optional). Show in version history. Permissions: only users with edit permission can create versions, only owner can delete versions. Cleanup: keep all versions for 30 days, then keep daily versions for 1 year, then weekly versions indefinitely (configurable per user/plan).

instruction: Implement a dashboard analytics system with customizable widgets. Requirements: allow users to create custom dashboards, add widgets (charts, tables, metrics), configure widget data sources and filters, share dashboards with team members, schedule automated reports, handle large data aggregations efficiently.
reasoning: Dashboard customization requires a flexible widget configuration schema. Data sources need to be abstracted to support different metrics. Large data aggregations can be slow - need pre-computation or caching. Sharing requires permission management. Scheduled reports need reliable job scheduling. Widget rendering needs to handle loading, error, and empty states. Need to support different chart types and data transformations.
answer: Data model: dashboards table (id, name, user_id, shared_with (array), layout (JSON)), widgets table (id, dashboard_id, type, config (JSON), position (JSON)). Widget types: line_chart, bar_chart, pie_chart, metric_card, table, heatmap. Widget config: {dataSource: 'orders', metric: 'revenue', filters: {dateRange: 'last_30_days', status: 'completed'}, groupBy: 'day'}. Data sources: define in code as data_source_definitions {orders: {table: 'orders', metrics: {revenue: 'SUM(amount)', count: 'COUNT(*)'}, dimensions: ['status', 'created_at']}}. Dashboard builder UI: drag-and-drop widgets, resize and position, configure data source and filters. Widget rendering: fetch data from /api/analytics/query with config, render appropriate chart (use Recharts or Chart.js). Handle states: loading (skeleton), error (retry button), empty ('No data for selected filters'). Large data: pre-compute common aggregations in materialized views, refresh periodically. For custom queries: use clickhouse or similar OLAP database for fast aggregations. Caching: cache query results for 5 minutes (keyed by query hash). Sharing: shared_with array contains user IDs or 'team:all'. Check permission before loading dashboard. Scheduled reports: create schedule (daily, weekly, monthly), job generates PDF/image of dashboard, emails to recipients. Export: allow exporting dashboard as PDF or individual widget data as CSV. Templates: provide pre-built dashboard templates for common use cases (sales, marketing, operations).

instruction: Add a multi-step approval workflow for purchase requests. Requirements: define approval chains based on amount (e.g., <$1000: manager approval, >$1000: manager + director), allow parallel and sequential approvals, send notifications at each step, track approval status and history, allow delegation of approval authority, handle timeouts and escalations.
reasoning: Approval workflows require a state machine to track request progress through approval chain. Conditional routing based on amount needs rule evaluation. Parallel approvals require waiting for all approvers. Delegation needs to track original vs delegated approver. Timeouts need escalation logic. Need to handle approver unavailability and reassignments. Audit trail is critical for compliance.
answer: Data model: approval_workflows table (id, name, rules (JSON)), approval_requests table (id, workflow_id, requester_id, amount, status, current_step, created_at), approval_steps table (id, request_id, step_number, approver_id, status, approved_at, comment). Workflow rules: {conditions: [{amount_max: 1000, approvers: ['manager']}], [{amount_min: 1000, amount_max: 10000, approvers: ['manager', 'director']}], [{amount_min: 10000, approvers: ['manager', 'director', 'vp']}]}]. Request creation: POST /api/approval-requests with amount, description. System evaluates rules, creates approval_steps records, sets status to 'pending_approval', notifies first approver(s). Sequential approval: step 2 only starts after step 1 approved. Parallel approval: all approvers in step notified simultaneously, step completes when all approve. Approval action: POST /api/approval-steps/:id/approve with comment. Update step status, if all steps in current step complete, move to next step. If all steps complete, mark request as 'approved'. Rejection: any approver can reject, marks request as 'rejected', notifies requester. Delegation: approver can delegate to another user, creates delegation record, delegate receives notification and can approve on behalf of original approver (tracked in audit log). Timeouts: if no action in 3 days, send reminder. After 7 days, escalate to next level or manager. Status tracking: show current step, approvers, history of actions. Notifications: email and in-app at each step (request created, approval needed, approved, rejected). Dashboard: show pending approvals, my requests, approval history.

instruction: Implement a geolocation-based feature for finding nearby stores. Requirements: get user's location (with permission), find stores within radius, show on map, allow filtering by store features (e.g., open now, has parking), calculate distance and ETA, handle location permission denial gracefully, optimize for mobile with offline support.
reasoning: Geolocation requires user permission and fallback for denial. Distance calculations need to account for Earth's curvature (Haversine formula) or use database geo queries. Map integration requires clustering for many markers. Filtering needs to happen efficiently (database-level geo filtering). ETA calculation requires routing API integration. Offline support needs service worker and IndexedDB. Battery life considerations for continuous location tracking.
answer: Frontend: request location permission with navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition. Handle permission states: granted, denied, prompt. If denied: show manual location input (zip code or address, geocode with Google Maps API). If granted: get lat/lng, use for queries. Backend: stores table with lat, lng columns, create PostGIS geography column for geo queries. Find nearby: SELECT *, ST_Distance(location, ST_MakePoint(:lng, :lat)::geography) as distance FROM stores WHERE ST_DWithin(location, ST_MakePoint(:lng, :lat)::geography, :radius_meters) ORDER BY distance. Alternative: use MongoDB geospatial queries or Elasticsearch geo_distance. Filtering: add WHERE clauses for features (is_open, has_parking). is_open requires checking current time against store hours (stored as JSON). Map display: use Mapbox GL JS or Google Maps. Add markers for each store, cluster markers when zoomed out. Click marker shows store details popup. Store details: show distance, address, hours, features. ETA calculation: integrate Google Maps Directions API or Mapbox Directions, show driving/walking time. Mobile optimization: use high accuracy for initial location, lower accuracy for updates to save battery. Offline support: cache user's last location and nearby stores in IndexedDB, service worker serves cached data when offline, sync when back online. Performance: cache nearby store results for 5 minutes, invalidate on location change >1km. Privacy: don't store user location history, only use for current session.

instruction: Add a comprehensive error handling and recovery system. Requirements: categorize errors (user error, system error, external service error), provide user-friendly error messages, implement circuit breaker pattern for external services, add retry logic with exponential backoff, collect error metrics, provide debugging information for developers.
reasoning: Error handling requires distinguishing between different error types to provide appropriate responses. User errors need actionable messages, system errors need generic messages (don't expose internals). Circuit breaker prevents cascading failures when external services are down. Retry logic handles transient failures. Error metrics help identify systemic issues. Need to balance user experience with debugging needs. Correlation IDs help trace requests across services.
answer: Error categorization: define error classes - UserError (400, validation), NotFoundError (404), AuthError (401/403), SystemError (500), ExternalServiceError (503). Error handler middleware: catch errors, determine type, return appropriate response. User-friendly messages: map error codes to human-readable messages in i18n files. Example: ValidationError -> 'Please check your input and try again', ExternalServiceError -> 'We're experiencing technical difficulties, please try again later'. Don't expose stack traces or internal details to users. Circuit breaker: wrap external service calls with circuit breaker (opossum library). States: closed (normal), open (failing, reject immediately), half-open (test if recovered). Trip circuit after 5 failures in 1 minute, reset after 30 seconds. When circuit open: return cached response or degraded service. Retry logic: retry idempotent operations (GET, PUT) on transient failures (timeout, 503). Exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, max 30s. Don't retry non-idempotent operations (POST) without idempotency key. Error metrics: log errors with context (user_id, endpoint, error_type, stack_trace). Send to monitoring system (Sentry, DataDog).
