Alert on error rate spikes. Correlation ID: generate unique ID per request, pass to all downstream services, include in logs and error responses. Helps trace request flow. Debugging info: in development, show full error details. In production, return error_id, user can provide to support for investigation. Graceful degradation: if non-critical service fails, continue with reduced functionality (e.g., recommendations service down, show popular items instead).

instruction: Implement a real-time collaborative whiteboard feature. Requirements: allow multiple users to draw simultaneously, sync drawing operations in real-time, support different tools (pen, eraser, shapes, text), show other users' cursors, persist whiteboard state, support undo/redo, handle network latency and conflicts.
reasoning: Collaborative drawing requires broadcasting drawing operations efficiently. Vector operations (not pixel data) are more efficient to sync. Conflict resolution is needed when users draw simultaneously. Cursor positions need low-latency updates. Persistence requires serializing drawing state. Undo/redo needs to be user-specific (not affect other users' drawings). Network latency compensation needs prediction and interpolation.
answer: Data model: whiteboards table (id, project_id, created_at), whiteboard_elements table (whiteboard_id, element_data (JSON), user_id, created_at, order). Element data: {type: 'path', points: [[x,y], ...], color: '#000', width: 2} or {type: 'rectangle', x: 10, y: 20, width: 100, height: 50, color: '#000'}. Real-time sync: use WebSocket (Socket.io). On draw: client sends drawing operation (start point, current point, tool, color). Server broadcasts to other users in whiteboard room. Use requestAnimationFrame for smooth rendering. Tools: pen (freehand path), eraser (path with destination-out blend mode), rectangle, circle, line (click and drag), text (click to place, type text). Cursor sync: send cursor position every 50ms (throttled), render other users' cursors with name label and color. Persistence: save elements to database every 5 seconds or after 10 operations. On load: fetch all elements, render in order. Undo/redo: maintain operation stack per user. Undo: remove user's last operation, broadcast removal. Don't affect other users' operations. Network latency: use operational transformation for text, last-write-wins for drawing. Interpolate cursor positions for smooth movement. Conflict resolution: each operation has timestamp and user_id, apply in order. If two users draw at same location, both drawings appear (no conflict). Performance: use HTML5 Canvas for rendering, batch operations, use layers (background elements, active drawing, cursors). Large whiteboards: implement infinite canvas with viewport culling (only render visible elements). Export: allow exporting as PNG/SVG.

instruction: Add a comprehensive testing infrastructure. Requirements: support unit, integration, and end-to-end tests, achieve >80% code coverage, run tests in CI/CD pipeline, parallelize test execution, generate test reports, handle test data setup and teardown, support visual regression testing.
reasoning: Testing infrastructure requires different test types for different purposes. Unit tests are fast and isolated, integration tests verify component interactions, E2E tests verify user workflows. Code coverage helps identify untested code but 100% coverage doesn't guarantee quality. CI/CD integration ensures tests run on every change. Test parallelization speeds up execution. Test data management prevents flaky tests. Visual regression testing catches unintended UI changes.
answer: Test types: Unit tests (Jest): test individual functions/components in isolation, mock dependencies. Integration tests (Jest + React Testing Library): test component interactions, use real implementations where possible. E2E tests (Cypress/Playwright): test complete user workflows in real browser. Test organization: __tests__ folder next to source files for unit/integration, cypress/e2e for E2E. Test data: use factories (e.g., faker.js) to generate test data, avoid hardcoded data. Setup/teardown: use beforeEach/afterEach to reset state. For database tests: use transactions (rollback after each test) or test database with migrations. Code coverage: configure Jest to collect coverage, set thresholds (80% lines, 70% branches). Exclude generated code and types. CI/CD integration: run tests on every PR, block merge if tests fail or coverage drops. Use GitHub Actions or CircleCI. Parallelization: Jest runs tests in parallel by default. For E2E: use Cypress parallelization or run multiple specs concurrently. Test reports: use jest-junit for JUnit XML reports, integrate with CI dashboard. Upload coverage to Codecov or Coveralls for tracking over time. Visual regression: use Percy or Chromatic to capture screenshots, compare with baseline, flag differences for review. Run on component library and key pages. Flaky test handling: quarantine flaky tests, investigate and fix, don't ignore. Retry flaky tests once before failing. Test environment: use Docker Compose to spin up test dependencies (database, Redis). Seed with test data. Test utilities: create helper functions for common operations (login, create test user, mock API responses). Performance tests: use k6 or Artillery to load test critical endpoints, set performance budgets. Accessibility tests: use jest-axe to check for accessibility violations in component tests.

instruction: Implement a data import/export system for bulk operations. Requirements: support CSV and Excel file formats, validate data before import, show import progress, handle large files (>100k rows) without timeout, allow mapping columns to fields, provide detailed error reports, support incremental imports and full replacements.
reasoning: Bulk data operations require streaming to handle large files without memory issues. Validation needs to check both format and business rules. Column mapping allows flexible file formats. Progress tracking helps with long operations. Error reporting needs to identify specific rows and columns with issues. Incremental vs full replacement needs careful handling to avoid data loss. Need to handle concurrent imports and conflicts.
answer: Data model: data_imports table (id, user_id, file_name, status, total_rows, processed_rows, errors (JSON), created_at). File upload: accept CSV/XLSX, store temporarily in S3. Column mapping UI: show file preview (first 10 rows), let user map file columns to system fields (e.g., 'Email Address' -> email). Auto-detect common mappings. Validation: stream file, validate each row (required fields, email format, unique constraints, foreign key existence). Collect errors with row number and field. Show error summary before proceeding. Import execution: use background job (Bull queue). Stream file again, process in batches (1000 rows). For each batch: insert into database within transaction, update progress. Handle duplicates: based on unique field (e.g., email), either skip, update, or error. Full replacement: mark existing records as deleted, insert new records. Use soft delete to allow rollback. Incremental: only insert/update, don't delete. Progress tracking: update processed_rows in database, frontend polls or uses WebSocket for updates. Show progress bar and ETA. Error handling: continue on errors, collect all errors. After completion: generate error report (CSV with row numbers, field names, error messages). Provide download link. Success report: show summary (rows imported, updated, skipped, errors). Large files: use streaming parsers (csv-parser for CSV, xlsx streaming for Excel). Process in background to avoid HTTP timeout. Set max file size (100MB). Concurrent imports: use advisory locks or queue to prevent multiple imports modifying same data. Rollback: if import fails catastrophically, restore from backup or use transaction rollback. Export: similar streaming approach, query data, write to CSV/XLSX in chunks, stream to client. Support filters to export subset of data.

instruction: Add a comprehensive caching layer with cache invalidation strategies. Requirements: implement multiple cache layers (browser, CDN, application, database), choose appropriate TTL for different data types, invalidate cache on data changes, handle cache stampedes, measure cache hit rates, provide cache warming for critical data.
reasoning: Multi-layer caching improves performance but increases complexity. Different data types need different TTLs (user profile: 5 min, product catalog: 1 hour, static content: 1 day). Cache invalidation is the hardest part - need to know when data changes. Cache stampedes occur when many requests hit expired cache simultaneously. Cache warming prevents cold start performance issues. Need to balance freshness with performance.
answer: Browser cache: set Cache-Control headers (max-age for public data, no-cache for personalized data). Use ETag for conditional requests. CDN cache (CloudFlare/CloudFront): cache static assets and public API responses. Set appropriate TTLs. Purge CDN cache on content updates. Application cache (Redis): cache API responses, computed data, session data. Use cache-aside pattern: check cache, if miss query database and populate cache. Database cache: use read replicas, materialized views for complex queries. Cache key design: include all relevant parameters. Example: user:123:profile, products:category:shoes:page:2. TTL strategy: frequently updated data (5 min), rarely updated (1 hour), static (1 day). Cache invalidation: when data changes, invalidate related cache keys. Use cache tags to invalidate groups (tag all product caches with 'products', invalidate all on product update). Event-driven invalidation: publish event on data change, cache invalidation service consumes event and invalidates keys. Cache stampede prevention: use locking (only one request rebuilds cache, others wait) or stale-while-revalidate (return stale data while rebuilding in background). Use probabilistic early expiration (refresh cache before TTL with probability based on time remaining). Cache warming: on deployment or schedule, pre-populate cache for critical data (popular products, homepage content). Use background job to query and cache data. Cache metrics: track hit rate, miss rate, eviction rate. Log cache operations for debugging. Set up alerts for low hit rates. Selective caching: don't cache everything. Skip caching for personalized data, frequently changing data, or data with low reuse. Cache size management: set max memory for Redis, use LRU eviction. Monitor memory usage. Debugging: provide cache bypass parameter (?nocache=true) for testing. Log cache hits/misses in development.

instruction: Implement a multi-environment deployment pipeline. Requirements: support development, staging, and production environments, automate deployments with CI/CD, manage environment-specific configurations, implement feature flags for safe rollouts, support blue-green deployments, provide rollback mechanisms.
reasoning: Multiple environments allow testing changes before production. CI/CD automation reduces human error and speeds up deployments. Environment-specific configs prevent configuration drift. Feature flags allow deploying code without enabling features. Blue-green deployments eliminate downtime. Rollback mechanisms are critical for quick recovery from issues. Need to manage secrets securely across environments.
answer: Environments: development (auto-deploy on merge to main), staging (manual trigger or auto-deploy from release branch), production (manual approval required). Infrastructure: use infrastructure as code (Terraform) to provision identical environments. Environment-specific configs: use environment variables for secrets and config. Store in AWS Parameter Store or HashiCorp Vault. Different values per environment (DATABASE_URL, API_KEYS). CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions/GitLab CI): stages - build (compile, bundle), test (unit, integration, E2E), deploy. Build once, deploy same artifact to all environments (ensures consistency). Feature flags: use LaunchDarkly or custom system. Deploy code with new feature behind flag, enable for percentage of users or specific segments. Monitor metrics, increase rollout if stable. Blue-green deployment: maintain two identical production environments (blue and green). Deploy to inactive environment (green), run smoke tests, switch load balancer to green. Keep blue available for quick rollback. Rollback: automated rollback on deployment failure (health check fails). Manual rollback: redeploy previous version. Keep last 5 versions available for quick rollback. Database migrations: run migrations before deploying new code (backward compatible). For breaking changes: use expand-contract pattern (add new column, migrate data, update code, drop old column over multiple deployments). Secrets management: never commit secrets to code. Use AWS Secrets Manager, rotate secrets regularly. Provide read-only access to developers for debugging. Monitoring: health check endpoint returns 200 if service healthy. Load balancer checks health, removes unhealthy instances. Set up alerts for error rates, latency, resource usage. Deployment notifications: notify Slack channel on deployment start, success, failure. Include version, deployer, changelog. Canary deployments: route small percentage of traffic to new version, monitor metrics, increase if stable. Feature flags vs canary: flags control feature visibility, canary controls code version. Combine for maximum safety.

instruction: Add session management with concurrent session limits. Requirements: allow users to view active sessions (device, location, last active), limit concurrent sessions to 3 per user, automatically logout oldest session when limit exceeded, force logout all other sessions option, handle session expiration, detect and prevent session hijacking.
reasoning: Session management requires tracking multiple sessions per user. Concurrent limits need real-time tracking and enforcement. Force logout needs to invalidate tokens across devices. Session hijacking detection needs IP/device fingerprinting. Expiration needs both absolute and idle timeouts. Session data needs to be shared across server instances.
answer: Data model: sessions table (id, user_id, token_hash, device_info (JSON), ip_address, last_active, created_at, expires_at). On login: create new session, generate JWT with session_id claim. Check concurrent limit: if user has 3+ active sessions, delete oldest (UPDATE sessions SET expires_at = NOW() WHERE id = oldest_id). Device info: parse User-Agent, store browser, OS, device type. Active sessions UI: GET /api/sessions returns user's active sessions (exclude current). Show device, location (from IP geolocation), last active time. Force logout: DELETE /api/sessions/:id invalidates specific session. DELETE /api/sessions/other invalidates all except current. Implementation: add revoked flag to session, check on every request. Session expiration: absolute timeout (7 days), idle timeout (2 hours). Update last_active on each request. Background job deletes expired sessions hourly. Hijacking detection: compare IP and device fingerprint on each request. If significant change (different country), require re-authentication. Fingerprint: hash of User-Agent, Accept-Language, screen resolution. Session binding: optionally bind session to IP (more secure, less convenient). Shared session store: use Redis to store session data, share across server instances. Token refresh: issue new token before expiration, invalidate old token. Graceful logout: clear session on server, delete token on client. Handle edge case: user changes password, invalidate all sessions.

instruction: Implement a dynamic form generator based on JSON schema. Requirements: render forms from JSON schema definition, support field types (text, number, select, date, file), apply validation rules, support conditional fields (show/hide based on other field values), handle nested objects and arrays, generate TypeScript types from schema.
reasoning: Dynamic forms require a schema interpreter that maps JSON to components. Conditional visibility needs dependency tracking. Nested structures need recursive rendering. Validation needs to be derived from schema. Type generation ensures type safety. Need to handle complex schemas with unions and references. Performance matters for large forms.
answer: Schema format: JSON Schema with extensions. Example: {type: 'object', properties: {name: {type: 'string', title: 'Full Name', minLength: 2}, age: {type: 'number', minimum: 0}, role: {type: 'string', enum: ['admin', 'user']}, adminCode: {type: 'string', 'x-visible-if': {role: 'admin'}}}}. Form generator component: recursively render schema. Map JSON Schema types to components: string -> TextInput, number -> NumberInput, enum -> Select, boolean -> Checkbox. Handle 'x-visible-if': evaluate condition against form values, show/hide field. Use react-hook-form for state management. Validation: convert JSON Schema validation keywords to yup schema (type, minLength, maximum, pattern, required). Custom validation: support 'x-validate' with custom function name. Nested objects: render as fieldset with nested fields. Arrays: render as repeatable sections with add/remove buttons. File upload: support 'x-file-upload' extension, render file input with preview. Conditional required: 'x-required-if' makes field required based on condition. Default values: use 'default' from schema. Help text: use 'description' for helper text below field. Type generation: use json-schema-to-typescript to generate TypeScript interfaces from schema. Import generated types for type-safe form data. Performance: memoize schema parsing, use React.memo for field components. Large forms: virtualize rendering for 100+ fields. Schema validation: validate schema itself before rendering (catch malformed schemas). Fallback: if schema has unsupported type, show warning and skip field.

instruction: Add a comment mentioning system with @mentions. Requirements: detect @mentions in comment text, show autocomplete dropdown with user suggestions, highlight mentions in rendered comment, send notifications to mentioned users, prevent mentioning non-members, handle edge cases (mentions in code blocks, deleted users).
reasoning: Mention detection requires parsing text for @username patterns. Autocomplete needs to filter users as user types. Rendering needs to convert @mentions to links. Notifications need to identify mentioned users and send appropriate notifications. Edge cases: don't trigger mentions inside code blocks, handle deleted users gracefully. Need to prevent abuse (mentioning hundreds of users).
answer: Detection: on text input, detect when user types '@' followed by 2+ characters. Extract mention query (text after @ until space or end). Autocomplete: fetch users matching query (GET /api/projects/:id/members?search=query), show dropdown with avatar and name. Keyboard navigation: up/down arrows, enter to select, escape to close. On select: replace @query with @username in text, add space after. Rendering: parse comment text with regex /@(\w+)/g, replace matches with @username. Verify user exists before linking (fetch user data). Styling: highlight mentions with background color. Notifications: on comment save, extract all @mentions, validate users are project members, send notification to each mentioned user (skip commenter). Prevent abuse: limit mentions to 20 per comment, show warning if exceeded. Edge cases: don't detect mentions inside code blocks (``` or `). Use markdown parser to identify code blocks first. Deleted users: if mentioned user is deleted, show @username as plain text (not link). Self-mentions: don't send notification if user mentions themselves. Duplicate mentions: send only one notification per user even if mentioned multiple times. Mention permissions: only allow mentioning users the commenter can see (respect privacy settings). Group mentions: support @team or @all to mention groups (with appropriate permissions). Edit handling: if comment is edited and new mentions added, send notifications for new mentions only. Performance: debounce autocomplete fetch (300ms), cache recent search results.

instruction: Implement a responsive navigation system with nested menus. Requirements: support multi-level nested dropdowns, show on hover (desktop) and click (mobile), handle keyboard navigation, indicate active route, support mega menus with rich content, animate transitions, ensure accessibility.
reasoning: Nested navigation requires careful state management to track which menus are open. Desktop and mobile need different interaction patterns. Keyboard navigation needs arrow keys and escape. Active route detection needs to match current URL. Mega menus need flexible layouts. Animations must not interfere with interaction. Accessibility requires ARIA attributes and focus management.
answer: Data structure: navigation items array with nested children. Example: [{label: 'Products', href: '/products', children: [{label: 'Shoes', href: '/products/shoes', children: [...]}]}]. Desktop: on hover, show dropdown after 200ms delay (prevent accidental triggers). Use onMouseEnter/onMouseLeave. Keep open while mouse is over dropdown. Mobile: on click, toggle dropdown. Show hamburger menu icon. Nested levels: indent or use breadcrumbs. Active route: compare item.href with router pathname, highlight active item and all parent items. Keyboard navigation: Tab moves between top-level items, Arrow Down opens dropdown and moves to first child, Arrow Up/Down navigates within dropdown, Arrow Right opens submenu, Arrow Left closes submenu, Escape closes current dropdown, Enter activates link. Focus management: trap focus within open dropdown, return focus to trigger on close. Mega menus: for items with many children or rich content, use mega menu layout (full-width dropdown with columns). Render custom content (images, descriptions, CTAs). ARIA attributes: aria-haspopup='true' on items with children, aria-expanded on dropdown trigger, aria-current='page' on active item, role='menubar' on nav, role='menu' on dropdown, role='menuitem' on items. Animations: CSS transitions for opacity and transform (slide down). Use transform: translateY for performance. Prevent layout shift by reserving space or using position: absolute. Breadcrumbs: show current path on mobile for context. Search: add search input in navigation for quick access. Sticky header: keep navigation visible on scroll. Performance: lazy load mega menu content on first open. Code splitting: load routes on navigation item click.

instruction: Add optimistic UI updates with conflict resolution. Requirements: immediately update UI on user action, send request to server, handle conflicts when server state differs, show loading indicators, provide undo capability, handle network failures gracefully.
reasoning: Optimistic updates improve perceived performance but require handling conflicts when server state differs from optimistic state. Need to track previous state for rollback. Loading indicators prevent confusion about state. Undo improves UX for accidental actions. Network failures need retry logic. Conflicts need resolution strategy (server wins, client wins, or merge).
answer: Implementation pattern: 1) Store previous state before optimistic update. 2) Update UI immediately. 3) Send API request. 4) On success: confirm update, clear previous state. 5) On conflict (409): server returns current state, show conflict dialog or auto-merge. 6) On error: rollback to previous state, show error message. Example - todo toggle: previousState = todo.completed, set todo.completed = !todo.completed, send PATCH request. On success: done. On 409: server returns {completed: true}, show 'Todo was modified by another user, keep your change or use server version?' On error: set todo.completed = previousState, show 'Failed to update, please try again'. Loading indicators: show spinner or skeleton during request. Disable related actions to prevent duplicate requests. Undo: show 'Undo' button in toast for 5 seconds after action. Clicking undo sends reverse request. Store action in undo stack (max 10 actions). Conflict resolution strategies: server wins (accept server state), client wins (retry with force flag), merge (combine changes if possible). Choose based on data type. For text: use operational transformation. For simple fields: last write wins with timestamp. Network failures: retry with exponential backoff (3 attempts). After max retries, show 'Offline, changes saved locally' and sync when back online (use IndexedDB). Queue failed mutations, retry on reconnect. Conflict detection: include version number or timestamp in request. Server compares with current version, returns 409 if mismatch. Include both client and server versions in response for resolution. User experience: show clear feedback for each state (optimistic, confirmed, failed, conflicted). Don't silently fail.

instruction: Implement a comprehensive form validation system. Requirements: validate on blur and submit, show inline error messages, support async validation (e.g., check username availability), validate dependent fields, show field-level and form-level errors, support custom validation rules, integrate with i18n for error messages.
reasoning: Form validation requires multiple validation triggers (blur for immediate feedback, submit for final check). Async validation needs debouncing to avoid excessive requests. Dependent fields need validation order (validate field A before B if B depends on A). Error display needs to be accessible and clear. Custom rules need extensibility. i18n ensures error messages are localized.
answer: Validation library: use Yup or Zod for schema definition. Example schema: {username: string().min(3).test('unique', 'Username taken', async (value) => await checkUsername(value)), email: string().email(), password: string().min(8).matches(/[A-Z]/, 'Must contain uppercase'), confirmPassword: string().oneOf([ref('password')], 'Passwords must match')}. Validation triggers: validate field on blur (after user interacts), validate all fields on submit. Use react-hook-form with yupResolver. Async validation: debounce async validators (500ms). Show 'Checking...' message during validation. Cancel pending validation if field value changes (AbortController). Dependent fields: validate in order. If password changes, revalidate confirmPassword. Use watch() to track dependencies. Error display: show error message below field in red. Use aria-invalid='true' on field, aria-describedby pointing to error message. Don't show errors until field is touched (to avoid overwhelming user on load). Form-level errors: show summary of all errors at top of form on submit failure. Custom rules: extend Yup with addMethod. Example: strongPassword rule checking multiple criteria. i18n: store error message keys in schema, resolve to translated messages. Example: .min(3, 'errors.minLength') maps to 'Must be at least {min} characters'. Validation feedback: show checkmark icon for valid fields (optional). Disable submit button while async validation is pending. Field-level submission: allow submitting individual fields (e.g., 'Save email' button). Show field-level success/error messages. Complex validation: cross-field validation (start date before end date), conditional validation (field required only if another field has value). Performance: validate only changed fields, not entire form. Memoize validation schemas. Accessibility: announce errors to screen readers with aria-live='polite'. Focus first invalid field on submit.

instruction: Add a drag-and-drop file upload zone with preview. Requirements: show drop zone with visual feedback, validate file types and sizes, show upload progress, allow multiple files, generate thumbnails for images, allow removing files before upload, handle upload failures with retry.
reasoning: Drag-and-drop requires handling multiple drag events (enter, over, leave, drop). Visual feedback helps users understand drop target. File validation needs to happen before upload to save bandwidth. Progress tracking requires XHR (fetch doesn't support upload progress). Thumbnail generation needs client-side image processing. Multiple files need individual state tracking. Retry logic handles transient failures.
answer: Drop zone component: render div with onDragEnter, onDragOver, onDragLeave, onDrop handlers. Prevent default on dragover to allow drop. On dragenter: set isDragging state, show highlighted border (dashed blue). On dragleave: check if leaving drop zone (not entering child), clear isDragging. On drop: prevent default, get files from event.dataTransfer.files. File validation: check file.type against allowed types (image/jpeg, image/png, application/pdf). Check file.size against max (10MB). Show error for invalid files. Multiple files: accept multiple attribute on input, handle array of files. File list: show each file with name, size, thumbnail (for images), progress bar, remove button. Thumbnail generation: for images, use FileReader to read as data URL, resize with canvas if needed (max 200x200). Upload: use XMLHttpRequest for progress tracking. Create FormData with file, send POST to /api/uploads. Track progress with xhr.upload.onprogress, update progress bar. Allow cancel with xhr.abort(). Remove before upload: remove from file list, don't upload. Upload failures: on error, show 'Failed' status with retry button. Retry: re-upload same file. Success: show checkmark, return file URL. Drag-and-drop vs click: also support click to open file picker (hidden input). Paste support: listen for paste event, get files from clipboard. Folder upload: support webkitdirectory attribute for folder selection (optional). Accessibility: make drop zone focusable, allow keyboard upload (Enter to open file picker). Announce upload progress to screen readers. Performance: limit concurrent uploads (3 at a time), queue remaining files. Compress large images client-side before upload (use browser-image-compression).

instruction: Implement a virtualized list for rendering large datasets. Requirements: render only visible items, handle variable height items, support scrolling to specific items, maintain scroll position on data updates, handle keyboard navigation, ensure accessibility.
reasoning: Virtualization is critical for performance with large lists (10k+ items). Only visible items should be rendered. Variable heights require measuring items and calculating positions. Scroll-to-item needs to calculate offset. Data updates shouldn't reset scroll position. Keyboard navigation needs to work with virtualization. Accessibility requires proper ARIA attributes.
answer: Use react-window or react-virtualized library. Basic usage: <FixedSizeList height={600} itemCount={items.length} itemSize={50} width='100%'> renders only visible items plus overscan (extra items above/below for smooth scrolling). Variable height items: use VariableSizeList. Provide itemSize function that returns height for each item. Measure items after render with itemSizer. Cache measured sizes for performance. Scroll to item: call listRef.scrollToItem(index, align). Align options: 'start' (item at top), 'center', 'end', 'auto' (scroll only if not visible). Maintain scroll position: store scroll offset before data update, restore after. Use scrollOffset prop. Handle item additions/removals: adjust scroll offset if items added/removed above current position. Keyboard navigation: make list focusable, handle Arrow Up/Down to move selection, Enter to activate. Track selectedIndex in state. Scroll selected item into view. Accessibility: role='listbox' on list, role='option' on items, aria-selected on selected item. Use aria-setsize and aria-posinset to communicate total size and position to screen readers. Announce scroll position changes. Infinite scroll: detect when user scrolls near end, load more items. Use onItemsRendered callback to check visibleStopIndex. Loading state: show loading indicator at bottom while fetching. Empty state: show message when list is empty. Error state: show error with retry button if data fetch fails. Search/filter: filter items before passing to list. Update itemCount and reset scroll to top. Performance: use React.memo for item components to prevent re-renders. Avoid inline functions in item renderer. Use itemKey prop for stable keys. Handle rapid scrolling: increase overscan for smoother experience. Responsive: adjust height based on container. Use ResizeObserver to detect container size changes.

instruction: Add a comprehensive error boundary system. Requirements: catch JavaScript errors in component tree, show user-friendly fallback UI, log errors with context, allow retry, prevent entire app from crashing, handle async errors, provide different error UIs for different contexts.
reasoning: Error boundaries catch render errors but not all errors (event handlers, async code need explicit handling). Fallback UI should be helpful, not just 'Something went wrong'. Error logging needs component stack and user context. Retry allows recovery from transient errors. Different contexts need different error UIs (modal vs page vs widget). Need to handle cascading errors.
answer: Error boundary component: class component with componentDidCatch(error, errorInfo) and getDerivedStateFromError(error). Render fallback UI when error caught. Fallback UI: show friendly message 'Something went wrong', provide 'Try again' button (resets error state), 'Go home' link. Log error: send to Sentry/error tracking service with error message, stack trace, componentStack from errorInfo, user context (user ID, URL). Async errors: error boundaries don't catch errors in event handlers or async code. Wrap async operations in try/catch, call error boundary's setError manually or use error boundary hook. Context-specific error UIs: PageErrorBoundary - full page error with navigation. ModalErrorBoundary - error within modal, close modal option. WidgetErrorBoundary - small error message within widget, retry button. TableErrorBoundary - show error row in table. FormErrorBoundary - show error in form field. Error recovery: 'Try again' button resets error state, re-renders children. For data fetch errors, retry fetch. For render errors, may need to reset component state. Cascading errors: if error boundary itself errors, parent boundary catches it. Have root error boundary that shows 'Critical error, please refresh page'. Error details: in development, show error details and stack trace. In production, show generic message but log full details. Provide error ID to user for support reference. Prevent crashes: wrap entire app in root error boundary. Wrap individual routes in route-level boundaries. Wrap third-party components in boundaries. Reset error state: provide resetKeys prop - when these props change, reset error state (useful when navigating to different page). Testing: intentionally throw errors in development to test boundaries. Use error boundary in Storybook to document error states.

instruction: Implement a multi-select component with search and grouping. Requirements: allow selecting multiple options, search/filter options, group options by category, show selected items as tags, allow removing selected items, handle large option lists (10k+), support async loading, ensure keyboard accessibility.
reasoning: Multi-select requires managing selected state and search state separately. Grouping needs hierarchical rendering. Tags need to be removable and accessible. Large lists require virtualization. Async loading needs debouncing and loading states. Keyboard navigation needs to work with search and selection. Need to handle edge cases (selecting all, clearing all).
answer: Component structure: input field for search, dropdown with options, selected items as tags above input. Search: filter options as user types (debounce 300ms for async). Highlight matching text in options. Grouping: group options by category, show group headers. Collapse/expand groups. Selected items: render as tags with remove button. Click tag or press Backspace to remove. Show count if many selected ('+5 more'). Large lists: virtualize dropdown options (react-window). Only render visible options. Async loading: on search, fetch options from API. Show loading spinner. Cache results. Debounce to avoid excessive requests. Keyboard navigation: Arrow Down opens dropdown, Arrow Up/Down navigates options, Enter selects option, Escape closes dropdown, Backspace removes last selected item. Type to search. Accessibility: role='combobox', aria-expanded, aria-activedescendant on current option, aria-multiselectable='true'. Announce selection changes. Selected items: role='list', each tag role='listitem' with remove button. Select all/clear all: provide buttons for bulk operations. Disable if max selection reached. Max selection: limit number of selected items, show warning when limit reached. Custom rendering: allow custom option renderer (avatar + name, icon + label). Disabled options: show but don't allow selection. Create new option: if search doesn't match, show 'Create "search term"' option. Value format: store selected values as array of IDs or objects. Provide onChange callback with selected values. Controlled vs uncontrolled: support both modes. Performance: memoize filtered options. Use stable keys for options. Debounce search for async. Validation: validate selection (min/max items, required). Show validation errors.

instruction: Add a toast notification system with queuing. Requirements: show multiple toasts simultaneously, position toasts (top-right, bottom-center, etc.), auto-dismiss after timeout, allow manual dismiss, queue toasts when many are triggered, support different types (success, error, warning, info), ensure accessibility.
reasoning: Toast notifications need to be non-intrusive but noticeable. Multiple toasts need stacking without overlap. Auto-dismiss needs to be pausable on hover. Queuing prevents overwhelming users with many toasts. Different types need different styling and icons. Accessibility requires ARIA live regions and keyboard dismissal.
answer: Toast system: use react-hot-toast or build custom with context. Toast types: success (green, checkmark), error (red, X), warning (yellow, exclamation), info (blue, i). Each type has default duration (success: 3s, error: 5s, info: 4s). Positioning: support top-right, top-left, bottom-right, bottom-left, top-center, bottom-center. Stack toasts vertically with gap. Auto-dismiss: start timer on show, dismiss after duration. Pause timer on hover (onMouseEnter), resume on leave (onMouseLeave). Manual dismiss: show close button, click to dismiss immediately. Swipe to dismiss on mobile. Queuing: limit visible toasts (max 3). Additional toasts queue and show when space available. Show 'X more notifications' indicator. API: toast.success('Item saved'), toast.error('Failed to save'), toast.loading('Saving...'). Can update toast: const id = toast.loading('Saving'), toast.success('Saved', {id}). Persistent toasts: set duration: Infinity for toasts that require action. Include action button (e.g., 'Undo'). Accessibility: role='alert' or role='status', aria-live='polite' for non-urgent, aria-live='assertive' for errors. Announce toast content to screen readers. Allow keyboard dismissal (Escape key dismisses focused toast). Don't steal focus from user's current task. Styling: use CSS animations for enter/exit (slide in from edge, fade out). Respect prefers-reduced-motion. Customization: allow custom toast components for complex content (progress bar, rich text). Global configuration: set default position, duration, styling. Toast groups: prevent duplicate toasts (e.g., don't show 'Saved' 10 times if user saves rapidly). Use unique ID or message deduplication. Error handling: for errors, include 'Retry' action button. Log errors when toast is shown. Testing: provide test utilities to trigger toasts in tests. Mock toast in unit tests to avoid timing issues.

instruction: Implement a data table with inline editing. Requirements: display data in table format, allow clicking cells to edit inline, validate edits, save on blur or Enter, cancel on Escape, show loading state during save, handle edit failures, support different field types (text, number, select, date).
reasoning: Inline editing requires switching between display and edit modes. Validation needs to happen before save. Different field types need different input components. Save needs to be debounced or explicit. Failures need rollback. Need to handle concurrent edits. Keyboard navigation is critical for efficiency.
answer: Table structure: use HTML table or grid component. Each cell has display mode and edit mode. Click to edit: on cell click, switch to edit mode, focus input. Store editing state: {rowId, columnId, value}. Edit mode: render appropriate input based on column type. Text: TextInput. Number: NumberInput with validation. Select: Select dropdown with options. Date: DatePicker. Checkbox: toggle immediately (no edit mode). Validation: validate on change or blur. Show error message below cell if invalid. Disable save if invalid. Save triggers: blur (click outside), Enter key. Cancel: Escape key reverts to original value. Debounce saves for rapid edits (500ms) or save immediately on trigger. Save implementation: send PATCH /api/resource/:id with {field: value}. Show loading spinner in cell during save. On success: update local state, show subtle success indicator (green border flash). On failure: revert to original value, show error toast with retry option. Concurrent edits: include version number in save request. If version mismatch (409), show 'Data was modified, reload to see latest' warning. Batch edits: allow editing multiple cells, save all on 'Save changes' button. Track dirty cells. Undo: maintain edit history, allow undo last edit (Ctrl+Z). Keyboard navigation: Tab moves to next cell, Shift+Tab to previous, Enter saves and moves down, Escape cancels. Arrow keys navigate between cells when not editing. Accessibility: announce edit mode changes to screen readers. Provide edit button for keyboard users (not just click). Performance: use React.memo for cells to prevent re-renders. Only re-render edited cell. For large tables: virtualize rows. Editable columns config: define which columns are editable, validation rules, input type. Example: {field: 'name', editable: true, type: 'text', validate: (v) => v.length > 0}. Read-only rows: disable editing based on permissions or row state.

instruction: Add a comprehensive loading state system. Requirements: show different loading states for different operations (initial load, pagination, form submission), prevent layout shift with skeleton loaders, show progress for long operations, handle loading errors, allow cancellation of loading operations, ensure accessibility.
reasoning: Loading states improve perceived performance and prevent confusion. Different operations need different loading UIs. Skeleton loaders prevent layout shift by matching content dimensions. Progress indicators help with long operations. Error handling during loading needs retry logic. Cancellation prevents wasted resources. Accessibility requires announcing loading state changes.
answer: Loading state types: Initial load: full-page skeleton or spinner. Pagination: inline skeleton at bottom of list. Form submission: disable button, show spinner in button, disable form fields. Background operations: toast or banner with progress. Skeleton loaders: create skeleton components matching actual content structure. SkeletonText for text, SkeletonRect for images, SkeletonCircle for avatars. Use CSS animations (pulse or shimmer) to indicate loading. Match dimensions exactly to prevent layout shift. Progress indicators: for long operations (file upload, data export), show progress bar with percentage. Use determinate progress when possible (known total), indeterminate when not. Update progress via WebSocket or polling. Error handling: if loading fails, show error state with retry button. Don't leave skeleton indefinitely. Set timeout (30s), show error if exceeded. Cancellation: for cancellable operations (file upload, search), provide cancel button. Use AbortController to cancel fetch requests. Clean up on component unmount. Accessibility: announce loading state changes with aria-live='polite'. Use aria-busy='true' on loading containers. Don't trap focus in loading states. Provide escape (cancel button). Reduce motion: respect prefers-reduced-motion, use fade instead of pulse for skeletons. Loading state management: use loading state in component (isLoading) or global loading context. For data fetching: use React Query's isLoading, isFetching states. Distinguish between initial load (no data) and refetch (has stale data). Optimistic updates: show immediate feedback, loading indicator for confirmation. Timeout handling: set reasonable timeouts for different operations. Show 'Still working...' message if operation takes longer than expected. Partial loading: load critical content first, lazy load secondary content. Show skeleton for secondary while loading.

instruction: Implement a modal system with focus trapping. Requirements: support multiple modals (stacked), trap focus within modal, close on Escape key, close on backdrop click (optional), prevent body scroll when modal open, ensure accessibility, handle nested modals, support different sizes and positions.
reasoning: Modals require careful focus management to trap keyboard navigation. Multiple modals need stacking with proper z-index. Body scroll prevention needs to preserve scroll position. Nested modals need proper focus restoration. Accessibility requires ARIA attributes and focus management. Different sizes need flexible styling.
answer: Modal component: use portal to render outside component tree (avoid z-index issues). Props: isOpen, onClose, title, children, size (sm, md, lg, xl), closeOnBackdrop, closeOnEscape. Focus trapping: on open, focus first focusable element (or element with autoFocus prop). Use focus-trap library or implement manually. Tab cycles through focusable elements within modal. Shift+Tab cycles backward. On close, return focus to trigger element (button that opened modal). Escape key: close modal if closeOnEscape is true. Backdrop: render semi-transparent overlay behind modal. Click backdrop closes if closeOnBackdrop is true. Prevent accidental closes: require confirmation for forms with unsaved changes. Body scroll: on open, add overflow: hidden to body, store current scroll position. On close, restore scroll position. Handle mobile: prevent scroll on iOS with position: fixed on body. Stacked modals: maintain modal stack. Each new modal adds to stack. Closing top modal reveals previous. Adjust backdrop opacity for depth. ARIA attributes: role='dialog', aria-modal='true', aria-labelledby (title ID), aria-describedby (content ID). Announce modal open to screen readers. Sizes: sm (400px), md (600px), lg (800px), xl (1000px), full (100vw/100vh). Center modal vertically and horizontally. On mobile: full screen or bottom sheet. Animation: fade in backdrop, scale up modal. Use CSS transitions. Respect prefers-reduced-motion. Nested content: support scrollable content within modal. Sticky header/footer. Form support: handle form submission, show loading state, close on success or show errors. Confirmation dialogs: specialized modal with title, message, confirm/cancel buttons. Destructive actions use red confirm button. Toast integration: show toast after modal closes for success feedback. Performance: lazy render modal content (only when open). Unmount on close to reset state. Testing: provide test utilities to open/close modals in tests.

instruction: Add a comprehensive search system with filters and faceting. Requirements: support full-text search across multiple fields, provide filter options (category, price range, date), show faceted search results (count per category), highlight search terms in results, support advanced search syntax, handle search suggestions and autocomplete.
reasoning: Full-text search needs efficient indexing and ranking. Filters need to work with search (not replace it). Facets show available filter options with counts. Highlighting helps users see why results matched. Advanced syntax (quotes, boolean operators) needs parsing. Autocomplete improves discoverability. Performance is critical for search responsiveness.
answer: Search implementation: backend uses Elasticsearch or PostgreSQL full-text search. Index searchable fields (title, description, tags). Rank by relevance (TF-IDF or BM25). Frontend: search input with debouncing (300ms). On input: fetch results and facets from /api/search?q=query&filters={...}. Filters: sidebar with filter options. Category: checkboxes for each category with count. Price range: dual-handle slider or min/max inputs. Date: date range picker. Apply filters: add to URL params (?q=shoes&category=running&price_min=50&price_max=100). Fetch filtered results. Facets: show available filter values with counts based on current search and filters. Example: Categories: Running (45), Walking (23), Casual (12). Update facets when filters change. Highlighting: backend returns highlighted snippets with <mark> tags. Frontend renders with dangerouslySetInnerHTML (sanitize first). Highlight in title and description. Advanced syntax: support "exact phrase", AND, OR, NOT, field:value. Parse query client-side or send to backend parser. Show syntax help tooltip. Autocomplete: as user types, fetch suggestions (top 5 queries, top 5 products). Show in dropdown. Click suggestion searches for it. Use search history (localStorage) for personalized suggestions. Recent searches: show 'Recent searches' when search input focused. Allow clearing history. Search results: show result count, sort options (relevance, price, date), pagination or infinite scroll. Empty results: show 'No results found' with suggestions (check spelling, try different keywords, remove filters). Search analytics: track search queries, click-through rates, zero-result searches. Use to improve search relevance and content. Performance: cache common searches (5 min TTL). Use search-as-you-type for instant results (with throttling). Accessibility: announce result count changes. Provide skip to results link. Keyboard navigation for suggestions and filters.

instruction: Implement a comprehensive state persistence system. Requirements: persist state across page refreshes, support different storage backends (localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB), handle storage quota limits, encrypt sensitive data, sync state across tabs, provide migration for schema changes.
reasoning: State persistence improves UX by remembering user preferences and in-progress work. Different data needs different storage (session vs persistent). Storage quotas require size management. Sensitive data needs encryption. Multi-tab sync prevents inconsistencies. Schema migrations handle evolving data structures. Need to handle storage failures gracefully.
answer: Storage backends: localStorage (5-10MB, persistent), sessionStorage (5-10MB, session only), IndexedDB (50MB+, persistent, async). Choose based on data size and lifetime. Small prefs: localStorage. Session data: sessionStorage. Large data: IndexedDB. Persistence library: use zustand persist middleware, redux-persist, or custom implementation. Configuration: specify which state slices to persist, storage backend, serialization. Example: persist({name: 'user-preferences', storage: localStorage, partialize: (state) => ({theme: state.theme, language: state.language})}. Storage quota: check available space before writing. If quota exceeded, implement LRU eviction (delete oldest entries). Compress data with lz-string for text. Show warning when approaching quota. Sensitive data: encrypt with Web Crypto API before storing. Use user's session key or derive from password. Never store passwords, tokens in localStorage (use httpOnly cookies). Multi-tab sync: use BroadcastChannel API or storage event. When state changes in one tab, broadcast to others. Other tabs update state. Handle conflicts: last write wins or merge strategy. Debounce broadcasts to avoid excessive updates. Schema migration: version persisted data. On load, check version, apply migrations if needed. Example: if (version < 2) { data.newField = defaultValue; version = 2; }. Maintain migration functions. Fallback: if storage fails (private browsing, quota), fall back to in-memory state. Don't crash app. Selective persistence: don't persist everything. Persist: user preferences, form drafts, UI state (expanded sections). Don't persist: auth tokens, sensitive data, frequently changing data. Expiration: set TTL for persisted data. Auto-delete after expiration. Example: form drafts expire after 7 days. Debugging: provide dev tools to view/clear persisted state. Show storage usage. Testing: mock storage in tests. Test quota exceeded scenarios. Performance: batch writes, debounce rapid state changes. Use requestIdleCallback for non-critical persistence.

instruction: Add a comprehensive API client with interceptors. Requirements: centralize API configuration, add authentication headers automatically, handle token refresh, implement request/response interceptors, provide consistent error handling, support request cancellation, add request/response logging.
reasoning: API client centralizes HTTP configuration and common logic. Interceptors allow cross-cutting concerns (auth, logging, error handling). Token refresh needs to queue requests during refresh. Consistent error handling improves debugging. Request cancellation prevents memory leaks. Logging helps with debugging but needs to be disabled in production.
answer: API client setup: use axios or fetch wrapper. Base configuration: baseURL from environment, timeout (30s), default headers (Content-Type: application/json). Authentication interceptor: request interceptor adds Authorization: Bearer {token} header. Get token from auth context or cookie. Token refresh: response interceptor catches 401 errors. If refresh token exists and not already refreshing: initiate refresh, queue failed request, retry after refresh. Use promise to queue requests during refresh. If refresh fails: clear tokens, redirect to login. Request interceptor: add request ID header (X-Request-ID: uuid) for tracing. Add timestamp for cache busting if needed. Response interceptor: extract data from response.data, handle common response formats. Error interceptor: normalize errors. Map HTTP status codes to error types (400: ValidationError, 401: AuthError, 404: NotFoundError, 500: ServerError). Include error message, status code, request ID. Request cancellation: use AbortController. Return cancel function from API call. Cancel on component unmount. Example: const {data, cancel} = api.get('/users'); useEffect(() => cancel, []); Logging: in development, log requests and responses (method, URL, status, duration). Use performance.now() for timing. Disable in production or log only errors. Retry logic: retry idempotent requests (GET) on network errors or 503. Max 3 retries with exponential backoff. Don't retry POST/PUT/DELETE without idempotency key. Request deduplication: if same GET request is in flight, return existing promise instead of making new request. Cache key: method + URL + params. Cache responses: cache GET responses in memory (5 min TTL). Invalidate on mutations. Provide cache clear method. File uploads: handle FormData, show upload progress with onUploadProgress callback. Set appropriate timeout for large files. Pagination helpers: provide methods for paginated APIs. Example: api.getPaginated('/users', {page: 1, limit: 20}) returns {data, total, hasMore}. Type safety: use TypeScript generics for request/response types. Example: api.get<User[]>('/users') returns Promise<User[]>. Testing: provide mock API client for tests. Record/playback requests.

instruction: Implement a comprehensive theming system with CSS variables. Requirements: support light and dark themes, allow custom themes, use CSS custom properties for theme values, provide theme context for React components, support theme preview before applying, handle theme transitions smoothly.
reasoning: Theming requires a systematic approach to colors, spacing, and other design tokens. CSS variables provide runtime theming without CSS-in-JS overhead. Theme context allows components to access theme values. Custom themes need validation. Transitions need to be smooth but respect reduced motion. Need to handle theme in SSR.
answer: Design tokens: define tokens for colors, spacing, typography, shadows, borders. Example: colors: {primary: '#0066cc', secondary: '#6c757d', background: '#ffffff', text: '#212529'}. Spacing: {xs: '4px', sm: '8px', md: '16px', lg: '24px', xl: '32px'}. CSS variables: generate :root with all tokens as CSS variables (--color-primary, --spacing-md). Theme definitions: light theme and dark theme with different token values. Dark theme: --color-background: #121212, --color-text: #ffffff. Theme provider: React context providing current theme and setTheme function. On theme change: update data-theme attribute on <html>, CSS variables change automatically. CSS variables approach: components use var(--color-primary) instead of hardcoded colors. Works with any CSS-in-JS solution or plain CSS. Custom themes: allow users to create custom themes by overriding tokens. Validate custom theme has required tokens. Store in localStorage. Theme preview: show preview of theme before applying. Apply temporarily, revert if user cancels. Smooth transitions: add transition: background-color 0.3s, color 0.3s to body. Respect prefers-reduced-motion: use instant transition if enabled. Theme persistence: store selected theme in localStorage. On app load: read from localStorage, apply before React hydrates (inline script in <head> to prevent flash). System preference: detect prefers-color-scheme media query. Provide 'system' option that follows OS setting. Listen for changes and update theme. SSR: inject theme script server-side. Read theme from cookie (set on theme change) and apply in initial HTML. Component API: useTheme hook returns {theme, setTheme, tokens}. Components can access tokens for dynamic styling. Theme-aware components: all components use theme tokens. Audit codebase for hardcoded colors. Provide theme validation: check contrast ratios meet WCAG AA. Theme documentation: show all tokens and their values. Provide theme playground for testing. Performance: CSS variables are efficient, no runtime overhead. Avoid theme prop drilling. Accessibility: ensure all themes meet contrast requirements. Test with color blindness simulators.

instruction: Add a comprehensive form state management system. Requirements: track field values, touched state, dirty state, validation errors, support field arrays, handle nested objects, provide form-level and field-level submission, integrate with UI components, support controlled and uncontrolled modes.
reasoning: Form state management requires tracking multiple states per field (value, touched, error). Field arrays need special handling for add/remove/reorder. Nested objects need path-based access. Form-level submission differs from field-level. UI integration needs to be flexible. Controlled vs uncontrolled modes affect performance. Need to handle large forms efficiently.
answer: Form library: use react-hook-form, formik, or final-form. Core state: values (field values), touched (which fields user interacted with), dirty (which fields changed from initial), errors (validation errors), isSubmitting, submitCount. Field registration: components register with form using name path. Example: register('user.email') or register('addresses[0].city'). Values access: getValues('user.email') or watch('user.email') for reactive updates. Touched tracking: mark field as touched on blur. Use for showing errors only after interaction. Dirty tracking: compare current value to initial value. Use to enable/disable save button or show unsaved changes warning. Validation: define validation schema (yup/zod) or inline rules. Validate on blur, change, or submit. Show errors: {errors.user?.email?.message}. Field arrays: useFieldArray hook for dynamic arrays. Provides append, remove, move, insert methods. Track field identity with key field. Nested objects: use dot notation for paths. Flatten/unflatten utilities for API conversion. Form submission: handleSubmit(onSubmit) validates then calls onSubmit with values. Disable button during submission. Show loading state. Field-level submission: allow saving individual fields. Example: 'Save email' button validates and saves only email field. Controlled vs uncontrolled: uncontrolled (default) uses refs, better performance for large forms. Controlled uses state, needed for some UI libraries. UI integration: create wrapper components (TextField, Select) that integrate with form. Pass register, error, touched props. Reset: reset() resets to initial values. resetField('email') resets single field. Keep values on reset if needed. Performance: for large forms (100+ fields), use uncontrolled mode, avoid watching all fields, use React.memo for field components. Accessibility: associate labels with fields, show errors with aria-describedby, mark invalid fields with aria-invalid. Complex validation: cross-field validation (password confirmation), async validation (username availability), conditional validation (required if other field has value).

instruction: Implement a comprehensive data fetching strategy with React Query. Requirements: cache API responses, handle loading and error states, support optimistic updates, implement infinite scrolling, prefetch data, invalidate queries on mutations, handle background refetching, provide retry logic.
reasoning: Data fetching requires balancing freshness with performance. Caching reduces server load and improves UX. Optimistic updates improve perceived performance. Infinite scrolling needs cursor-based pagination. Prefetching improves perceived speed. Invalidation keeps cache fresh. Background refetching updates stale data. Retry logic handles transient failures.
answer: React Query setup: configure QueryClient with defaults: staleTime (5 min), cacheTime (30 min), retry (3), refetchOnWindowFocus (true). Basic fetching: useQuery(['users', {page: 1}], fetchUsers). Returns {data, isLoading, error, isFetching}. Loading states: show skeleton on isLoading (no cache), show spinner overlay on isFetching (refetching with cache). Error states: show error message with retry button. Use error boundary for critical errors. Caching: React Query caches by query key. Same key returns cached data. Data is stale after staleTime, refetched in background. Optimistic updates: useMutation with onMutate. Example: toggleTodo mutation. onMutate: cancel queries, snapshot previous data, update cache optimistically. onError: rollback to snapshot. onSettled: invalidate queries to refetch. Infinite scrolling: useInfiniteQuery with getNextPageParam. Fetch next page when user scrolls near bottom. Flatten pages for rendering. Prefetching: queryClient.prefetchQuery(['user', 123], fetchUser) on hover or route change. Data ready when user navigates. Invalidation: after mutation, invalidateQueries(['users']) refetches all user queries. Invalidate specific queries with filters. Background refetching: refetchInterval (poll every 30s), refetchOnWindowFocus, refetchOnReconnect. Configure per query. Retry logic: retry: 3, retryDelay: (attempt) => Math.min(1000 * 2 ** attempt, 30000). Exponential backoff. Don't retry 4xx errors. Parallel queries: useQueries for multiple independent queries. Fetch in parallel, render as each completes. Dependent queries: use enabled option. Second query enabled only after first completes. Query key best practices: include all parameters that affect data. ['users', {status: 'active', sort: 'name'}]. Use objects for complex params. Select: transform data with select option. Example: select: (data) => data.users (extract from wrapper). Placeholder data: show placeholder while loading. Example: placeholderData: {users: []}. Keep previous data: keepPreviousData: true shows old data while fetching new page. Server state vs UI state: use React Query for server state, useState/context for UI state. Don't mix. Devtools: use React Query Devtools in development to inspect cache, queries, mutations.

instruction: Implement a progressive web app (PWA) with offline support. Requirements: install as app on mobile/desktop, work offline with cached data, sync changes when back online, show install prompt, handle app updates, provide offline-first experience with background sync.
reasoning: PWAs require service workers for caching and offline support. Offline-first needs careful data synchronization strategy. Install prompts need to be non-intrusive. App updates need to handle service worker lifecycle. Background sync queues mutations for when connectivity returns. Need to handle storage limits and cache invalidation.
answer: Service worker: use Workbox library for caching strategies. Register service worker in main entry point. Caching strategies: static assets (JS, CSS, images) use Cache First (serve from cache, update in background). API responses use Network First (try network, fall back to cache). Use Stale While Revalidate for frequently accessed data. App manifest: create manifest.json with name, short_name, icons (192x192, 512x512), start_url, display: standalone, theme_color, background_color. Link in HTML head. Install prompt: listen for beforeinstallprompt event, store prompt, show custom install button. Don't show immediately, wait for user engagement. Offline data: use IndexedDB for storing app data offline. On API fetch failure (offline), read from IndexedDB. Queue mutations: when offline, store mutations in IndexedDB queue (outbox). When back online (navigator.onLine + online event), process queue by sending mutations to server. Handle conflicts with server state. Background sync: use Background Sync API for reliable delivery. Register sync event, service worker processes queue even if app is closed. App updates: service worker checks for updates on app start. When new version available, show 'Update available' banner. User clicks to activate new service worker and reload. Skip waiting phase with skipWaiting() and clients.claim(). Offline UI: show offline indicator banner when navigator.onLine is false. Disable features requiring network. Show cached data with 'Last updated X ago' timestamp. Storage management: monitor storage usage with navigator.storage.estimate(). Request persistent storage with navigator.storage.persist(). Implement cache cleanup for old entries. Testing: use Chrome DevTools Application tab to test offline, inspect cache, simulate slow networks.

instruction: Add WebSocket-based real-time updates with reconnection logic. Requirements: establish persistent WebSocket connection, handle disconnections gracefully, implement exponential backoff reconnection, queue messages during disconnection, authenticate WebSocket connections, handle server-initiated disconnections.
reasoning: WebSockets provide real-time communication but connections can drop. Reconnection logic needs exponential backoff to avoid overwhelming server. Message queuing prevents data loss during disconnection. Authentication needs to happen on connection and be refreshed. Server may disconnect clients for maintenance. Need to handle concurrent connections and message ordering.
answer: WebSocket client: create singleton service managing connection lifecycle. Connection: connect to wss://api.example.com/ws with JWT in query param or first message. Authenticate: send auth message on open {type: 'auth', token: jwt}. Server validates and subscribes to user channels. Reconnection: on close/error, attempt reconnect with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, max 30s). Add jitter to prevent thundering herd. Reset backoff on successful connection. Max retries: 10, then show 'Connection lost, refresh to reconnect' message. Message queuing: when disconnected, queue outgoing messages in array. On reconnect, send queued messages in order. Persist queue in IndexedDB for page refresh. Message handling: parse incoming JSON messages, route to handlers based on type. Example: {type: 'notification', data: {...}} triggers notification handler. Use event emitter pattern for components to subscribe. Heartbeat: send ping every 30s, expect pong. If no pong in 10s, consider disconnected and reconnect. Server-initiated disconnect: server sends {type: 'disconnect', reason: 'maintenance'} before closing. Show user-friendly message. Connection state: expose state (connecting, connected, disconnected) via observable. UI shows connection status indicator. Components subscribe to specific event types. Example: useWebSocket('order:updated', handler). Multiple tabs: use BroadcastChannel to share WebSocket across tabs. Only one active connection, others receive messages via broadcast. Graceful degradation: if WebSocket fails repeatedly, fall back to polling. Reconnection events: emit 'reconnecting', 'reconnected' events. On reconnect, sync missed data by fetching updates since last message timestamp. Security: use wss:// (TLS), validate origin on server, implement rate limiting. Performance: batch multiple updates into single message, compress large messages.

instruction: Implement server-side rendering (SSR) with hydration. Requirements: render React components on server, send HTML to client, hydrate on client-side, handle data fetching on both server and client, manage meta tags, handle authentication state differences, optimize for performance.
reasoning: SSR improves initial load performance and SEO. Hydration attaches event handlers to server-rendered HTML. Data fetching needs to work in both environments. Meta tags need server-side injection for SEO. Authentication state differs (server has no cookies initially). Performance optimization includes streaming and selective hydration.
answer: Framework choice: Next.js provides SSR out of box, or implement with React DOM Server. Server rendering: use renderToString or renderToPipeableStream (React 18). Render app with initial data, inject into HTML template. Data fetching: create data loader functions that work in both environments. Server: fetch data before render, pass as props. Client: use initial data from window.__INITIAL_DATA__, fetch on navigation. Hydration: use hydrateRoot (React 18) or hydrate (older). Attaches event handlers to existing DOM. Must match server render exactly or hydration mismatch occurs. Meta tags: use react-helmet or Next.js Head component. Server extracts meta tags and injects into <head>. Include title, description, og:image for social sharing. Authentication: server renders public view or uses cookies for authenticated view. Client upgrades to full auth state after hydration. Use cookie-based auth for SSR compatibility. Streaming SSR: React 18 renderToPipeableStream streams HTML as components resolve. Use Suspense boundaries for loading states. Client receives partial HTML immediately, rest streams in. Selective hydration: React 18 hydrates Suspense boundaries independently. Interactive parts hydrate first. Use lazy() for code splitting. Performance: cache rendered pages (ISR - Incremental Static Regeneration). Revalidate in background. Use CDN for static pages. Optimize server render time (profile slow components). Hydration errors: common causes - date formatting differences, random values, browser-only APIs. Use useEffect for client-only code. Suppress with suppressHydrationWarning for unavoidable differences (but fix root cause). SEO: ensure all content is in initial HTML (not loaded client-only). Test with Google's Mobile-Friendly Test. Sitemap and robots.txt. Error handling: catch render errors, fall back to client-side rendering. Log errors for monitoring.

instruction: Add comprehensive accessibility (a11y) audit and fixes. Requirements: achieve WCAG 2.1 AA compliance, add ARIA labels and roles, ensure keyboard navigation, provide sufficient color contrast, add focus indicators, support screen readers, test with accessibility tools.
reasoning: Accessibility ensures all users can use the application regardless of abilities. WCAG AA is the standard for most applications. ARIA attributes help screen readers understand UI. Keyboard navigation is essential for motor-impaired users. Color contrast affects low-vision users. Focus indicators help keyboard users track position. Automated testing catches common issues but manual testing is also needed.
answer: Audit: run automated tools (axe-core, Lighthouse, WAVE) to identify issues. Fix critical errors first. ARIA labels: add aria-label to icon buttons (aria-label='Close'), aria-labelledby for complex labels, aria-describedby for help text. Don't overuse ARIA - prefer semantic HTML (button, nav, main). Roles: use role='alert' for important messages, role='dialog' for modals, role='tablist' for tabs. Landmarks: use <main>, <nav>, <header>, <footer> for page structure. Add skip to main content link. Keyboard navigation: ensure all interactive elements are focusable (tabindex='0' or native). Tab order should be logical. Don't trap focus (except modals). Provide keyboard shortcuts for common actions. Focus management: visible focus indicators (outline: 2px solid blue). Don't remove outline without replacement. Manage focus on route changes (focus main content). Return focus after modal closes. Color contrast: check all text meets 4.5:1 ratio (3:1 for large text). Use contrast checker tool. Don't rely on color alone (add icons, patterns). Support high contrast mode. Screen readers: test with NVDA (Windows), VoiceOver (Mac/iOS), TalkBack (Android). Ensure content is announced correctly. Use aria-live for dynamic content. Hide decorative elements with aria-hidden='true'. Forms: associate labels with inputs (for/id). Show errors with aria-invalid and aria-describedby. Announce errors with aria-live region. Images: add alt text for informative images, alt='' for decorative. Provide longdesc for complex images. Tables: use <th> with scope attribute. Provide caption for data tables. Dynamic content: announce updates with aria-live='polite' (non-urgent) or 'assertive' (urgent). Use aria-busy during loading. Reduced motion: respect prefers-reduced-motion. Disable non-essential animations. Testing: manual testing with keyboard only, screen reader. Automated testing in CI (jest-axe, pa11y). User testing with disabled users. Documentation: create accessibility guidelines for developers. Include in code review checklist.

instruction: Implement a comprehensive logging system. Requirements: log at different levels (debug, info, warn, error), include context (user ID, request ID, timestamp), send logs to centralized service, handle sensitive data masking, support structured logging, provide log search and filtering.
reasoning: Logging is critical for debugging and monitoring. Different log levels help filter noise. Context makes logs useful for debugging. Centralized logging enables searching across services. Sensitive data must be masked for security. Structured logs (JSON) are easier to parse and search. Log volume needs management to avoid storage costs.
answer: Logging library: use winston (Node.js), pino (high performance), or console with formatting. Log levels: debug (detailed info for development), info (normal operations), warn (potential issues), error (failures). Configure minimum level per environment (debug in dev, info in prod). Structured logging: output JSON with consistent fields. Example: {level: 'info', message: 'User login', userId: 123, requestId: 'abc', timestamp: '2024-01-15T10:00:00Z', service: 'auth'}. Context: create logger with context. Example: const logger = baseLogger.child({userId, requestId}). All logs include context automatically. Request ID: generate UUID for each request, pass through all layers (middleware, services, database queries). Enables tracing request flow across services. Sensitive data masking: define patterns to mask (email, phone, credit card, SSN). Use regex to detect and replace with [MASKED]. Never log passwords, tokens, API keys. Centralized logging: send logs to ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana), Datadog, or CloudWatch. Use log shipper (Filebeat, Fluentd) or send directly via HTTP. Log aggregation enables searching across all services. Log rotation: rotate log files daily or by size (100MB). Keep 30 days of logs locally. Compress old logs. Search and filtering: Kibana/Datadog provide search UI. Query by level, service, user ID, time range. Create dashboards for error rates, slow requests. Alerting: alert on error spikes, specific error patterns. Use log-based metrics. Performance: use async logging to avoid blocking. Buffer logs and flush periodically. Don't log in hot paths (every request). Sample logs (log 1% of successful requests, 100% of errors). Frontend logging: send error logs to backend via beacon API. Include browser, OS, URL, user ID. Rate limit to avoid spam. Don't log sensitive data from frontend. Correlation: link frontend errors to backend logs via request ID. Show request ID in error UI for user to report. Compliance: retain logs per policy (90 days for general, 7 years for financial). Implement log deletion. Audit logs: separate audit log for security events (login, permission changes). Immutable, longer retention. Testing: mock logger in tests, verify log calls. Don't pollute test output.

instruction: Add database connection pooling and query optimization. Requirements: configure connection pool, optimize slow queries, add database indexes, implement query caching, handle connection failures, monitor database performance, prevent SQL injection.
reasoning: Connection pooling improves performance by reusing connections. Slow queries need identification and optimization (EXPLAIN, indexes). Indexes speed up queries but slow down writes. Query caching reduces database load. Connection failures need retry logic. Performance monitoring catches issues early. SQL injection prevention is critical for security.
answer: Connection pooling: use pg-pool (PostgreSQL), mysql2/pool (MySQL). Configure pool size (min: 5, max: 20 per server instance). Too many connections overwhelm database. Connection timeout: 10s. Idle timeout: 30s. Share pool across application. Query optimization: identify slow queries with pg_stat_statements (PostgreSQL) or slow query log (MySQL). Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see query plan. Look for sequential scans, missing indexes. Add indexes: CREATE INDEX on frequently queried columns. Composite indexes for multi-column WHERE clauses. Don't over-index (slows writes, uses storage). Use partial indexes for filtered queries. Query patterns: avoid SELECT *, specify needed columns. Use pagination (LIMIT/OFFSET or cursor-based). Avoid N+1 queries (use JOINs or batch loading). Parameterized queries: always use parameterized queries or prepared statements. Never concatenate user input into SQL. Example: db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1', [userId]). ORM: use Prisma, TypeORM, or Knex for type-safe queries. Still use raw SQL for complex queries. Query caching: cache query results in Redis for read-heavy queries. Invalidate on writes. Use cache tags for bulk invalidation. Transaction management: use transactions for multi-step operations. Keep transactions short. Use appropriate isolation level (READ COMMITTED default).
