Connection failures: retry with exponential backoff (3 attempts). Circuit breaker: stop trying if database is down. Queue writes for later. Health checks: ping database every 30s. Remove unhealthy instances from load balancer. Monitoring: track query duration, connection count, error rates. Use APM (Application Performance Monitoring) like New Relic. Set alerts for slow queries (>1s), connection pool exhaustion. Migrations: use migration tool (Knex migrations, Prisma migrate). Test migrations on staging first. Backup before production migrations. Read replicas: route read queries to replicas, writes to primary. Reduces load on primary. Handle replication lag. Partitioning: for large tables (>10M rows), partition by date or key. Improves query performance.

instruction: Implement comprehensive input validation and sanitization. Requirements: validate all user inputs, sanitize HTML to prevent XSS, validate file uploads, implement CSRF protection, prevent SQL injection, handle validation errors gracefully, validate on both client and server.
reasoning: Input validation is the first line of defense against attacks. Client-side validation improves UX but can be bypassed - server validation is mandatory. HTML sanitization prevents XSS. File uploads need type and size validation. CSRF protection prevents cross-site attacks. SQL injection prevention requires parameterized queries. Validation errors need user-friendly messages.
answer: Client-side validation: use form validation library (react-hook-form, formik) with schema validation (yup, zod). Validate on blur and submit. Show inline errors. Server-side validation: validate all inputs again on server. Use same schema if possible. Return structured errors {field: 'email', message: 'Invalid email format'}. Input sanitization: trim whitespace, normalize (lowercase emails), escape special characters. Use validator.js for common validations (isEmail, isURL, isAlphanumeric). XSS prevention: sanitize HTML with DOMPurify before rendering user content. Use dangerouslySetInnerHTML only with sanitized content. Prefer text content over HTML. Set Content-Security-Policy header to restrict script sources. File upload validation: validate file type (check MIME type and extension), size (max 10MB), and content (magic bytes). Scan for malware with ClamAV. Store files outside web root or in S3. Generate random filenames to prevent path traversal. CSRF protection: use CSRF tokens (double-submit cookie pattern). Generate token on session creation, include in forms/headers. Validate token on state-changing requests (POST, PUT, DELETE). Use SameSite cookie attribute (Strict or Lax). SQL injection: always use parameterized queries or ORM. Never concatenate user input. Example: db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', [email]). NoSQL injection: validate and sanitize MongoDB queries. Don't pass user input directly to query operators. Rate limiting: limit requests per IP/user to prevent brute force and DoS. Use express-rate-limit or similar. Authentication: validate credentials securely. Use bcrypt for password hashing (cost factor 12). Implement account lockout after failed attempts. Use multi-factor authentication for sensitive operations. Error messages: don't leak sensitive info. Generic errors for auth failures ('Invalid credentials' not 'User not found'). Log detailed errors server-side. Content Security Policy: set CSP headers to prevent XSS. Restrict script sources, disable inline scripts, report violations. Security headers: set X-Frame-Options (DENY), X-Content-Type-Options (nosniff), Strict-Transport-Security. Use helmet.js middleware. Dependency scanning: regularly scan for vulnerabilities with npm audit, Snyk. Update dependencies promptly.

instruction: Add comprehensive error monitoring and alerting. Requirements: capture and group errors, track error rates and trends, set up alerts for error spikes, provide error context for debugging, integrate with issue tracking, measure error impact on users.
reasoning: Error monitoring helps identify and prioritize fixes. Error grouping prevents alert fatigue from duplicate errors. Tracking trends shows if issues are improving or worsening. Alerts need appropriate thresholds to avoid noise. Context (user, request, stack trace) speeds debugging. Integration with issue tracking streamlines workflow. Impact measurement helps prioritize.
answer: Error tracking service: integrate Sentry, Rollbar, or Bugsnag. Capture errors: global error handler (window.onerror, window.onunhandledrejection), React error boundaries, try/catch in async code, Express error middleware. Error grouping: service groups errors by stack trace fingerprint. Same error reported 1000 times shows as one issue with count. Error context: capture user ID, URL, browser, OS, request headers, component stack (React), breadcrumbs (user actions leading to error). Custom context: add business context (order ID, cart value). Sampling: capture 100% of errors, sample successful requests for breadcrumbs. Error details: include error message, stack trace (with source maps for readable production stacks), request/response data (sanitize sensitive fields), environment info. Alerting: configure alerts for error rate spikes (e.g., >5% of requests error in 5 min), new error types, critical errors (payment failures). Send to Slack, PagerDuty, email. Set different severity levels. Alert fatigue: tune thresholds, use alert grouping, set maintenance windows. Trend tracking: dashboard showing error count over time, top errors, error rate by endpoint. Compare before/after deployments. Issue tracking integration: link Sentry issues to Jira/GitHub Issues. Auto-create issue for new critical errors. Track resolution status. Impact measurement: calculate percentage of users affected by each error. Prioritize errors affecting many users. Track error-free sessions as metric. User feedback: allow users to report errors with description. Correlate with error event. Release tracking: tag errors with release version. See which release introduced error. Mark as resolved in new release. Sourcemaps: upload sourcemaps to Sentry on deployment. Maps minified code to original source. Privacy: don't capture PII (email, name) unless necessary. Mask sensitive data. Comply with GDPR. Performance impact: error tracking adds overhead. Use sampling in high-traffic scenarios. Send errors asynchronously. Testing: test error tracking in staging. Verify errors are captured with correct context. Don't send test errors to production project.

instruction: Implement a comprehensive API rate limiting and throttling system. Requirements: limit requests per user/IP/endpoint, implement different limits for different endpoints, return proper rate limit headers, handle rate limit exceeded gracefully, allow rate limit increases for premium users, prevent abuse.
reasoning: Rate limiting protects APIs from abuse and ensures fair usage. Different endpoints need different limits based on cost and sensitivity. Rate limit headers inform clients of their quota. Exceeded limits need clear error responses. Premium users may need higher limits. Implementation needs to be distributed (shared across servers).
answer: Rate limiting strategies: Fixed window (reset every minute), Sliding window (more accurate), Token bucket (allows bursts), Leaky bucket (smooths traffic). Use token bucket for most APIs. Distributed rate limiting: use Redis to share rate limit state across servers. Key: ratelimit:{userId|IP}:{endpoint}. Implementation: use rate-limiter-flexible library or build custom with Redis. Configure per endpoint: /api/search (100 req/min), /api/signup (10 req/min), /api/upload (5 req/min). Store configs in database for dynamic updates. Rate limit headers: add to all responses: X-RateLimit-Limit (max requests), X-RateLimit-Remaining (requests left), X-RateLimit-Reset (Unix timestamp when limit resets). Rate limit exceeded: return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After header (seconds to wait). Include message explaining limit. Client-side handling: check rate limit headers, slow down requests when approaching limit. On 429, wait Retry-After seconds before retrying. Show user-friendly message. User identification: use JWT user ID for authenticated users, IP address for anonymous. Handle proxies (use X-Forwarded-For, but validate). Rate limit tiers: free users (100 req/min), premium (1000 req/min), enterprise (custom). Check user tier in rate limit middleware. Burst handling: allow short bursts above limit (e.g., 2x for 10 seconds). Token bucket naturally allows bursts. Gradual backoff: if user hits limit repeatedly, increase wait time exponentially. Abuse prevention: detect and block IPs with sustained high traffic. Use CAPTCHA for suspicious activity. Implement request fingerprinting. Whitelisting: allow trusted IPs (internal services, partners) to bypass limits. Monitoring: track rate limit hits, top users, abuse patterns. Alert on unusual activity. API keys: require API key for programmatic access. Rate limit per API key. Allow users to view/regenerate keys. Documentation: clearly document rate limits in API docs. Provide examples of handling rate limits. Testing: test rate limiting in staging. Verify limits are enforced correctly. Don't rate limit health checks.

instruction: Add comprehensive performance monitoring and optimization. Requirements: measure Core Web Vitals (LCP, FID, CLS), track custom performance metrics, identify performance bottlenecks, implement performance budgets, optimize bundle size, optimize images and assets, monitor server performance.
reasoning: Performance directly impacts user experience and SEO. Core Web Vitals are Google's metrics for user experience. Custom metrics track business-specific performance. Bottlenecks need profiling to identify. Budgets prevent regressions. Bundle size affects load time. Image optimization reduces bandwidth. Server performance affects API response times.
answer: Core Web Vitals: use web-vitals library to measure LCP (Largest Contentful Paint, <2.5s), FID (First Input Delay, <100ms), CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift, <0.1). Send to analytics (Google Analytics, custom backend). LCP optimization: optimize largest element (usually hero image). Preload critical images, use responsive images (srcset), lazy load below-fold images. FID optimization: reduce JavaScript execution time. Code split, defer non-critical JS, use web workers for heavy computation. CLS optimization: reserve space for images/videos (width/height), avoid inserting content above existing content, use transform for animations. Custom metrics: track Time to Interactive, page load time, API response time, search result time. Use Performance API (performance.mark, performance.measure). Performance budgets: set limits (bundle <200KB, LCP <2.5s, API <500ms). Fail CI if exceeded. Use bundlesize or webpack-bundle-analyzer. Bundle optimization: code split by route (React.lazy), tree shake unused code, use dynamic imports for large libraries. Analyze with webpack-bundle-analyzer. Remove moment.js (use date-fns), lodash (use lodash-es or individual imports). Image optimization: use modern formats (WebP, AVIF) with fallbacks. Compress with ImageOptim or squoosh. Use responsive images. Lazy load with loading='lazy'. CDN: serve static assets from CDN (CloudFlare, CloudFront). Set long cache headers (1 year) with content hash in filename. Caching: cache API responses (React Query), use service worker for offline caching. Implement cache invalidation strategy. Server performance: use APM (New Relic, Datadog) to track slow endpoints. Profile with Node.js profiler. Optimize database queries, add indexes, use connection pooling. Compression: enable gzip/brotli compression on server. Compress text responses (HTML, JSON, CSS, JS). Monitoring: create performance dashboard showing metrics over time. Alert on regressions. Track performance by page, device, connection type. Testing: use Lighthouse CI in CI/CD. Test on real devices and slow networks (3G throttling). User experience: show loading skeletons, use optimistic updates, provide feedback for slow operations.

instruction: Implement a comprehensive testing strategy with unit, integration, and E2E tests. Requirements: achieve >80% code coverage, test critical user flows, mock external dependencies, run tests in CI/CD, parallelize test execution, handle flaky tests, provide fast feedback.
reasoning: Testing ensures code quality and prevents regressions. Unit tests verify individual functions, integration tests verify component interactions, E2E tests verify user flows. Coverage helps identify untested code but 100% isn't always necessary. Mocking isolates tests from external dependencies. CI/CD ensures tests run on every change. Parallelization speeds up test runs. Flaky tests undermine confidence and need fixing.
answer: Test pyramid: many unit tests (fast, isolated), fewer integration tests (slower, test interactions), few E2E tests (slowest, test critical flows). Unit tests (Jest): test pure functions, utilities, reducers. Mock dependencies with jest.mock(). Test edge cases and error paths. Example: test('calculates total with tax', () => { expect(calculateTotal(items, 0.1)).toBe(110); }). Integration tests (React Testing Library): test components with real DOM. Use real implementations where possible, mock API calls with MSW (Mock Service Worker). Test user interactions, not implementation details. Example: test('submits form', async () => { render(<Form />); fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText('Name'), {target: {value: 'John'}}); fireEvent.click(screen.getByText('Submit')); await waitFor(() => expect(mockApi.submit).toHaveBeenCalled()); }). E2E tests (Cypress/Playwright): test critical user flows (signup, login, checkout). Run against real backend (test environment). Test across browsers. Example: test('user can complete purchase', () => { cy.visit('/products'); cy.contains('Add to cart').click(); cy.contains('Checkout').click(); cy.get('input[name=card]').type('4242...'); cy.contains('Pay').click(); cy.contains('Order confirmed'); }). Test organization: __tests__ folder next to source, cypress/e2e for E2E. Use describe/it for grouping. Test data: use factories (faker.js) to generate test data. Avoid hardcoded data. Seed database before E2E tests. Mocking: MSW for API mocking (intercepts network requests). jest.mock() for module mocking. Avoid over-mocking (test real behavior). Code coverage: configure Jest to collect coverage. Set thresholds (80% lines, 70% branches). Upload to Codecov. Exclude generated code. CI/CD: run tests on every PR. Block merge if tests fail or coverage drops. Use GitHub Actions. Parallelization: Jest runs tests in parallel by default. Shard E2E tests across multiple machines. Use Cypress Dashboard or Playwright sharding. Fast feedback: run unit tests first (fast), then integration, then E2E (slow). Use test impact analysis to run only affected tests. Flaky tests: identify flaky tests (pass sometimes, fail sometimes). Quarantine them, investigate root cause (timing, test data, network). Fix or delete. Retry flaky tests once before failing. Test utilities: create helpers for common operations (renderWithProviders, login, createTestData). Reduce boilerplate. Snapshot testing: use sparingly for complex output (JSON, serialized components). Update snapshots intentionally. Visual regression: use Percy or Chromatic to catch unintended UI changes. Run on component library. Performance tests: use k6 or Artillery to load test APIs. Set performance budgets (p95 <500ms). Accessibility tests: use jest-axe to check components for a11y violations.

instruction: Add comprehensive API documentation with OpenAPI/Swagger. Requirements: generate documentation from code, provide interactive API explorer, include request/response examples, document authentication, version API documentation, keep docs in sync with code.
reasoning: API documentation is essential for developer experience. Auto-generation from code keeps docs in sync. Interactive explorer allows testing without writing code. Examples make APIs easier to understand. Authentication documentation is critical. Versioning helps manage API evolution. Manual documentation gets outdated quickly.
answer: OpenAPI specification: write API spec in YAML/JSON following OpenAPI 3.0 standard. Define paths, methods, parameters, request bodies, responses, authentication. Or generate from code with decorators (NestJS, tsoa). Code-first approach: use decorators to annotate routes. Example (NestJS): @ApiTags('users') @ApiOperation({summary: 'Get user'}) @ApiResponse({status: 200, type: User}) @Get(':id') getUser(@Param('id') id: string). Generate OpenAPI spec from decorators. Swagger UI: serve interactive documentation at /api-docs. Users can explore endpoints, see parameters, try requests. Auto-generate client SDKs from OpenAPI spec. Request/response examples: provide examples in spec. Example: responses: {'200': {content: {'application/json': {example: {id: 1, name: 'John', email: 'john@example.com'}}}}}. Include multiple examples for different scenarios (success, error). Authentication docs: document auth methods (JWT, API key, OAuth). Show how to obtain tokens, include in requests. Provide example authenticated request. Error documentation: document common error responses (400, 401, 404, 500). Explain error format and codes. Versioning: maintain separate docs for each API version (/v1/docs, /v2/docs). Show changelog between versions. Deprecation notices for old versions. Keeping docs in sync: generate docs in CI/CD. Fail build if docs are outdated. Use contract testing to verify implementation matches spec. Postman collection: export OpenAPI spec to Postman collection. Share with API consumers. Provide environment templates. Changelog: maintain API changelog documenting changes (new endpoints, parameter changes, deprecations). Follow semantic versioning. SDK generation: use OpenAPI Generator to create client SDKs in multiple languages (JavaScript, Python, Java). Publish to package managers. Testing documentation: test documentation examples in CI. Verify example requests work and return expected responses. Developer portal: create developer portal with guides, tutorials, API reference. Use Docusaurus or ReadMe. Feedback: allow users to provide feedback on documentation. Track common questions to improve docs. Rate limiting docs: document rate limits, how to handle 429 responses, how to request higher limits. Webhooks docs: document webhook events, payload format, how to verify signatures. Provide example webhook handlers.

instruction: Implement comprehensive data validation and transformation layer. Requirements: validate incoming data against schemas, transform data formats (snake_case to camelCase), handle nested objects and arrays, provide detailed validation errors, support custom validators, ensure type safety.
reasoning: Data validation ensures data integrity and prevents errors. Transformation normalizes data formats between frontend and backend. Nested structures need recursive validation. Detailed errors help debugging. Custom validators handle business rules. Type safety prevents runtime errors. This layer sits between raw input and business logic.
answer: Validation library: use Zod (TypeScript-first) or Yup. Define schemas for each API endpoint. Example: const userSchema = z.object({name: z.string().min(2).max(100), email: z.string().email(), age: z.number().int().min(0).optional()}). Validation middleware: validate request body, query params, and URL params against schemas. On validation error, return 400 with detailed errors. Error format: {errors: [{path: 'email', message: 'Invalid email', code: 'invalid_string'}]}. Include all errors, not just first. Data transformation: transform snake_case (backend) to camelCase (frontend) and vice versa. Use libraries like humps or custom transformers. Apply in middleware. Example: {user_name: 'John'} -> {userName: 'John'}. Nested objects: schemas handle nesting recursively. Example: z.object({address: z.object({street: z.string(), city: z.string()})}). Arrays: validate array items. Example: z.object({tags: z.array(z.string()).min(1).max(10)}). Custom validators: add custom validation logic. Example: .refine((val) => isValidPassword(val), {message: 'Password must contain uppercase, lowercase, and number'}). Coercion: coerce string inputs to numbers/booleans. Example: z.coerce.number() converts '42' to 42. Be explicit about coercion. Optional fields: use .optional() for optional fields, .nullable() for fields that can be null, .default() for default values. Date handling: parse date strings to Date objects. Validate date format. Example: z.string().datetime() for ISO 8601. Enum validation: validate against allowed values. Example: z.enum(['active', 'inactive', 'pending']). Union types: accept multiple types. Example: z.union([z.string(), z.number()]). Type safety: TypeScript infers types from schemas. Example: type User = z.infer<typeof userSchema>. Use inferred types throughout application. Partial updates: for PATCH requests, make all fields optional. Example: userSchema.partial(). Strict validation: reject unknown fields with .strict(). Prevents typos and unexpected data. Sanitization: trim strings, normalize emails (lowercase), escape HTML. Apply before validation. File validation: validate file uploads (type, size, dimensions). Example: z.instanceof(File).refine((f) => f.size < 5000000, 'File too large'). Performance: compile schemas once, reuse. Zod schemas are compiled on first use. Testing: test validation schemas with valid and invalid inputs. Verify error messages are clear.

instruction: Add comprehensive state management with Redux Toolkit. Requirements: organize state into slices, handle async operations with thunks, implement optimistic updates, persist state, handle loading and error states, use selectors for derived state, ensure type safety.
reasoning: State management organizes application state for predictability and maintainability. Slices divide state by domain. Thunks handle async logic. Optimistic updates improve UX. Persistence improves UX across sessions. Loading/error states need consistent handling. Selectors prevent prop drilling and enable memoization. Type safety prevents bugs.
answer: Redux Toolkit setup: configure store with slices. Example: const store = configureStore({reducer: {users: usersSlice.reducer, products: productsSlice.reducer}, middleware: (getDefaultMiddleware) => getDefaultMiddleware().concat(api.middleware)}). Slices: create slice for each domain. Example: const usersSlice = createSlice({name: 'users', initialState: {items: [], loading: false, error: null}, reducers: {...}, extraReducers: (builder) => {...}}). State structure: normalize state (store by ID, not arrays). Example: {byId: {1: {id: 1, name: 'John'}, 2: {...}}, allIds: [1, 2]}. Use normalizr for normalization. Async operations: use createAsyncThunk for API calls. Example: const fetchUsers = createAsyncThunk('users/fetch', async () => { const response = await api.get('/users'); return response.data; }). Handle states: extraReducers handles pending, fulfilled, rejected. Set loading: true on pending, update data on fulfilled, set error on rejected. Optimistic updates: update state immediately in reducer, send API request, rollback on error. Example: toggleTodo updates state, sends request, reverts if request fails. Persistence: use redux-persist to persist state to localStorage. Configure which slices to persist. Handle migrations for schema changes. Selectors: create selectors for derived state. Example: const selectActiveUsers = createSelector([selectUsers], (users) => users.filter(u => u.active)). Memoize with reselect to prevent unnecessary re-renders. Type safety: use TypeScript with Redux Toolkit. Infer types from slice. Example: type UsersState = ReturnType<typeof usersSlice.reducer>. Use TypedUseSelectorHook for useSelector. Actions: define action creators in slice. Example: reducers: {addUser: (state, action: PayloadAction<User>) => {state.items.push(action.payload)}}. Dispatch actions with dispatch(addUser(user)). Middleware: add custom middleware for logging, analytics, error handling. RTK Query: use RTK Query for data fetching (alternative to thunks). Auto-generates hooks, handles caching, invalidation. Example: const {data, isLoading} = useGetUsersQuery(). DevTools: use Redux DevTools extension to inspect state, time travel debug, track actions. Performance: use React.memo for components, memoize selectors, avoid inline selectors. Split large slices into smaller ones. Testing: test reducers with different actions. Test thunks with mock API. Test selectors with different state.

instruction: Implement comprehensive error handling and recovery strategies. Requirements: categorize errors, provide user-friendly messages, implement retry logic, use circuit breakers for external services, implement graceful degradation, log errors with context, provide debugging information.
reasoning: Error handling improves application resilience and user experience. Categorization helps provide appropriate responses. User-friendly messages improve UX without exposing internals. Retry logic handles transient failures. Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures. Graceful degradation maintains partial functionality. Logging enables debugging. Context helps reproduce issues.
answer: Error categorization: define error types - ValidationError (400, user input), NotFoundError (404), AuthError (401/403), NetworkError (no connection), TimeoutError, ServerError (500), ExternalServiceError. Each type has different handling. User-friendly messages: map error codes to human-readable messages. Example: 'ERR_NETWORK' -> 'Connection problem. Please check your internet and try again.' Don't expose stack traces or internal details. Use i18n for localized messages. Retry logic: retry idempotent operations (GET, PUT) on transient failures (network error, 503, timeout). Exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, max 30s. Max retries: 3. Don't retry non-idempotent (POST) without idempotency key. Circuit breaker: use opossum library. Wrap external service calls. States: closed (normal), open (failing, reject immediately), half-open (test recovery). Trip after 5 failures in 1 minute. Reset after 30 seconds. When open: return cached response or degraded service. Graceful degradation: if non-critical service fails, continue with reduced functionality. Example: recommendations service down, show popular items. Payment service down, show 'Try again later' message. Error boundaries: catch React render errors with error boundary component. Show fallback UI, log error. Don't crash entire app. Async error handling: wrap async operations in try/catch. Use error boundary hook for unhandled promise rejections. Don't silently swallow errors. Error logging: log errors with context (user ID, URL, action, stack trace). Send to Sentry or similar. Include breadcrumbs (user actions before error). Correlation ID: generate unique ID per request, pass through all services. Include in logs and error responses. Helps trace request flow. Debugging info: in development, show full error details. In production, return error ID for support reference. Show 'Something went wrong. Error ID: abc123. Please contact support.' Recovery strategies: offer retry button, suggest alternative actions, provide workaround. Example: 'Upload failed. Try again or use a smaller file.' Offline handling: detect offline state, queue mutations, sync when back online. Use IndexedDB for offline storage. Show offline indicator. Timeout handling: set reasonable timeouts (30s for API, 5min for file upload). Show 'Still working...' for long operations. Allow cancellation. Error recovery testing: intentionally cause errors in staging. Verify error handling works correctly. Test offline scenarios.

instruction: Add comprehensive internationalization (i18n) and localization (l10n). Requirements: support multiple languages, detect user's preferred language, allow language switching, handle RTL languages, translate all UI text, format dates/numbers/currency by locale, handle pluralization and gender.
reasoning: Internationalization makes app translatable to multiple languages. Localization adapts to specific locales. Language detection improves UX. RTL support requires layout adjustments. All UI text needs extraction to translation files. Date/number formatting varies by locale. Pluralization rules differ by language. This is a cross-cutting concern affecting all text.
answer:
I18n library: use react-i18next or react-intl. Setup: initialize with translations, default language, detection options. Translation files: create JSON files per language. Example: en.json: {welcome: 'Welcome, {{name}}!', items: {one: '{{count}} item', other: '{{count}} items'}}. Organize by namespace (common, auth, dashboard). Extract strings: replace hardcoded strings with t() function. Example:

{t('welcome', {name: user.name})}

. Use translation keys, not English text as keys. Language detection: check localStorage, then navigator.language, then default. Priority: user preference > browser > default. Language switcher: dropdown in header or settings. Save preference to localStorage and user profile. RTL support: detect RTL languages (Arabic, Hebrew). Set dir='rtl' on . Use CSS logical properties (margin-inline-start instead of margin-left). Mirror icons and layouts. Date formatting: use Intl.DateTimeFormat with locale. Example: new Intl.DateTimeFormat('fr-FR').format(date) -> '15 janvier 2024'. Don't hardcode date formats. Number formatting: use Intl.NumberFormat. Example: new Intl.NumberFormat('de-DE').format(1234.56) -> '1.234,56'. Currency: use Intl.NumberFormat with currency option. Example: new Intl.NumberFormat('ja-JP', {style: 'currency', currency: 'JPY'}).format(1000). Pluralization: use ICU message syntax. Example: {count, plural, =0 {No items} one {# item} other {# items}}. Different languages have different plural rules. Gender: handle gender-specific translations. Example: {gender, select, male {He} female {She} other {They}}. Translation workflow: use translation management system (Phrase, Lokalise, Crowdin). Export keys, translators translate, import back. Track translation progress. Missing translations: fallback to default language (English). Log missing translations for review. Show key in development mode. Pseudo-localization: transform strings to identify untranslated text. Example: 'Welcome' -> '[Ẇēļçõḿē]'. Test UI with longer strings (German is 30% longer). Context for translators: provide context and screenshots. Explain placeholders. Example: 'welcome': 'Welcome message shown on homepage. {{name}} is user's first name.' Dynamic content: don't translate user-generated content. Translate only UI strings. SEO: use hreflang tags for multilingual pages. Example: . Serve language-specific URLs (/fr/, /de/) or use language subdomain. Performance: lazy load translation files. Load only current language. Preload common namespaces. Testing: test all supported languages. Check for layout issues with longer strings. Verify RTL layout. Test date/number formatting.

instruction: Implement a role-based dashboard with customizable widgets. The existing app has admin and user roles. Add a dashboard where users can add, remove, resize, and rearrange widgets. Admin users see additional analytics widgets. Widget data must be fetched independently with loading and error states. Layout must persist across sessions.
reasoning: This combines RBAC with drag-and-drop layout persistence. Each widget needs independent data fetching to avoid coupling. Layout persistence requires serializing positions and sizes. Admin-only widgets need both frontend hiding and backend API protection. The grid system must handle responsive breakpoints while preserving user customizations.
answer: Data model: dashboard_layouts table (user_id, layout (JSON)), widgets table (id, type, config (JSON), allowed_roles (array)). Layout library: use react-grid-layout for drag-and-drop grid. Each widget is a grid item with x, y, w, h properties. Layout state: store array of {i: widgetId, x, y, w, h}. On layout change: debounce save (1s) to PUT /api/dashboard/layout. Widget registry: map widget type to component. Each widget component handles its own data fetching with useQuery. Loading: show skeleton within widget bounds. Error: show retry button within widget. Admin widgets: check user.role === 'admin' before rendering. Backend: GET /api/analytics/* endpoints require admin role middleware. Don't rely on frontend hiding alone. Responsive: define breakpoints (lg: 1200px, md: 996px, sm: 768px, xs: 480px). Store layout per breakpoint. Mobile: stack widgets vertically, disable drag. Widget marketplace: modal showing available widgets with add button. User selects widget, configure options (e.g., date range for chart). Widget config: store per-widget settings in layout JSON. Settings modal on widget header gear icon. Performance: lazy load widget components with React.lazy. Only fetch data for visible widgets. Memoize widget components to prevent re-renders when other widgets update. Default layout: provide default layout for new users. Reset to default button. Export/import: allow sharing dashboard layouts as JSON.

instruction: Add a bulk operations system to the user management table. Requirements: select multiple users with checkboxes, perform bulk actions (activate, deactivate, delete, assign role), show confirmation dialog with count, handle partial failures (some succeed, some fail), maintain selection across pages, show progress for long operations.
reasoning: Bulk operations require tracking selection state across paginated data. Partial failures need clear reporting of which items succeeded and which failed. Select all on current page vs select all across all pages are different operations. Confirmation dialogs must show accurate counts. Progress tracking prevents user confusion during long operations. The implementation must not break existing single-item operations.
answer: Selection state: track selectedIds (Set<string>) and selectAllMode (boolean for 'select all across pages'). Checkbox column: individual checkboxes toggle selectedIds. Header checkbox: toggles all visible items on current page. 'Select all N users' link appears when all visible selected, sets selectAllMode. Bulk action bar: shows when selectedIds.size > 0. Displays count, action buttons (activate, deactivate, delete, assign role). Confirmation dialog: 'Are you sure you want to deactivate 15 users? This action cannot be undone.' For selectAllMode: 'Are you sure you want to deactivate all 1,234 users?' Progress: for >50 items, show progress bar. Use background job for large batches. API: POST /api/users/bulk-action with {action: 'deactivate', userIds: [...]} or {action: 'deactivate', filter: {status: 'active'}} for selectAllMode. Response: {succeeded: 14, failed: [{id: 'abc', reason: 'User is admin, cannot deactivate'}]}. Partial failure UI: show toast '14 users deactivated, 1 failed'. Expandable error details. Selection persistence: clear selection on page navigation unless selectAllMode. Store selection in component state, not URL (avoid URL bloat). Performance: for select all, don't load all IDs client-side. Send filter to backend, backend applies to query. Undo: for reversible actions (activate/deactivate), show undo toast for 10 seconds. Permissions: check bulk action permissions before showing buttons. Require confirmation for destructive actions (delete).

instruction: Implement a notification delivery system with multiple channels. The system must support email, in-app, push, and SMS notifications. Each user has preferences per notification type and channel. The system must handle delivery failures, respect quiet hours, deduplicate notifications, and track delivery status.
reasoning: Multi-channel notification delivery requires a routing layer that checks user preferences before sending. Quiet hours need timezone-aware logic. Delivery failures need different handling per channel (email bounce vs SMS failure). Deduplication prevents notification spam. Status tracking enables debugging delivery issues. The system must be extensible for new channels without modifying core logic.
answer: Architecture: notification service with channel adapters (strategy pattern). Data model: notification_types table (id, name, default_channels), user_notification_prefs table (user_id, notification_type, channel, enabled, quiet_hours_start, quiet_hours_end, timezone), notifications table (id, user_id, type, data, created_at), notification_deliveries table (notification_id, channel, status, sent_at, delivered_at, error). Routing logic: when event triggers notification, look up user prefs for that type. For each enabled channel: check quiet hours (convert to user timezone, skip if in quiet hours unless urgent). Check deduplication: don't send same notification type to same user within 5 minutes (configurable). Queue delivery job per channel. Channel adapters: EmailAdapter (SendGrid/SES), PushAdapter (Firebase/OneSignal), SMSAdapter (Twilio), InAppAdapter (WebSocket + database). Each adapter implements send(notification, user) method. Delivery tracking: update status (queued, sent, delivered, failed, bounced). Email: track opens/clicks via webhook. Push: track delivery receipts. SMS: track delivery status from Twilio webhook. Failure handling: email bounce -> mark email as invalid, notify user to update. SMS failure -> fall back to email. Push failure -> fall back to in-app. Retry transient failures (3 attempts, exponential backoff). Batch sending: for notifications to many users (e.g., announcement), use bulk email API, batch push notifications. Rate limiting: respect channel rate limits (SMS: 1/second per number). Analytics: track delivery rates, open rates, click rates per channel and notification type. Identify underperforming channels. User digest: option to receive daily/weekly digest instead of individual notifications. Aggregate notifications, send single email.

instruction: Add an undo/redo system for a document editor. Requirements: track all editing operations (insert text, delete text, format, move), support undo/redo with keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+Z/Ctrl+Y), handle collaborative editing (don't undo other users' changes), maintain operation history with memory limits, support selective undo from history panel.
reasoning: Undo/redo requires an operation stack that records inverse operations. In collaborative editing, operations from other users interleave with local operations, requiring careful filtering. Memory limits prevent unbounded growth of history. Selective undo requires understanding operation dependencies (can't undo a format if the formatted text was deleted). The implementation must integrate with the existing editor without performance impact.
answer: Operation model: each operation has type, data, inverse, userId, timestamp. Example: InsertText operation stores position and text, inverse is DeleteText at same position with same length. Operation stack: maintain two stacks - undoStack and redoStack. On new operation: push to undoStack, clear redoStack. Limit stack size to 100 operations (configurable). Use circular buffer for memory efficiency. Undo: pop from undoStack, execute inverse operation, push original to redoStack. Redo: pop from redoStack, execute operation, push to undoStack. Keyboard shortcuts: listen for Ctrl+Z (undo), Ctrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z (redo). Prevent default browser undo. Collaborative filtering: tag each operation with userId. Undo only affects current user's operations. When undoing, skip other users' operations in stack but maintain their position. Conflict resolution: if another user modified the same text, show conflict warning. Don't silently undo over someone else's changes. Selective undo: history panel shows list of operations with timestamps and descriptions. Click to undo specific operation. Check dependencies: if operation B depends on A (e.g., format depends on insert), undoing A requires undoing B first. Show warning: 'This will also undo 2 dependent changes'. Batch operations: group related operations (e.g., typing a word creates multiple InsertText ops). Group into single undo step. Debounce: group operations within 500ms window. Performance: don't store full document snapshots. Store only operation deltas. Use structural sharing for large operations. Integration: wrap editor commands to automatically record operations. Hook into existing editor events (onInsert, onDelete, onFormat). Persistence: optionally save operation history to enable undo across sessions. Store in IndexedDB with size limit. Clear history on document close (configurable).

instruction: Implement a database migration that adds a new required column to a high-traffic table without downtime. The users table has 10 million rows and receives 1000 writes per second. The new column 'status' must default to 'active' and eventually be NOT NULL. The deployment must not lock the table or cause downtime.
reasoning: Adding a NOT NULL column to a large table can lock it for extended periods, causing downtime. The solution requires a multi-phase approach: add nullable column, backfill data, add constraint, update code. Each phase must be independently deployable. The migration must handle concurrent writes during backfill. Rollback strategy is needed for each phase.
answer: Phase 1 (Migration 1): Add nullable column with default. ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'active'. This is instant in PostgreSQL 11+ (doesn't rewrite table). Deploy code that writes status on new records but doesn't require it. Phase 2 (Backfill script): Update existing rows in batches. DO $$ DECLARE batch_size INT := 10000; updated INT; BEGIN LOOP UPDATE users SET status = 'active' WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM users WHERE status IS NULL LIMIT batch_size); GET DIAGNOSTICS updated = ROW_COUNT; EXIT WHEN updated = 0; PERFORM pg_sleep(0.1); -- throttle to reduce load END LOOP; END $$; Run as background job, not during migration. Monitor database load. Phase 3 (Code update): Deploy code that reads and writes status column. All new records include status. All queries handle status column. Phase 4 (Migration 2): Add NOT NULL constraint. ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN status SET NOT NULL. In PostgreSQL, this requires a table scan but doesn't lock for writes if all rows have values. Verify no NULLs before running: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE status IS NULL. Phase 5 (Cleanup): Remove any backward compatibility code. Each phase is a separate deployment, can be rolled back independently. Concurrent writes during backfill: new writes already include status (Phase 1 default), so backfill only touches old rows. No race condition. Rollback: Phase 1 rollback: ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN status. Phase 2 rollback: no-op (re-running is safe). Phase 4 rollback: ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN status DROP NOT NULL. Monitoring: track migration progress, database CPU, query latency. Pause backfill if load exceeds threshold. Communication: coordinate with team, schedule during low-traffic period.

instruction: Add a file preview system supporting PDFs, images, videos, and Office documents. Requirements: show inline preview in the file list, open full-screen preview modal, support annotations on PDFs and images, handle large files without loading entirely in browser, provide download and share options, work on mobile devices.
reasoning: File preview requires different rendering strategies per file type. Large files need streaming or server-side conversion. PDF annotations require overlaying canvas on rendered pages. Mobile preview needs touch gestures (pinch zoom, swipe). Office documents typically need server-side conversion to PDF or images. The system must gracefully handle unsupported file types.
answer: File type detection: use MIME type and file extension. Route to appropriate viewer. Image preview: use tag with loading='lazy'. For large images (>5MB): generate thumbnail server-side (sharp/ImageMagick), show thumbnail in list, full image in modal. Support zoom (CSS transform: scale), pan (mouse drag), pinch-zoom on mobile. PDF preview: use PDF.js library. Render pages to canvas. For large PDFs: render only visible pages (virtualization). Annotations: overlay transparent canvas on PDF page. Draw annotations (highlight, text, drawing) on canvas. Save annotations separately from PDF (annotations table with page_number, type, coordinates, content). Video preview: use

instruction: Implement a real-time collaborative code editor with syntax highlighting and multiple cursors. Requirements: support multiple users editing simultaneously, show other users' cursors and selections in real-time, provide syntax highlighting for multiple languages, handle conflict resolution, support code execution, persist document state.
reasoning: Collaborative code editing requires CRDT or OT for conflict-free merging. Syntax highlighting needs language detection and efficient tokenization. Multiple cursors need low-latency position broadcasting. Code execution requires sandboxed environments for security. The editor must handle large files efficiently. Persistence needs to handle version history.
answer: Editor library: use CodeMirror 6 or Monaco editor as base. Both support collaborative editing extensions. CRDT integration: use Yjs with y-codemirror.next binding. Each character is a CRDT node that can be independently edited. Operations merge automatically regardless of order. Real-time sync: WebSocket connection shares Yjs document updates. On local edit: Yjs generates update, sent to server, broadcast to other clients. On remote update: apply to local Yjs document, editor updates automatically. Syntax highlighting: CodeMirror has built-in language modes. Support JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, Go, Rust, SQL, HTML, CSS. Auto-detect language from file extension or content. Allow manual language selection. Multiple cursors: each user has unique color and name label. Broadcast cursor position and selection range via Yjs awareness protocol. Render remote cursors as colored lines with name tooltip. Show remote selections as colored highlights. User presence: show avatar bar with connected users. Show 'X users editing' indicator. Conflict resolution: CRDT handles conflicts automatically. For structural operations (rename variable), use LSP (Language Server Protocol) for workspace-wide refactoring. Code execution: send code to backend execution service. Use Docker containers for isolation (one container per execution). Support multiple languages with appropriate runtimes. Show output in terminal panel below editor. Limit execution time (30s) and memory (256MB). Persistence: save document to database every 30 seconds or after 50 edits. Use Yjs's built-in persistence (y-indexeddb for client, y-redis for server). Version history: save snapshots every 100 edits. Allow viewing and restoring previous versions. Performance: virtualize editor lines for large files (10k+ lines). Lazy load language modes. Debounce cursor broadcasts (50ms). Offline support: continue editing offline with Yjs IndexedDB persistence. Sync changes on reconnect. Show offline indicator.

instruction: Add a comprehensive search system with Elasticsearch integration. Requirements: full-text search across multiple content types (users, posts, comments), support faceted search with filters, provide search suggestions and autocomplete, highlight matching terms, support advanced search syntax, handle search relevance tuning.
reasoning: Full-text search with Elasticsearch requires proper index mapping and analysis. Multi-type search needs either unified index or multi-index queries. Faceted search requires aggregations alongside search results. Autocomplete needs separate suggest index or completion suggester. Relevance tuning requires understanding of scoring and boosting. The system must handle index updates when content changes.
answer: Elasticsearch setup: create indices per content type (users_index, posts_index, comments_index). Mapping: define field types and analyzers. Example: posts_index: {title: {type: 'text', analyzer: 'english', boost: 3}, body: {type: 'text', analyzer: 'english'}, author: {type: 'keyword'}, tags: {type: 'keyword'}, created_at: {type: 'date'}}. Indexing: on content create/update, sync to Elasticsearch. Use change data capture (Debezium) or application-level sync. Handle deletes. Batch updates for performance. Search endpoint: GET /api/search?q=query&type=posts&tags=javascript&date_from=2024-01-01&page=1. Backend constructs Elasticsearch query: multi_match for text search, bool query for filters, aggregations for facets. Multi-type search: use multi-index query (indices: ['posts_index', 'comments_index']). Group results by type. Faceted search: add aggregations to query. Terms aggregation for tags, date_histogram for dates, range for prices. Return facet counts alongside results. UI: sidebar with filter checkboxes showing counts. Filters: apply as bool filters (don't affect scoring). Highlight: use Elasticsearch highlight feature. Returns matched text with <em> tags. Render with sanitized HTML. Autocomplete: use completion suggester or search_as_you_type field type. Debounce input (300ms). Show top 5 suggestions with type icon. Recent searches: store in localStorage, show when input focused. Advanced syntax: support "exact phrase", AND, OR, NOT, field:value. Parse query and convert to Elasticsearch query_string or simple_query_string. Relevance tuning: boost important fields (title > body). Use function_score for recency boost. Synonyms: configure synonym filter (js = javascript). Tune based on click-through analytics. Pagination: use search_after for deep pagination (not from/size beyond 10k results). Performance: cache common searches (5 min TTL). Use Elasticsearch request cache. Optimize shard count. Analytics: track search queries, clicks, zero-result searches. Use to improve relevance and identify content gaps.

instruction: Implement a responsive email template system. Requirements: create reusable email templates with dynamic content, ensure compatibility across email clients (Gmail, Outlook, Apple Mail), support both HTML and plain text versions, handle images and attachments, provide preview before sending, track opens and clicks.
reasoning: Email HTML is notoriously difficult due to inconsistent client support. Outlook uses Word rendering engine, requiring table-based layouts. Gmail strips certain CSS and HTML. Images need to be hosted with tracking pixels. Plain text fallback is required for accessibility. Templates need variable interpolation with escaping. Open/click tracking requires modifying HTML and URLs.
answer: Email framework: use MJML or Foundation for Emails. These compile to email-compatible HTML with table layouts and inline CSS. Templates: create MJML templates with variables. Example: <mj-text>Hello {{name}}, your order #{{orderId}} is confirmed.</mj-text>. Compile to HTML at build time or runtime. Variable interpolation: use Handlebars or Mustache. Escape HTML in variables to prevent XSS. Provide default values for missing variables. Template registry: store templates in database with name, subject, html_body, text_body, variables list. Admin UI to edit templates with live preview. HTML compatibility: inline all CSS (email clients strip <style> tags). Use table-based layouts. Avoid flexbox, grid, modern CSS. Test with Litmus or Email on Acid for cross-client preview. Images: host on CDN with public URLs. Use absolute URLs. Add width/height attributes. Include alt text. Don't rely on images for critical content (some clients block images). Plain text version: generate from HTML by stripping tags and formatting. Or write separately for better formatting. Send as multipart/alternative. Tracking: open tracking - add 1x1 transparent pixel image at bottom of email. Image URL includes unique tracking ID. When pixel loads, record open event. Click tracking - rewrite all links to go through tracking redirect (https://track.example.com/click?id=xyz&url=original). Record click, then redirect to original URL. Sending: use transactional email service (SendGrid, SES, Postmark). Queue emails for bulk sending. Respect rate limits. Handle bounces and unsubscribes. Preview: admin UI shows rendered email with sample data. Send test email to specified address. Show both HTML and plain text versions. Unsubscribe: include unsubscribe link in all marketing emails (legally required). One-click unsubscribe via List-Unsubscribe header. Process unsubscribe requests immediately. Analytics: track sent, delivered, opened, clicked, bounced, unsubscribed. Show per-template and per-campaign metrics. A/B testing: send variants with different subjects, measure open rates.

instruction: Add a comprehensive data export system supporting CSV, Excel, PDF, and JSON formats. Requirements: export filtered data from any table view, handle large datasets (100k+ rows) without timeouts, support custom column selection, format data appropriately per format, schedule recurring exports, email exports when ready.
reasoning: Data export of large datasets requires streaming to avoid memory issues and timeouts. Different formats need different libraries and formatting logic. Column selection requires mapping display columns to data fields. Scheduling requires background jobs and notification system. The implementation must handle concurrent exports without overwhelming the server.
answer: Export request: user selects table, filters, columns, format. POST /api/exports with {table: 'orders', filters: {status: 'completed'}, columns: ['id', 'customer', 'total', 'date'], format: 'csv'}. Returns export ID. Background job: queue export job (Bull/BullMQ). Worker streams data from database using cursor (not loading all rows). CSV export: use csv-stringify with streaming. Write header row, then stream data rows. Handle special characters (quotes, commas, newlines) with proper escaping. Excel export: use exceljs with streaming workbook. Add worksheet, write header with bold formatting. Stream data rows. Add auto-filter, freeze top row. Set column widths. PDF export: use pdfkit or puppeteer for HTML-to-PDF. Generate HTML table, render to PDF. Include header with title, date, filters. Add page numbers. JSON export: stream JSON array with proper formatting. Progress tracking: update export record with progress (rows processed / total). Frontend polls or uses WebSocket for progress updates. Show progress bar in UI. Completion: upload file to S3/storage. Update export record with download URL. Notify user via in-app notification and optionally email. Download: GET /api/exports/:id/download returns signed URL or streams file. URL expires after 24 hours. Column selection: show available columns with checkboxes. Map column IDs to data fields and formatters. Example: {id: 'total', label: 'Order Total', format: 'currency'}. Data formatting: apply format functions per column. Currency: format with symbol and decimals. Date: format per locale. Enum: map codes to labels. Scheduling: allow recurring exports (daily, weekly, monthly). Create cron job that runs export with saved filters. Email results to specified addresses. Large dataset handling: stream in batches (1000 rows). Set job timeout (30 minutes). Show estimated time based on progress. Allow cancellation. Concurrent exports: limit concurrent export jobs (5 per server). Queue additional requests. Rate limit export requests per user (10/hour) to prevent abuse. Cleanup: delete export files after 7 days. Delete export records after 30 days.

instruction: Implement a permission-based API gateway that routes requests to microservices. Requirements: authenticate requests, check permissions, rate limit per user/service, route to appropriate service, aggregate responses from multiple services, handle service failures gracefully, provide API versioning.
reasoning: API gateway centralizes cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limiting, routing). Permission checking requires resolving user roles and matching against route permissions. Response aggregation needs parallel requests with timeout handling. Service failures need circuit breakers and fallback responses. Versioning allows API evolution without breaking clients. The gateway must add minimal latency.
answer: Gateway setup: use Express/Fastify with middleware chain. Authentication: verify JWT token, extract user ID and roles. Attach to request context. Permission checking: define route permissions in configuration. Example: {path: '/api/orders/*', methods: ['GET'], roles: ['user', 'admin']}, {path: '/api/orders/*', methods: ['POST', 'PUT', 'DELETE'], roles: ['admin']}. Middleware checks user role against route permissions. Return 403 if unauthorized. Rate limiting: per-user and per-route limits. Use Redis for distributed rate counting. Different limits for different tiers (free: 100/min, pro: 1000/min). Return 429 with Retry-After header. Routing: map request paths to service URLs. Example: /api/users/* -> user-service:3001, /api/orders/* -> order-service:3002. Use http-proxy-middleware or build custom proxy. Forward headers (X-Request-ID, X-User-ID). Response aggregation: for endpoints needing data from multiple services, make parallel requests. Example: GET /api/dashboard aggregates from user-service, order-service, analytics-service. Use Promise.allSettled with timeout (5s per service). Handle partial failures: return available data with error indicators. Circuit breaker: per-service circuit breaker (opossum). Trip after 5 failures in 1 minute. Return cached response or degraded service when open. Fallback: if service is down, return cached data with stale indicator. For writes: queue request for retry when service recovers. API versioning: support version in URL (/api/v1/orders, /api/v2/orders) or header (Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json). Route to appropriate service version. Maintain old versions for backward compatibility. Deprecation: add Sunset header to deprecated versions. Document migration path. Request/response transformation: transform request/response formats between gateway and services. Example: gateway uses camelCase, service uses snake_case. Logging: log all requests with method, path, user, service, status, duration. Send to centralized logging. Tracing: propagate trace ID through services. Use OpenTelemetry. Performance: keep gateway lightweight. Use connection pooling to services. Compress responses. Cache GET responses where appropriate. Health checks: aggregate health from all services. Return 503 if critical services are down.

instruction: Add a comprehensive form wizard with conditional steps and data persistence. Requirements: multi-step form with progress indicator, show/hide steps based on previous answers, validate each step before proceeding, persist partial progress across sessions, support going back to edit previous steps, handle step dependencies correctly.
reasoning: Form wizards with conditional steps require a dependency graph to determine which steps to show. Validation must happen per-step before allowing progression. Persistence needs to handle schema changes between sessions. Going back to edit previous steps may invalidate later steps if they depend on changed values. The progress indicator must accurately reflect visible steps, not total steps.
answer: Step configuration: define steps as array with conditions. Example: [{id: 'personal', title: 'Personal Info', fields: ['name', 'email']}, {id: 'employment', title: 'Employment', fields: ['status', 'company'], condition: (data) => data.age >= 18}, {id: 'company', title: 'Company Details', fields: ['companyName', 'role'], condition: (data) => data.status === 'employed'}, {id: 'review', title: 'Review', fields: []}]. Step evaluation: on mount and when data changes, evaluate conditions to determine visible steps. Build visibleSteps array. Current step must be in visible steps. If current step becomes hidden, navigate to nearest visible step. Progress indicator: show step number relative to visible steps (Step 2 of 4, not Step 2 of 6). Show completed checkmarks for finished steps. Click completed steps to navigate back. Validation: each step has validation schema (yup/zod). On 'Next': validate current step. If valid, save data and advance. If invalid, show errors, stay on step. Don't validate hidden steps. Data persistence: save form data to localStorage on each step change. Key by form ID and user session. On mount: check for saved data, prompt 'Continue where you left off?' Clear on successful submission. Expiry: delete saved data after 7 days. Step dependencies: if user changes answer in step 2 that affects step 4's visibility or validation, clear step 4's data when navigating back through step 2. Show warning: 'Changing this will reset later steps'. Conditional fields within steps: same pattern - show/hide fields based on other field values. Clear hidden field values. Review step: show summary of all entered data organized by step. Allow clicking section to edit that step. Final submit: validate all visible steps, send complete data to API. Show loading state, handle errors. Accessibility: announce step changes to screen readers. Use aria-current='step' on current step. Keyboard navigation between steps. Mobile: show progress bar instead of step numbers. Swipe between steps.

instruction: Implement a real-time analytics dashboard with live charts and drill-down capabilities. Requirements: display real-time metrics updating every second, support multiple chart types (line, bar, pie, heatmap), allow clicking data points to drill down into details, handle large time ranges efficiently, provide date range selection, support custom metric definitions.
reasoning: Real-time analytics requires efficient data streaming and chart updates without causing re-render cascading. Drill-down needs to maintain context while showing detailed data. Large time ranges need server-side aggregation (can't render millions of points). Custom metrics need a query builder that translates user definitions to database queries. Charts must handle empty data, loading states, and errors gracefully.
answer: Data pipeline: metrics collected by application -> time-series database (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, ClickHouse) -> WebSocket stream to dashboard. Time-series storage: store metrics with timestamp, value, and tags (dimensions). Example: measurement: page_views, tags: {page: '/home', browser: 'chrome'}, value: 1. Aggregation: for large time ranges, pre-aggregate data. Minute-level for last hour, hour-level for last 7 days, day-level for last year. Query appropriate resolution based on date range. Real-time updates: WebSocket pushes new data points every second. Charts append new point, remove oldest (sliding window). Use requestAnimationFrame for smooth updates. Chart library: use Recharts, Chart.js, or Apache ECharts. Line charts for time series, bar charts for comparisons, pie charts for proportions, heatmaps for patterns. Performance: limit rendered points (max 500 per chart). Use data sampling or aggregation for larger datasets. Debounce chart interactions. Drill-down: clicking a data point opens detail view. Example: click on 'page views at 2pm' opens breakdown by page URL. Maintain breadcrumb for navigation back. Pass filters and time range to drill-down query. Date range: preset ranges (Last hour, Today, Last 7 days, Last 30 days) and custom range picker. Update all charts when range changes. Custom metrics: metric builder UI where users define: metric name, aggregation (COUNT, SUM, AVG), source (table/event), filters, group by. Save as custom metric. Backend translates to SQL/query and executes. Dashboard layout: grid of chart widgets. Users can add, remove, resize, rearrange (use react-grid-layout). Save layout per user. Loading states: show skeleton for each chart during initial load. Show spinner overlay during range changes. Error states: show error message with retry button per chart. Empty states: show 'No data for selected range' with suggestion to adjust filters. Export: export chart as PNG/SVG. Export underlying data as CSV. Alerts: configure thresholds on metrics (e.g., alert if error rate > 5%). Send notification when threshold breached.

instruction: Add a comprehensive RBAC system with dynamic permissions and resource-level access control. Requirements: define roles with permission sets, assign roles to users, check permissions at route and component level, support resource-level permissions (user can edit their own posts but not others'), allow custom roles, audit permission changes.
reasoning: RBAC with resource-level permissions requires checking both role-based permissions and ownership. Route-level checks prevent unauthorized navigation. Component-level checks hide unauthorized UI elements. Backend checks are the security boundary - frontend is UX only. Custom roles need validation to prevent privilege escalation. Audit logs track who changed what permissions and when.
answer: Permission model: permissions table (id, name, resource, action). Example: ('posts.create', 'posts', 'create'), ('posts.edit', 'posts', 'edit'), ('posts.edit.own', 'posts', 'edit_own'). Roles table (id, name, permissions (array), is_system_role). System roles can't be deleted. Role assignments: user_roles table (user_id, role_id). Built-in roles: admin (all permissions), editor (content permissions), viewer (read-only). Custom roles: admin can create roles with selected permissions. Validate: can't create role with permissions exceeding creator's permissions. Permission checking middleware: extract user roles from JWT, load permissions, attach to request context. Route middleware: checkPermission('posts.edit') checks if user has permission. For resource-level: checkResourcePermission('posts.edit', postId) checks permission AND ownership (post.author_id === user.id). Frontend permission hook: usePermission('posts.edit') returns boolean. useResourcePermission('posts.edit', post) checks ownership. Conditionally render: {canEdit && <EditButton />}. Route guard: <PermissionRoute permission='admin.panel'> wraps admin routes. Redirect to 403 page if unauthorized. API protection: all endpoints check permissions in middleware. Return 403 with clear error message. Don't rely on frontend hiding. Ownership check: define ownership per resource. Posts: author_id. Comments: user_id. Projects: check project_members table. Use ownership resolvers that can be extended. Permission caching: cache user permissions in Redis (key: user:{id}:permissions, TTL: 5 min). Invalidate on role change. Reduces database queries. Permission changes: when admin changes user's role, immediately invalidate permission cache. Send notification to user. Audit log: record all permission changes (who changed, whose role, old role, new role, timestamp). Store in audit_logs table. UI for viewing audit log (admin only). UI components: <PermissionGuard permission='users.delete'> wraps delete button. Renders nothing or fallback if unauthorized. <PermissionGate> for conditional rendering. Role management UI: list roles with permission counts. Create/edit role with permission checkboxes grouped by resource. Assign roles to users in user management. Prevent privilege escalation: user can't assign roles they don't have. Can't modify roles that have permissions they don't have. Can't delete own role.

instruction: Implement a comprehensive caching strategy with cache invalidation for a full-stack application. Requirements: implement browser caching with proper headers, CDN caching for static assets, API response caching with React Query, database query caching with Redis, handle cache invalidation on data changes, prevent cache stampedes, provide cache warming.
reasoning: Multi-layer caching improves performance but creates invalidation challenges. Each layer has different TTL and invalidation strategies. Cache invalidation must propagate through all layers when data changes. Cache stampedes occur when many requests simultaneously miss an expired cache entry. Cache warming pre-populates cache for predictable performance. The strategy must balance freshness with performance.
answer: Browser cache: set Cache-Control headers on responses. Static assets: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable (1 year, with content hash in filename). API responses: Cache-Control: private, max-age=60 (1 minute for personalized data), or no-cache for real-time data. Use ETag for conditional requests. CDN cache: CloudFlare/CloudFront for static assets and public API responses. Set appropriate TTLs per content type. Purge CDN on content update via API. Cache public pages (homepage, blog posts), don't cache personalized pages. API response cache (React Query): configure staleTime (how long data is fresh), cacheTime (how long to keep unused data). Example: useQuery('posts', fetchPosts, {staleTime: 5 * 60 * 1000, cacheTime: 30 * 60 * 1000}). Stale-while-revalidate: show cached data immediately, fetch fresh data in background. Server-side cache (Redis): cache expensive computations and database queries. Cache key includes all parameters: 'posts:list:page:1:sort:date:filter:published'. TTL: 5 minutes for frequently changing data, 1 hour for rarely changing. Cache invalidation: on data mutation, invalidate related cache keys. Use cache tags: tag all post-related caches with 'posts'. On post update, invalidate all 'posts' tagged keys. Event-driven: publish cache invalidation events, cache service consumes and invalidates. Cache stampede prevention: use mutex/lock so only one request rebuilds cache, others wait. Or use stale-while-revalidate: return stale data while rebuilding. Probabilistic early expiration: refresh cache before TTL with increasing probability as TTL approaches. Cache warming: on deployment, pre-populate cache for popular pages and queries. Scheduled job refreshes cache for top 100 queries. Warm cache after invalidation. Selective caching: don't cache everything. Skip: personalized data, frequently changing data, data with low reuse. Cache: public data, expensive computations, frequently accessed data. Monitoring: track cache hit rate, miss rate, eviction rate. Alert on low hit rates. Log cache operations for debugging. Debugging: provide cache bypass parameter (?nocache=true) for testing. Show cache status in response headers (X-Cache: HIT/MISS).

instruction: Add a comprehensive notification system with batching and digest options. Requirements: collect notifications from multiple sources, batch related notifications, offer daily/weekly digest emails, respect user preferences for frequency, prevent notification fatigue, provide notification center with read/unread state, support marking all as read.
reasoning: Notification batching groups related notifications to reduce noise. Digest emails summarize notifications over a period. User preferences for frequency prevent fatigue. The notification center needs efficient read/unread tracking. Batch logic must handle timing (wait for more notifications or send immediately). The system must scale to millions of notifications without performance issues.
answer: Notification sources: define notification triggers across application. User mentioned in comment, order shipped, new follower, payment received, etc. Each trigger creates notification event with type, recipient, data. Batching logic: group notifications by type and time window. Example: 5 likes on user's post within 10 minutes -> single notification '5 people liked your post'. Use Redis to collect notifications in time window, then flush as batch. Digest: collect notifications for daily/weekly digest. Store in notification_queue table with digest_group. Cron job at scheduled time (9 AM user's timezone) compiles digest email. Include notification count summary, top items, link to notification center. User preferences: notification_settings table per user. Configure per notification type: immediate, batched (hourly), digest (daily), off. Configure per channel: email, push, in-app. Respect quiet hours. Notification fatigue detection: if user hasn't interacted with last 10 notifications, reduce frequency. Suggest adjusting preferences. Notification center: GET /api/notifications?unreadOnly=true&cursor=... Returns paginated list. Each notification: id, type, data, read (boolean), created_at. Mark as read: PATCH /api/notifications/:id/read on click. Mark all read: PATCH /api/notifications/read-all. Unread count: GET /api/notifications/unread-count. Update in real-time via WebSocket. Notification rendering: map notification type to render function. Example: 'mention' -> '{actor} mentioned you in {post_title}'. Include action link. Icons per type. Real-time: WebSocket event 'notification:new' adds to list, increments unread count. Show toast for immediate notifications. Performance: partition notifications table by user_id for fast queries. Archive old notifications (older than 90 days) to separate table. Use cursor-based pagination. Cleanup: delete read notifications older than 30 days. Keep unread indefinitely. Archive to cold storage for compliance. Analytics: track notification delivery, open rates, click rates per type. Identify underperforming notifications. A/B test notification copy and timing.

instruction: Implement a secure file sharing system with expiring links and access controls. Requirements: generate shareable links for files, set expiration dates, password-protect links, track link usage (view/download counts), revoke links, support folder sharing with inherited permissions, prevent unauthorized access and hotlinking.
reasoning: Secure file sharing requires signed URLs that can't be forged. Expiration needs both link-level and file-level controls. Password protection adds authentication layer. Usage tracking helps monitor sharing effectiveness. Folder sharing needs permission inheritance with override capability. Hotlinking prevention requires referrer checking or signed URLs. The system must prevent path traversal and unauthorized file access.
answer: Share link generation: create share record with file_id, token (random 32-char string), expires_at, password_hash (optional), max_views, created_by. Share URL: https://app.example.com/s/{token}. Token is unguessable. Link access: GET /api/shares/{token} validates: not expired, not revoked, view count not exceeded. If password-protected: show password form, verify hash. On valid access: return file metadata or redirect to signed download URL. Signed download URL: generate S3 presigned URL or similar with 5-minute expiry. Prevents direct linking. Don't expose actual storage URL. Password protection: bcrypt hash stored in share record. Prompt for password on first access. Store password verification in session cookie (don't re-prompt). Expiration: set expires_at on creation. Options: 1 hour, 1 day, 7 days, 30 days, custom date, never. Background job cleans up expired shares hourly. Usage limits: track views and downloads in share record. Increment on each access. Disable link when max reached. Show 'Link has expired' message. Link management: list all active shares for a file. Revoke: set revoked_at timestamp. Edit: change expiration, add password, adjust limits. Tracking: record each access with timestamp, IP, user agent. Show access log to file owner. Folder sharing: share folder generates link for folder. Recipients see file list, can download individual files or zip of folder. Inherited permissions: files in shared folder inherit share settings. Allow per-file override. Prevent unauthorized access: validate file ownership on share creation. Can only share files you own or have share permission for. Path traversal: never use user input in file paths directly. Use file IDs mapped to storage paths. Hotlinking prevention: use signed URLs with short expiry. Check Referer header (optional, can be spoofed). Serve through CDN with token authentication. Security: rate limit share link access (10/min per IP). Log suspicious activity. Scan uploaded files for malware. Content-Security-Policy headers. Audit: log all share creation, access, revocation. Include who shared, what file, when accessed.

instruction: Add a comprehensive data validation middleware pipeline for a REST API. Requirements: validate request body against JSON schema, validate query parameters, validate URL parameters, sanitize inputs, transform data formats, provide detailed error responses, support custom validation rules, handle file upload validation.
reasoning: API validation middleware needs to handle multiple input sources (body, query, params) with different validation rules. JSON schema validation provides structure checking. Sanitization prevents injection attacks. Data transformation normalizes formats. Error responses must be detailed enough for API consumers to fix issues. Custom rules handle business logic. File uploads need separate validation.
answer: Validation middleware chain: validateParams -> validateQuery -> validateBody -> sanitize -> transform. Each middleware validates one input source and calls next() on success. Request params validation: extract params from URL. Validate against schema. Example: /users/:id -> {id: z.string().uuid()}. Return 400 with {errors: [{field: 'id', message: 'Must be valid UUID', value: 'abc'}]}. Query params validation: parse and validate query string. Handle arrays (?tags=a&tags=b), numbers (?page=2), booleans (?active=true). Coerce types appropriately. Example: {page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1), limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100), sort: z.enum(['name', 'date', 'price']).optional()}. Body validation: validate JSON body against schema. Use Zod for TypeScript integration. Support nested objects, arrays, unions, discriminated unions. Custom validators: .refine() for business rules. Example: .refine(data => data.endDate > data.startDate, {message: 'End date must be after start date', path: ['endDate']}). Async validation: check uniqueness, validate references. Example: email uniqueness check with debounce. Sanitization: trim strings, normalize emails (lowercase), escape HTML in text fields. Use DOMPurify for HTML content. Remove unexpected fields (.strict()). Data transformation: convert snake_case to camelCase (or vice versa). Parse date strings to Date objects. Transform enum values. Apply after validation. Error response format: {status: 400, error: 'Validation Error', details: [{field: 'email', message: 'Invalid email format', code: 'invalid_string', received: 'notanemail'}]}. Include all errors, not just first. File upload validation: validate file type (check MIME and extension), size (max limit), dimensions (for images), content (magic bytes). Reject before processing. Use multer with file filter. Validation composition: create reusable validators. Example: const paginationSchema = z.object({page: z.coerce.number().min(1), limit: z.coerce.number().min(1).max(100)}). Compose: const getUsersQuery = z.object({...paginationSchema.shape, search: z.string().optional()}). OpenAPI integration: generate OpenAPI spec from Zod schemas using zod-to-openapi. Keep documentation in sync with validation. Performance: compile schemas once, reuse. Zod schemas compile on first use. Don't validate in hot paths unnecessarily.

instruction: Implement a multi-step onboarding flow for new users.
