Requirements: guide users through initial setup (profile, preferences, team invitation), track onboarding progress, allow skipping steps, resume onboarding if interrupted, show progress indicator, adapt steps based on user type (individual vs team), trigger onboarding only for new users.
reasoning: Onboarding needs to handle different user types with different required steps. Progress tracking must persist across sessions. Skipping steps needs to handle dependencies (can't skip step B if step C depends on it). Resuming requires detecting where user left off. The flow must not interfere with existing users. Adaptation based on user type requires branching logic. Analytics on completion rates help improve the flow.
answer: Onboarding state: onboarding_status table (user_id, current_step, completed_steps (JSON), started_at, completed_at, skipped_steps (JSON)). Initialize on user creation. Step configuration: define steps with conditions and requirements. Example: [{id: 'profile', title: 'Complete your profile', required: true}, {id: 'preferences', title: 'Set preferences', required: false}, {id: 'team', title: 'Invite team members', condition: (user) => user.plan !== 'individual', required: false}, {id: 'integrations', title: 'Connect tools', required: false}, {id: 'tutorial', title: 'Quick tutorial', required: true}]. Flow component: OnboardingWizard renders current step. Each step is a separate component receiving onNext, onSkip, onBack handlers. Progress tracking: update current_step on navigation. Add to completed_steps on step completion. Add to skipped_steps on skip. Progress indicator: show completed/current/remaining steps. Visual progress bar. Step adaptation: evaluate conditions to determine visible steps. Individual users skip team step. Enterprise users see SSO setup step. Resume: on login, check if onboarding_status exists and completed_at is null. If yes: show 'Continue setup' banner. Navigate to current_step. Skip logic: allow skipping optional steps. Required steps cannot be skipped. Show 'You can complete this later in Settings' message. Track skipped steps for reminders. Completion: when all required steps done (or all steps), set completed_at. Show completion celebration. Don't show onboarding again. Reminders: if onboarding incomplete after 3 days, send email reminder. Show in-app banner. Reduce frequency over time. Analytics: track step completion rates, time per step, drop-off points. Identify problematic steps. A/B test step order and content. Exit option: 'Skip setup for now' button always visible. Link to complete later in settings. Mobile: optimize steps for mobile. Shorter forms, larger touch targets. Swipe between steps. Integration: after onboarding, redirect to main app. Deep link to specific feature based on onboarding choices.

instruction: Add a comprehensive audit trail system for a healthcare application. Requirements: log all data access and modifications, track who viewed/edited patient records, ensure audit logs are tamper-proof, support compliance reporting (HIPAA), provide audit log search and filtering, handle high-volume logging without performance impact.
reasoning: Healthcare audit trails have strict compliance requirements (HIPAA). Every data access must be logged, not just modifications. Logs must be tamper-proof (append-only, cryptographic integrity). High volume (every page view generates logs) requires efficient storage and querying. Compliance reporting needs specific formats and retention periods. The system must not impact application performance.
answer: Audit event model: audit_events table (id, event_type, user_id, patient_id, resource_type, resource_id, action, details (JSON), ip_address, user_agent, timestamp). Partitioned by month for efficient querying and archival. Event types: record_viewed, record_created, record_updated, record_deleted, record_exported, login, logout, permission_changed, search_performed. Logging middleware: intercept all API requests. Log: who (user_id), what (resource and action), when (timestamp), where (IP address), how (user agent). Include relevant details (which fields changed, search query). Patient record access: log every view of patient data, even read-only. Include patient_id for patient-specific audit reports. This is a HIPAA requirement. Tamper-proof: append-only table (no UPDATE/DELETE grants). Cryptographic hash chain: each event includes hash of previous event. Tampering breaks the chain. Write to write-once storage (S3 Object Lock) for long-term retention. High volume handling: async logging via message queue (Kafka/RabbitMQ). Application publishes events, separate consumer writes to database. Don't block request processing. Batch inserts (1000 events per batch). Separate audit database to not impact application database performance. Search and filtering: Elasticsearch index for fast searching. Filter by user, patient, date range, event type, resource. Full-text search on details. Compliance reporting: generate HIPAA audit reports. Patient access report: who accessed patient X's records and when. User activity report: what did user Y access in date range. Break-the-glass report: emergency access events. Retention: retain audit logs for 6 years (HIPAA requirement). Move to cold storage (S3 Glacier) after 1 year. Automated retention policy. Access control: only compliance officers and admins can view audit logs. Separate role for audit access. Can't view own audit logs (prevents cover-ups). Alerting: alert on suspicious patterns (accessing records outside department, bulk exports, after-hours access). Real-time alerts for critical events. Performance: audit logging must not add more than 5ms to request latency. Use async processing. Monitor audit pipeline lag.

instruction: Implement a comprehensive A/B testing framework. Requirements: define experiments with variants, randomly assign users to variants consistently, track conversion metrics, calculate statistical significance, support feature flags for experiments, allow targeting specific user segments, provide results dashboard.
reasoning: A/B testing requires consistent user assignment (same user always sees same variant). Statistical significance calculation determines if results are meaningful. Feature flags control variant exposure. Targeting allows testing on specific segments. The framework must not impact page load performance. Results need proper statistical analysis to avoid false conclusions.
answer: Experiment definition: experiments table (id, name, description, status, start_date, end_date, variants (JSON), target_segments (JSON), metrics (JSON)). Variants: [{id: 'control', weight: 50}, {id: 'variant_a', weight: 25}, {id: 'variant_b', weight: 25}]. Weights determine traffic split. User assignment: hash(userId + experimentId) % 100 determines bucket. Consistent: same user always gets same variant. Store assignment in user_experiments table and client-side (cookie/localStorage). Feature flag integration: experiment variants map to feature flags. useExperiment('checkout_button_color') returns 'control', 'variant_a', or 'variant_b'. Conditionally render based on variant. Targeting: limit experiment to user segments (premium users, US users, mobile users). Check segment before assignment. Non-matching users get control. Metrics tracking: define primary metric (conversion rate) and secondary metrics (revenue, time on page). Track events: button click, purchase, page view. Include experiment and variant in event data. Event: {type: 'purchase', userId: 123, experiment: 'checkout_button', variant: 'variant_a', value: 49.99}. Statistical analysis: calculate conversion rate per variant. Use chi-squared test for conversion rates, t-test for continuous metrics. Calculate p-value, confidence interval. Require 95% confidence before declaring winner. Account for multiple comparisons (Bonferroni correction). Minimum sample size: calculate required sample size before starting experiment. Show progress toward target. Results dashboard: show variant performance, confidence level, lift percentage, sample size. Visualize with charts. Show statistical significance indicator. Auto-stop: pause experiment if variant is significantly worse (guardrail metric drops >10%). Alert experiment owner. Experiment lifecycle: draft -> running -> analyzing -> completed/abandoned. Can't modify running experiment. Archive completed experiments with results. Client-side performance: load experiment assignments in initial payload (don't make extra API call). Cache assignments. Fallback to control if experiment service is unavailable. Server-side experiments: for testing backend changes (algorithm, pricing), assign in backend, pass variant to frontend. Multi-armed bandit: alternative to fixed split. Dynamically adjust weights based on performance. More traffic to winning variants. Use for optimization rather than hypothesis testing.

instruction: Add a comprehensive error recovery system with automatic retries, fallback strategies, and user communication. Requirements: automatically retry failed operations, implement fallback strategies when retries fail, communicate status to users, allow manual retry, queue operations for later retry when service recovers, prevent duplicate operations on retry.
reasoning: Error recovery needs different strategies for different failure types. Transient failures (network, timeout) benefit from retries. Persistent failures need fallback strategies. Users need clear communication about what's happening. Idempotency prevents duplicate operations on retry. Queue-based recovery handles extended outages. The system must distinguish between retryable and non-retryable errors.
answer: Error classification: retryable errors (network timeout, 503 Service Unavailable, 429 Too Many Requests, database deadlock) and non-retryable errors (400 Bad Request, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found). Only retry retryable errors. Retry strategy: exponential backoff with jitter. Attempt 1: immediate. Attempt 2: 1s + random(0-500ms). Attempt 3: 2s + random(0-1s). Attempt 4: 4s + random(0-2s). Max 4 attempts. Respect Retry-After header from 429/503 responses. Idempotency: include Idempotency-Key header on POST/PUT requests. Server stores key and result. Duplicate requests with same key return cached result. Generate key per operation (UUID). Prevents duplicate creates on retry. Fallback strategies: when retries exhausted, try alternative. API timeout -> serve cached data with 'stale data' indicator. Payment service down -> queue payment for later, confirm order as pending. Image upload fails -> compress and retry, then try different format. Operation queue: when service is unavailable, queue operations in IndexedDB (client) or database (server). Include operation type, payload, timestamp, retry count. When service recovers (detected by health check), process queue. Process in order, handle conflicts. User communication: show clear status for each state. Retrying: 'Retrying... (attempt 2 of 4)'. Queued: 'Your request will be processed when connection is restored'. Failed: 'Operation failed. [Retry] [Cancel]'. Use toast notifications for background operations. Manual retry: provide retry button on failed operations. Reset retry count. Show original error and option to modify input. Circuit breaker: if service has many consecutive failures, open circuit. Stop trying for cooldown period (30s). Return fallback immediately. Check periodically if service recovered (half-open state). Offline support: detect offline state (navigator.onLine). Queue all mutations. Sync when back online. Show offline banner. Optimistic updates with recovery: show optimistic UI immediately. On failure: rollback, show error, offer retry. On retry success: re-apply optimistic update. Monitoring: track retry rates, fallback usage, recovery success rates. Alert on high retry rates (indicates systemic issue). Log all retries with context for debugging.

instruction: Implement a virtualized data grid with editable cells, column resizing, and multi-row selection. The existing app uses a simple HTML table that becomes unresponsive with more than 500 rows. Requirements: render only visible rows, support inline cell editing with validation, allow column width adjustment via drag handles, enable Shift+Click multi-row selection, and export selected rows to CSV.
reasoning: Virtualization is essential for large datasets but complicates inline editing since DOM nodes are recycled. Column resizing needs to persist across scroll events. Multi-row selection requires tracking selected IDs separately from rendered rows. The CSV export must work with the full dataset, not just visible rows. Each feature interacts with the others in non-obvious ways.
answer: Use react-window VariableSizeList for row virtualization. Measure row heights after render and cache with itemSize callback. For cell editing: render input only for the active cell (track editingCell: {rowId, colId}). On cell click, set editingCell and focus input. On blur or Enter, validate and save. Column resize: add drag handle div on column header right edge. On mousedown, track mousemove to calculate new width. Store widths in state, persist to localStorage. Multi-row selection: track selectedIds as Set. On row click: if Shift held, select range from lastSelected to current. If Ctrl held, toggle single row. Otherwise, select only clicked row. Render checkbox column with indeterminate state for partial selection. CSV export: iterate all data (not just visible), filter to selectedIds, format with proper escaping. Use Blob and download link for client-side download.

instruction: Add an accessible date range picker component that supports keyboard navigation, predefined ranges (Last 7 days, This month), custom range selection, and disabled dates. The existing app has no date picker and uses native HTML date inputs which lack range selection and have inconsistent cross-browser behavior.
reasoning: Date range pickers are deceptively complex: they need two calendars, range highlighting, keyboard navigation across months, and proper ARIA attributes. Disabled dates (weekends, holidays) require date comparison logic. Predefined ranges need timezone-aware calculation. The component must work without a mouse for accessibility. Cross-browser consistency requires custom implementation over native inputs.
answer: Build with two Calendar components side by side (current month and next month). State: {startDate, endDate, hoverDate, focusedInput: 'start'|'end'}. Range highlighting: for each day, check if it falls between startDate and endDate (or hoverDate when selecting). Apply background color. Disabled dates: accept disabledDates array and isDateDisabled function. Skip disabled dates in keyboard navigation. Keyboard: Tab between start/end inputs. Arrow keys navigate days. Page Up/Down change months. Enter selects date. Escape closes. ARIA: role='dialog' on picker, role='grid' on calendar, aria-selected on selected dates, aria-disabled on disabled dates. Announce date changes with aria-live. Predefined ranges: buttons that set startDate/endDate using date-fns (subDays, startOfMonth, endOfMonth). Use user's timezone. Responsive: stack calendars vertically on mobile. Close picker on outside click (use click-outside hook).

instruction: Implement a command palette (Ctrl+K) for the application that searches across pages, actions, and recent items. Requirements: show fuzzy search results ranked by relevance, display keyboard shortcuts next to actions, support navigation with arrow keys, show recent commands first when input is empty, and execute selected command on Enter.
reasoning: Command palettes require fast fuzzy search across heterogeneous data types (pages, actions, recent items). Ranking must balance text relevance with recency and usage frequency. The palette must open instantly and feel responsive. Keyboard navigation needs focus management without stealing focus from the underlying app. Recent commands need persistent storage and decay over time.
answer: Use cmdk library or build custom with downshift. Data sources: static commands array [{id: 'new-project', label: 'Create new project', shortcut: '⌘N', action: () => navigate('/projects/new')}], dynamic pages from router config, recent commands from localStorage. Fuzzy search: use fuse.js with keys ['label', 'keywords', 'description']. Score by match quality and boost recent items. Input: debounce-free (search must be instant). Filter on every keystroke. Empty state: show 5 most recent commands and 5 suggested actions. Results: group by category (Actions, Pages, Recent). Show icon, label, description, shortcut badge. Keyboard: Arrow Up/Down navigate results, Enter executes, Escape closes. Ctrl+K toggles palette from anywhere (global event listener). Focus trap within palette. Recent tracking: on command execution, prepend to recent array in localStorage (max 20, deduplicate). Analytics: track command usage to improve suggestions. Performance: virtualize results for 100+ items. Lazy load command definitions. Mobile: full-screen overlay instead of modal.

instruction: Add a rich text editor with collaborative editing, slash commands, and media embedding. The existing app uses a plain textarea for content. Requirements: support formatting (bold, italic, headings, lists, code blocks), slash command menu (/heading, /image), embed images via upload or URL, show other users' cursors in real-time, and serialize to both HTML and Markdown.
reasoning: Rich text editors require a document model that supports formatting. Slash commands need trigger detection and a floating menu. Media embedding requires upload handling and responsive rendering. Collaborative editing needs CRDT or OT for conflict resolution. Dual serialization (HTML and Markdown) requires a format-agnostic internal representation. Each feature adds complexity to the document model.
answer: Use TipTap (ProseMirror-based) or Slate.js for the editor framework. Document model: tree of nodes (paragraph, heading, list, code_block) with marks (bold, italic, code). Slash commands: detect '/' at start of line or after space. Show floating menu with command list filtered by text after '/'. On select, replace slash command with corresponding block. Media: slash /image opens upload dialog. Upload to /api/uploads, insert image node with URL. Support paste from clipboard (read clipboardData.files). Also support URL input for external images. Collaborative: integrate Yjs with y-prosemirror binding. Each user's cursor and selection shown as colored decorations. Changes synced via WebSocket. Serialization: ProseMirror/TipTap has built-in HTML serializer. For Markdown: use prosemirror-markdown or custom serializer that walks the document tree. Store both formats in database (HTML for rendering, Markdown for editing). Toolbar: floating toolbar on text selection with formatting buttons. Keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I, Ctrl+Shift+H for heading). Performance: lazy load editor component. Debounce saves (2 seconds after last edit).

instruction: Implement a responsive navigation sidebar that collapses on mobile, supports nested menu items with expand/collapse, shows active route highlighting, and persists expanded state across page navigations. The existing app has a flat navigation bar that doesn't scale with growing feature set.
reasoning: Nested navigation requires recursive rendering and state management for expand/collapse. Active route detection needs to match current URL against menu items and highlight parent items. Persisting expanded state prevents jarring UX where menus collapse on navigation. Mobile collapse needs smooth animation and touch-friendly targets. The sidebar must integrate with the router without tight coupling.
answer: Data structure: nav items array with nested children. [{label: 'Dashboard', icon: HomeIcon, href: '/'}, {label: 'Projects', icon: FolderIcon, children: [{label: 'All Projects', href: '/projects'}, {label: 'Archived', href: '/projects/archived'}]}]. Recursive SidebarItem component renders itself for each child. Expand/collapse: track expandedItems Set in state. Toggle on click for items with children. Persist to localStorage (keyed by user). Restore on mount. Active route: use router's useLocation or useMatch. Highlight item if href matches current path. Highlight parent items if any child is active. Mobile: hamburger button toggles sidebar. Use CSS transform: translateX(-100%) for slide animation. Overlay backdrop when open. Close on navigation or backdrop click. Touch: swipe right from left edge to open (on mobile). Keyboard: Tab navigates items, Enter activates, Arrow keys navigate within expanded sections. Collapse: button at bottom toggles between full and icon-only modes. In icon-only mode, show tooltip on hover. Icons: use consistent icon library (lucide-react, heroicons). Accessibility: nav role='navigation', aria-label='Main navigation', aria-current='page' on active item, aria-expanded on expandable items.

instruction: Add a toast notification system that queues notifications, supports different severity levels, allows undo actions, and respects user focus. The current app uses alert() for all notifications which blocks the UI and provides poor UX.
reasoning: Toast systems need careful state management to handle queuing when multiple notifications fire simultaneously. Undo actions require maintaining references to the action that can be reversed. Respecting user focus means not stealing focus from the current task. Different severity levels need different auto-dismiss timers and visual treatment. The system must be callable from anywhere in the app without prop drilling.
answer: Create ToastProvider context with addToast function accessible globally via useToast hook. Toast types: success (green, 3s auto-dismiss), error (red, manual dismiss), warning (yellow, 5s), info (blue, 4s). State: toasts array with {id, type, message, action, duration}. Position: fixed bottom-right, stack vertically with gap. Animation: slide in from right, fade out on dismiss. Queue: limit visible toasts to 3. Additional toasts wait in queue, show when space available. Show '+N more' indicator. Undo action: toast includes {action: {label: 'Undo', onClick: undoFn}}. Example: after deleting item, show 'Item deleted' toast with Undo button that calls restore function. Auto-dismiss pauses on hover (onMouseEnter clears timeout, onMouseLeave restarts). Focus: don't steal focus from user's current task. Toasts are non-modal. Dismiss: X button or swipe right on mobile. Keyboard: Escape dismisses most recent toast. Accessibility: role='status' for info/success, role='alert' for errors. aria-live='polite' for non-urgent, 'assertive' for errors. Announce toast content to screen readers. API: toast.success('Saved'), toast.error('Failed', {action: {label: 'Retry', onClick: retry}}), toast.loading('Processing...'). Update: const id = toast.loading('Saving'); toast.success('Saved', {id}). Deduplication: don't show duplicate toasts within 1 second. Group similar notifications.

instruction: Implement an infinite scroll feed with pull-to-refresh, skeleton loading, error recovery, and scroll position restoration. The existing app loads all items at once causing slow initial load and high memory usage.
reasoning: Infinite scroll requires IntersectionObserver for efficient scroll detection, not scroll events. Pull-to-refresh needs touch gesture handling on mobile. Skeleton loading must match actual content dimensions to prevent layout shift. Error recovery needs retry without losing already-loaded content. Scroll position restoration is critical when navigating away and back. Each state (loading, error, empty, end-of-list) needs distinct UI handling.
answer: IntersectionObserver: place sentinel div at end of list. When visible, fetch next page. Debounce fetches (don't fetch if already fetching). Cursor-based pagination: API returns {items, nextCursor}. Pass cursor to next request. Pull-to-refresh: detect touch start/move/end. If overscroll at top and pull distance > 80px, trigger refresh. Show spinner during refresh. Refetch first page, prepend new items. Skeleton: render 5 skeleton items matching actual item height during initial load. Use CSS animation (pulse). Error: if page fetch fails, show 'Failed to load more' with Retry button at bottom. Don't lose already-loaded items. On retry, re-fetch same page. Empty state: show illustration and message when list is empty. End of list: show 'You've reached the end' message when nextCursor is null. Scroll restoration: save scroll position to sessionStorage on navigation away. On return, scroll to saved position after data loads. Use scrollRestoration='manual' on router. Virtualization: for lists with 1000+ items, use react-window to render only visible items. Measure item heights for variable-size lists. Performance: use React.memo for list items. Avoid inline functions in renderItem. Preload next page when user is 5 items from bottom.

instruction: Add a multi-select autocomplete component that fetches options from an API, supports creating new options inline, groups options by category, and handles keyboard navigation with proper ARIA attributes. The current app uses a basic select element that can't handle the growing number of options.
reasoning: Autocomplete with API-backed options requires debounced fetching and caching. Creating new options inline needs a 'Create new' option when no match is found. Grouping requires hierarchical rendering while maintaining flat keyboard navigation. ARIA attributes must correctly communicate the combobox pattern to screen readers. The component must handle loading, error, empty, and no-results states.
answer: Use downshift library for accessible combobox pattern. Input: text input with debounced API fetch (300ms). Cancel previous request on new input (AbortController). Cache results by query (Map<string, Option[]>). Dropdown: show when input focused and has value. Render grouped options with category headers. Highlight matching text in options. Create new: if no options match query, show 'Create "{query}"' option at bottom. On select, call create API, add to selected items. Multi-select: selected items shown as tags/chips above input with remove button. Input shows remaining space. Keyboard: Arrow Down opens dropdown and navigates options. Arrow Up navigates up. Enter selects highlighted option. Escape closes dropdown. Backspace removes last selected tag when input is empty. ARIA: role='combobox', aria-expanded, aria-controls (dropdown ID), aria-activedescendant (highlighted option ID). Options have role='option', aria-selected. Loading: show spinner in dropdown while fetching. Error: show 'Failed to load options' with retry. Empty: show 'No options available'. Accessibility: announce result count ('5 options available'). Announce selection changes. Performance: virtualize dropdown for 100+ options. Debounce fetch. Memoize filtered options.

instruction: Implement a drag-and-drop kanban board where cards can be moved between columns, reordered within columns, and edited inline. Requirements: show drop zones during drag, persist order changes optimistically, handle concurrent edits from other users, and support keyboard-accessible drag operations.
reasoning: Kanban drag-and-drop requires tracking drag state across columns. Optimistic persistence means updating local state immediately and syncing to backend. Concurrent edits from other users can conflict with local drag operations. Keyboard accessibility for drag-and-drop is often overlooked but required for WCAG compliance. The implementation must handle edge cases like dragging the last card from a column.
answer: Use @dnd-kit library for accessible drag-and-drop. Columns are droppable containers, cards are draggable items. State: columns object {todo: [cards], inProgress: [cards], done: [cards]}. On drag start: set activeId. Show drop zone indicators (dashed border) on all columns. On drag over: calculate new position based on mouse position relative to other cards. Show insertion indicator (line between cards). On drop: move card from source column to target column at calculated index. Optimistic update: update local state immediately. Send PATCH /api/board/cards/:id/move with {column, position}. On error: rollback to previous state, show error toast. Concurrent edits: include version number in move request. If version mismatch (409): fetch latest board state, show 'Board was updated by another user' notification. Don't silently overwrite changes. Keyboard: dnd-kit supports keyboard sensors. Space to pick up card, arrow keys to move, Space/Enter to drop, Escape to cancel. Announce movements to screen readers ('Card moved to In Progress, position 3'). Inline editing: click card title to edit. Show input, save on blur/Enter, cancel on Escape. Card details: click card body opens detail modal with full description, comments, attachments. Performance: use React.memo for cards. Only re-render dragged card and affected columns. Virtualize columns with 100+ cards.

instruction: Add a responsive data visualization dashboard with interactive charts that support zoom, pan, tooltip, and cross-filtering. The existing app shows static chart images. Requirements: line charts for time series, bar charts for categories, pie charts for proportions, with clicking one chart filtering data in others.
reasoning: Interactive charts require efficient re-rendering when data changes. Cross-filtering means selecting data in one chart filters all others, requiring coordinated state management. Zoom and pan need to work smoothly without lag. Tooltips must position correctly near the cursor without going off-screen. The charts must be responsive and handle empty/loading states.
answer: Use D3.js for custom charts or Recharts/Visx for React-friendly charts. Chart components: LineChart, BarChart, PieChart, each accepting data and config props. Cross-filtering: maintain global filter state in context. When user clicks bar in BarChart, set filter {category: 'selected_category'}. Other charts receive filtered data. Show active filters as removable chips above dashboard. Tooltip: custom tooltip component positioned near cursor. Calculate position to avoid viewport edges. Show relevant data (value, date, category). Debounce tooltip updates for smooth movement. Zoom: D3 zoom behavior or brush component for selecting time range. On zoom: update x-axis domain, re-render visible data points. Pan: drag to pan when zoomed. Reset zoom button. Responsive: use ResizeObserver to detect container size. Redraw charts on resize. Use viewBox for SVG scaling. Loading: show skeleton matching chart dimensions. Error: show error message with retry button. Empty: show 'No data for selected filters' with suggestion to adjust filters. Performance: for large datasets (>10k points), aggregate data server-side before sending. Use canvas rendering for very large datasets. Debounce filter changes. Memoize chart computations. Accessibility: provide data table alternative for screen readers. Include chart title and description. Keyboard navigation for chart interactions.

instruction: Implement a RESTful API endpoint for creating orders with inventory validation, payment processing, and email confirmation. The endpoint must handle partial failures (payment succeeds but inventory update fails), prevent duplicate orders from double-clicks, and return appropriate HTTP status codes for different failure scenarios.
reasoning: Order creation involves multiple systems (inventory, payment, email) that can fail independently. Partial failures require compensation logic (refund if inventory fails). Duplicate prevention needs idempotency keys. HTTP status codes must accurately represent the failure type. The endpoint must be atomic from the user's perspective while handling distributed system realities.
answer: Idempotency: require Idempotency-Key header on POST /api/orders. Store key in idempotency_keys table with result. If key exists, return cached response. Prevents duplicate orders from network retries or double-clicks. Validation: validate request body (items, quantities, shipping address). Check inventory availability for all items. Return 400 with detailed errors if invalid. Transaction flow: BEGIN TRANSACTION. 1) Create order record with status 'pending'. 2) Reserve inventory (decrement available_count, increment reserved_count). 3) Process payment via Stripe (create PaymentIntent, confirm). 4) Update order status to 'confirmed'. COMMIT. If payment fails: ROLLBACK, return 402 Payment Required. If inventory insufficient: ROLLBACK, return 409 Conflict with unavailable items. Email: send confirmation email asynchronously (queue job, don't block response). Use template with order details. Return 201 Created with order object. Error handling: catch specific errors (StripeCardError -> 402, InventoryError -> 409). Log all errors with context. Rate limiting: limit order creation to 10/minute per user. Monitoring: track order creation success rate, average processing time, failure reasons.

instruction: Add a webhook delivery system that reliably sends events to subscriber URLs with retry logic, signature verification, and delivery tracking. The system must handle subscriber endpoints that are slow, return errors, or are temporarily unavailable without blocking the main application.
reasoning: Webhook delivery must be reliable without impacting application performance. Slow subscriber endpoints can block workers if not handled correctly. Retry logic needs exponential backoff with jitter to avoid thundering herd. Signature verification allows subscribers to authenticate webhook payloads. Delivery tracking helps debug integration issues. The system must handle millions of deliveries without data loss.
answer: Webhook registration: POST /api/webhooks with {url, events: ['order.created', 'user.updated'], secret}. Generate HMAC secret for signature verification. Delivery queue: when event occurs, find subscribed webhooks, create delivery jobs in webhook_deliveries table (status: 'pending'). Use Bull queue for async processing. Delivery: POST to subscriber URL with JSON payload {event: 'order.created', data: {...}, timestamp: '...'}, signature in X-Webhook-Signature header (HMAC-SHA256 of payload with secret). Set timeout (10 seconds). Retry logic: if non-2xx response or timeout, retry with exponential backoff: 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 hours, 24 hours (5 attempts total). Add jitter (±20%) to prevent thundering herd. After max retries, mark as 'failed'. Delivery tracking: record each attempt (status_code, response_body, duration, error). Show delivery history in webhook management UI. Subscriber can manually retry failed deliveries. Security: use HTTPS only in production. Validate URL is not internal IP (prevent SSRF). Rate limit deliveries per webhook (100/hour). Performance: process deliveries in background workers. Don't block application. Batch deliveries for same event to multiple subscribers. Dead letter queue: after max retries, move to DLQ for manual inspection. Alert on high failure rates. Testing: provide test delivery button that sends sample event. Show request/response details. Local development: use ngrok or similar for testing webhooks locally.

instruction: Implement a database query builder that safely constructs SQL from a flexible filter API, supports joins, aggregations, and pagination, while preventing SQL injection. The API receives filter parameters like ?status=active&created_after=2024-01-01&sort=-name&fields=id,name,email and must translate them to efficient SQL.
reasoning: Dynamic query building requires mapping API parameters to SQL while preventing injection. Parameterized queries are essential - never concatenate user input. Joins need careful handling to avoid N+1 queries. Aggregations require GROUP BY and HAVING clauses. Pagination needs efficient OFFSET/LIMIT or cursor-based approaches for large datasets. The builder must produce readable SQL for debugging.
answer: Use Knex.js query builder for safe SQL construction. Parse filters: extract field filters (status=active), operators (created_after uses >), sort (prefix - for DESC), fields (select specific columns), pagination (page, limit). Build query: let query = knex('users').select(parseFields(fields)).where(parseFilters(filters)).orderBy(parseSort(sort)).limit(limit).offset((page-1)*limit). For joins: define allowed joins in config. If filter references joined table (e.g., orders.status), add join. Prevent arbitrary joins. Parameterized queries: Knex automatically parameterizes values. Never use raw SQL with user input. If raw SQL needed, use knex.raw('WHERE id = ?', [id]). Operators: map API operators to SQL. created_after -> where('created_at', '>', value). status_in -> whereIn('status', values). search -> where('name', 'ilike', `%${value}%`). Aggregations: support ?group_by=status&count=true. Add groupBy and count to query. Validate group_by fields are allowed. Pagination: for large tables (>100k rows), use cursor-based pagination instead of OFFSET. Return cursor (encoded last item ID) in response. Performance: add EXPLAIN logging in development. Identify slow queries. Add indexes for frequently filtered columns. Use query analysis to suggest indexes. Security: whitelist allowed filter fields. Reject unknown fields. Limit max page size (100). Rate limit complex queries. Response: return {data: rows, meta: {total, page, limit, hasMore}}. Include SQL in response only in development mode.

instruction: Add a file upload endpoint that handles multipart form data, validates file types and sizes, scans for malware, generates thumbnails for images, stores files in S3 with proper access controls, and returns signed URLs for download. The endpoint must handle concurrent uploads efficiently and provide upload progress.
reasoning: File upload involves multiple concerns: parsing multipart data, validation, virus scanning, image processing, cloud storage, and access control. Large files need streaming to avoid memory issues. Malware scanning must happen before storage. Thumbnail generation should be async to not block upload response. Signed URLs provide time-limited access without exposing storage credentials. Concurrent uploads need resource management.
answer: Multipart parsing: use multer with memory storage for small files (<10MB), disk storage for larger. Set file size limit (100MB). Validate: check MIME type against whitelist (image/jpeg, image/png, application/pdf, etc.). Verify file extension matches MIME type. Check magic bytes to prevent MIME type spoofing. Reject invalid files with 400. Virus scanning: stream file to ClamAV daemon before storage. If infected, delete and return 400. Run asynchronously for large files. Image processing: for images, generate thumbnails (small: 150x150, medium: 500x500) using sharp. Process in background job to not block response. Store original and thumbnails. S3 storage: upload to S3 with server-side encryption (AES-256). Use multipart upload for files >5MB. Set storage class (STANDARD for frequent access, GLACIER for archives). Organize by user: uploads/{userId}/{fileId}. Access control: set S3 objects as private. Generate signed URLs with 1-hour expiry for download. Use S3 presigned URLs. API: POST /api/uploads with multipart form data. Return {fileId, filename, url (signed), thumbnails: {small, medium}}. Upload progress: use XHR with progress event on client. Server doesn't need special handling. Concurrent uploads: limit concurrent uploads per user (5). Use connection pooling for S3. Queue image processing jobs. Cleanup: delete orphaned files (uploaded but never referenced) after 24 hours. Provide delete endpoint for users to remove their files. Metadata: store file metadata in database (id, userId, filename, mimeType, size, s3Key, createdAt). Query for user's files.

instruction: Implement a rate limiting middleware that uses a sliding window algorithm, supports different limits per endpoint and user tier, returns proper rate limit headers, and gracefully handles Redis failures by falling back to in-memory limiting. The system must work across multiple server instances.
reasoning: Sliding window rate limiting is more accurate than fixed windows but more complex to implement. Different endpoints need different limits based on cost and abuse potential. User tiers (free, pro, enterprise) need different quotas. Rate limit headers inform clients of their remaining quota. Redis failures shouldn't break the application - fallback to less accurate in-memory limiting. Distributed systems need shared state.
answer: Sliding window algorithm: for each request, use Redis sorted set with timestamp as score. Key: ratelimit:{endpoint}:{userId}. Add current timestamp with score, remove entries older than window, count remaining entries. If count > limit, reject with 429. Implementation: use rate-limiter-flexible library with Redis store. Configure per endpoint: {endpoint: '/api/search', window: 60, limit: 100}, {endpoint: '/api/auth/login', window: 300, limit: 5}. User tiers: check user.tier, apply tier multiplier. Free: 1x, Pro: 5x, Enterprise: 20x. Store tier limits in config. Headers: add to all responses: X-RateLimit-Limit (max requests in window), X-RateLimit-Remaining (requests left), X-RateLimit-Reset (Unix timestamp when window resets). On 429: add Retry-After header (seconds until reset). Redis failure handling: catch Redis connection errors. Fall back to in-memory rate limiting (per-server, less accurate). Log fallback events for monitoring. Restore Redis when connection recovers. Use circuit breaker to avoid hammering failed Redis. IP-based limiting: for unauthenticated requests, use IP address instead of userId. Handle proxies (trust X-Forwarded-For from known load balancers only). Whitelisting: maintain whitelist of IPs/users that bypass limits (internal services, partners). Gradual backoff: if user hits limit repeatedly, increase wait time. First violation: wait window duration. Second: 2x window. Third: 4x window. Reset after 1 hour of no violations. Monitoring: track rate limit hits by endpoint, user, IP. Alert on unusual patterns (DDoS indicators). Dashboard showing top rate-limited users. Testing: mock Redis in tests. Test fallback behavior. Verify limits are enforced correctly under load.

instruction: Implement a real-time collaborative document editor where multiple users can edit simultaneously with conflict resolution, presence indicators, and offline support. The existing app uses a simple textarea with save button. Requirements: show other users' cursors and selections, handle network disconnections gracefully, sync changes when reconnected, and persist document state.
reasoning: Real-time collaboration requires a conflict resolution strategy (OT or CRDT) that handles concurrent edits without losing data. Presence indicators need low-latency updates without overwhelming the server. Offline support requires local persistence and conflict resolution on reconnect. The transition from simple textarea to collaborative editor is a fundamental architecture change affecting data model, networking, and UI.
answer: CRDT implementation: use Yjs library for conflict-free replicated data types. Each character is a CRDT node with unique ID and lamport timestamp. Concurrent edits merge automatically without conflicts. Document model: Yjs Y.Text for rich text, Y.Array for comments, Y.Map for metadata. Real-time sync: WebSocket connection per document. On local edit: Yjs generates update, sent to server, broadcast to other clients via room. On remote update: apply to local Yjs document, editor updates automatically. Presence: Yjs awareness protocol shares cursor position and selection. Each user has color and name. Render remote cursors as colored lines with name tooltip. Show user avatars in header for connected users. Offline support: Yjs persists to IndexedDB automatically. Continue editing offline, changes stored locally. On reconnect: sync with server, merge changes. Show offline/online indicator. Persistence: save document state to database every 30 seconds or after 50 edits. Use Yjs's built-in persistence adapters. Version history: save snapshots every 100 edits. Allow viewing and restoring previous versions. Editor integration: use y-prosemirror or y-quill binding. These provide rich text editing with Yjs sync out of the box. Performance: batch updates (send every 100ms, not every keystroke). Compress updates. Limit document size (100k characters). Lazy load editor component. Conflict scenarios: two users edit same word - CRDT merges both edits. User deletes text another is editing - deletion wins. These are handled automatically by Yjs. Testing: simulate concurrent edits in tests. Verify document converges to same state regardless of operation order.

instruction: Add a comprehensive search feature with Elasticsearch that supports full-text search, faceted filtering, autocomplete suggestions, and search analytics. The existing app uses SQL LIKE queries which are slow and don't support relevance ranking. Requirements: search across multiple content types, show faceted counts, provide instant suggestions as user types, and track search performance.
reasoning: Migrating from SQL LIKE to Elasticsearch requires indexing strategy and keeping index in sync with database. Full-text search needs proper analyzers for stemming and stop words. Faceted search requires aggregations alongside search results. Autocomplete needs fast completion suggester. Search analytics help improve relevance over time. The system must handle index updates without downtime.
answer: Elasticsearch setup: create indices for each content type (posts, users, products). Mapping: define fields with appropriate types and analyzers. Example: posts index: {title: {type: 'text', analyzer: 'english', boost: 3}, body: {type: 'text', analyzer: 'english'}, tags: {type: 'keyword'}, author: {type: 'keyword'}, created_at: {type: 'date'}}. Indexing: on content create/update/delete, sync to Elasticsearch. Use application-level hooks (afterSave, afterDestroy) or change data capture (Debezium) for reliability. Batch updates for performance. Search endpoint: GET /api/search?q=query&type=posts&tags=javascript&date_from=2024-01-01. Backend constructs Elasticsearch query: multi_match for text search across title and body, bool query with filters for tags and date range, aggregations for facets. Faceted search: add terms aggregation for tags, date_histogram for created_at. Return facet counts alongside results. UI: sidebar with filter checkboxes showing counts. Clicking filter adds to query, updates results and facet counts. Autocomplete: use completion suggester or search_as_you_type field. Debounce input (300ms). Show top 5 suggestions grouped by type. Highlight matching text. Search analytics: log all searches with query, filters, result count, clicked results. Track zero-result searches to identify content gaps. Track click-through rate to measure relevance. Use analytics to tune relevance (boost important fields, add synonyms). Relevance tuning: boost title matches over body. Use function_score for recency boost. Add synonyms (js = javascript). Tune based on analytics. Pagination: use search_after for deep pagination (not from/size beyond 10k). Performance: cache common searches (5 min TTL). Use Elasticsearch request cache. Optimize shard count and replica settings. Monitoring: track search latency, error rate, zero-result rate. Alert on degradation. Reindexing: when mapping changes, create new index, reindex data, swap alias. Zero downtime.

instruction: Implement a notification system that delivers messages via multiple channels (in-app, email, push, SMS) based on user preferences, with batching to prevent notification fatigue, quiet hours support, and delivery tracking. The existing app sends immediate emails for every event which overwhelms users.
reasoning: Multi-channel notification delivery requires a routing layer that respects user preferences per notification type and channel. Batching prevents overwhelming users with many notifications in short time. Quiet hours need timezone-aware logic. Delivery tracking helps debug delivery issues and measure engagement. The system must scale to millions of notifications without impacting application performance.
answer: Notification types: define types (mention, reply, order_update, marketing) with default channels and urgency levels. User preferences: notification_preferences table (user_id, type, channel, enabled, quiet_hours_start, quiet_hours_end, timezone). Users configure per type and channel. Routing logic: when event triggers notification, look up user preferences. For each enabled channel: check quiet hours (convert to user timezone, skip if in quiet hours unless urgent). Queue delivery job. Batching: collect notifications in time window (5 minutes for non-urgent). If multiple notifications of same type for same user, combine into single notification. Example: '5 people liked your post' instead of 5 separate notifications. Daily digest: for low-priority notifications, collect throughout day, send single email at preferred time (9 AM user's timezone). Channel adapters: InAppAdapter: insert into notifications table, push via WebSocket. EmailAdapter: render template, send via SendGrid/SES. PushAdapter: send via Firebase/OneSignal. SMSAdapter: send via Twilio (only for urgent). Each adapter implements send(notification, user) with error handling. Delivery tracking: notification_deliveries table (notification_id, channel, status, sent_at, delivered_at, error). Update status on delivery confirmation or failure. Email: track opens/clicks via webhook. Push: track delivery receipts. Failure handling: email bounce -> mark email invalid, notify user. SMS failure -> fall back to email. Retry transient failures (3 attempts, exponential backoff). Unsubscribe: include unsubscribe link in marketing emails. One-click unsubscribe via List-Unsubscribe header. Process immediately. Analytics: track delivery rates, open rates, click rates per channel and type. Identify underperforming notifications. Performance: queue all notifications for async processing. Don't block application. Batch database inserts. Use connection pooling for external services.

instruction: Implement a session recording and replay feature for debugging user-reported issues. Requirements: record user interactions (clicks, scrolls, input changes, network requests), store session data efficiently, allow playback in a viewer, mask sensitive data (passwords, credit cards), and respect user consent settings.
reasoning: Session recording requires capturing DOM mutations efficiently without impacting performance. Sensitive data masking must happen client-side before transmission. Storage efficiency requires delta compression of DOM changes. Playback needs to reconstruct the page state at any point in time. User consent must be checked before recording starts. The implementation must handle single-page application navigation.
answer: Recording: use rrweb library which records DOM mutations, scroll positions, input changes, and mouse movements. Initialize on page load if user has consented. Masking: configure rrweb to mask input fields matching selectors (input[type=password], input[autocomplete=cc-number]). Replace text content with asterisks. Never record sensitive data. Storage: batch events every 10 seconds, compress with gzip, POST to /api/sessions/events. Store in S3 with lifecycle policy (delete after 30 days). Session metadata: store session_id, user_id, start_time, duration, page_count in database. Playback: viewer loads session events, reconstructs DOM at each timestamp. Use rrweb-player component. Provide timeline scrubber, play/pause, speed controls. Show network requests and console logs alongside replay. Consent: check cookie consent settings before recording. Provide opt-out option. Show recording indicator (red dot) when active. Performance: limit recording to 5 minutes per session. Drop events if buffer exceeds 1MB. Use requestIdleCallback for non-critical processing. Privacy: comply with GDPR. Allow users to request deletion of their recordings. Don't record on pages with sensitive content (payment, health).

instruction: Add a feature that allows users to schedule posts for future publication. Requirements: support scheduling with timezone awareness, show scheduled posts in a calendar view, send notifications when posts are published, handle timezone changes (DST), and allow editing/canceling scheduled posts.
reasoning: Scheduled publishing requires reliable job scheduling that handles timezone complexities including DST transitions. Calendar view needs to fetch and display posts across date ranges efficiently. Editing scheduled posts requires updating both the content and the scheduled time. The system must handle clock skew between servers and ensure posts publish at the correct time in the user's timezone.
answer: Data model: posts table with status (draft, scheduled, published), scheduled_at (UTC), author_timezone. When user schedules: convert local time to UTC using author's timezone, save with status='scheduled'. Calendar view: GET /api/posts/scheduled?from=2024-01-01&to=2024-01-31. Return posts with scheduled_at in range. Render with FullCalendar or react-big-calendar. Show post title, time in user's timezone. Job scheduler: use node-cron or Bull scheduled jobs. Every minute, query posts where scheduled_at <= NOW() AND status = 'scheduled'. Publish: update status to 'published', trigger notifications. Timezone handling: store user's timezone in profile. Use date-fns-tz for conversions. Handle DST: if user schedules for 2:30 AM on DST spring-forward day (doesn't exist), show warning and suggest alternative. Editing: allow editing scheduled posts. Update content and/or scheduled time. If time changes, reschedule job. Canceling: set status back to 'draft', cancel scheduled job. Notifications: when post publishes, send notifications to followers (respect their preferences). Show 'Your scheduled post is now live' to author. Reliability: use database-level scheduling (not in-memory). If server restarts, jobs resume. Add monitoring for missed publications. Admin dashboard: show upcoming scheduled posts, ability to publish immediately or cancel.

instruction: Implement a URL shortener service with custom aliases, click tracking, geographic analytics, and QR code generation. Requirements: generate short URLs, redirect to original URL, track clicks with referrer and user agent, prevent abuse (malicious URLs), support custom aliases, and provide analytics dashboard.
reasoning: URL shortening requires efficient lookup for redirects (high throughput, low latency). Click tracking must not slow down redirects. Custom aliases need validation and conflict detection. Abuse prevention requires URL validation and blacklisting. Geographic analytics needs IP geolocation. QR codes need to be generated on demand. The redirect endpoint is on the critical path and must be extremely fast.
answer: Short URL generation: use base62 encoding of auto-incrementing ID for short codes (e.g., 'abc123'). For custom aliases: validate format (alphanumeric, 3-20 chars), check availability, reject reserved words. Store in urls table (id, short_code, original_url, user_id, created_at, clicks_count). Redirect: GET /:shortCode. Look up in Redis cache first (cache hot URLs), fall back to database. 301 redirect to original URL. If not found: 404 page. Track clicks asynchronously: after redirect response, queue click event with timestamp, IP, user agent, referrer. Process in background: parse user agent (browser, OS, device), geolocate IP (MaxMind GeoIP), store in clicks table. Don't block redirect for tracking. Abuse prevention: validate URL format, check against URL blacklist (phishing, malware databases). Scan destination with Google Safe Browsing API. Rate limit URL creation (50/hour per user). Require authentication for URL creation. Custom aliases: validate no profanity, no reserved paths (/api, /admin). Check availability with unique constraint. Analytics dashboard: show total clicks, clicks over time (chart), top referrers, geographic distribution (map), devices/browsers breakdown. Date range filter. QR code: generate QR code for short URL using qrcode library. Allow customizing size, colors, adding logo. Cache generated QR codes. Performance: cache redirects in Redis (TTL 1 hour). Use read replicas for analytics queries. Don't run analytics on redirect path. Cleanup: delete URLs with no clicks after 6 months. Archive old click data.

instruction: Add a comprehensive form auto-save feature that periodically saves form data to prevent data loss. Requirements: auto-save every 30 seconds, show save status indicator, restore auto-saved data on page return, handle conflicts between auto-save and manual save, and clean up auto-saves after successful submission.
reasoning: Auto-save must balance frequency (prevent data loss) with performance (not overwhelm server). Save status indicator builds user trust. Restoring auto-saved data requires detecting unsaved work on page return. Conflicts arise when auto-save and manual save happen simultaneously. Cleanup prevents storage bloat. The feature must work across browser crashes and accidental navigation.
answer: Auto-save implementation: use useEffect with setInterval (30 seconds). On interval: compare current form values with last saved values. If different: send PATCH /api/forms/:id/autosave with changed fields only. Show status: 'Saving...' during save, 'Saved' with timestamp after success, 'Offline' if no connection. Store last save timestamp in state. LocalStorage backup: also save to localStorage every 5 seconds (faster than network). On page load: check localStorage for auto-save data newer than server data. Prompt 'We found unsaved changes. Restore?' with Restore/Discard options. Conflict handling: manual save takes priority. If auto-save is in progress when user clicks Save, wait for auto-save to complete first. Use AbortController to cancel auto-save if manual save initiated. After successful submission: delete auto-save from server (DELETE /api/forms/:id/autosave) and localStorage. Redirect to success page. Status indicator: show in form header. Green checkmark with 'All changes saved'. Yellow dot with 'Saving...'. Red with 'Auto-save failed, your changes may be lost'. Click to retry. Debouncing: don't auto-save if user is actively typing (wait 2 seconds after last input). Use form state 'isDirty' to determine if save is needed. Performance: send only changed fields (diff). Compress large form data. Queue saves if offline, sync when back online. Cleanup: server-side cron job deletes auto-saves older than 7 days. Client-side: clear localStorage auto-saves on successful submission.

instruction: Implement a content moderation queue where moderators review flagged content. Requirements: show flagged content with reason for flagging, allow approve/reject/escalate actions, track moderator performance metrics, prevent moderators from reviewing their own content, and support bulk moderation actions.
reasoning: Moderation queues need prioritization (reported content first, then auto-flagged). Preventing self-review requires filtering based on content author. Performance metrics help identify training needs and ensure quality. Bulk actions speed up moderation for clear-cut cases. The system must handle appeals and track decision history for consistency.
answer: Queue system: moderation_queue table (content_id, content_type, flag_reason, flag_source (user_report|automated), priority, assigned_to, status). Priority: user reports > automated flags, older > newer. Queue view: moderators see next unassigned item. Auto-assign on open (prevent two moderators reviewing same item). Content display: show flagged content with context (surrounding content, user history). Show flag reason and reporter's comment (if user report). Show automated detection confidence score. Actions: Approve (content is fine, remove from queue), Reject (remove content, warn user), Escalate (send to senior moderator). Each action requires reason (dropdown + optional comment). Self-review prevention: filter queue WHERE content.author_id != moderator.id. Also filter out content from moderator's friends/connections if applicable. Bulk actions: allow selecting multiple items with same flag reason. Apply same action to all. Show confirmation with count. Limit to 50 items per bulk action. Performance metrics: track per moderator: items reviewed per hour, approval rate, escalation rate, accuracy (measured by senior moderator spot-checks). Show in moderator dashboard. Don't use metrics punitively - use for training. Appeals: users can appeal rejected content. Create appeal record, re-enter queue for different moderator. Track original decision and appeal outcome. Use for improving automated detection. Audit trail: log all moderation decisions with moderator ID, action, reason, timestamp. Allow admins to review decisions. Consistency: show similar past decisions to moderators for reference. Automated detection: integrate Perspective API for text toxicity, AWS Rekognition for image safety. Flag content above threshold. Continuously improve thresholds based on moderator decisions.

instruction: Add a comprehensive API versioning strategy that supports multiple API versions simultaneously, provides deprecation warnings, and allows gradual migration. Requirements: version in URL path (/v1/, /v2/), maintain backward compatibility, document breaking changes, and sunset old versions with proper notice.
reasoning: API versioning allows evolution without breaking existing clients. Multiple versions must run simultaneously during migration periods. Deprecation warnings inform clients to migrate. Breaking changes must be clearly documented. Sunset headers tell clients when versions will be removed. The strategy must balance innovation (new features) with stability (not breaking clients).
answer: Versioning approach: URL path versioning (/api/v1/users, /api/v2/users). Each version has its own route handlers. Shared business logic in service layer. Version router: middleware extracts version from path, routes to appropriate handler. Fallback to latest version if not specified (with deprecation warning). Backward compatibility: within a version, never make breaking changes. Add new fields (additive changes are safe). Deprecate fields by marking in docs but still returning them. Breaking changes go in new version. Deprecation: when planning to remove v1, add Sunset header to all v1 responses: Sunset: Sat, 01 Jun 2025 00:00:00 GMT. Add Deprecation header: Deprecation: true. Log deprecated version usage. Email API consumers with migration guide and timeline. Migration guide: document all differences between versions. Provide code examples for migration. Offer migration assistance for enterprise clients. Version lifecycle: active (full support), deprecated (bug fixes only, sunset date set), sunsetted (removed, returns 410 Gone). Minimum 6 months between deprecation and sunset. Analytics: track API usage by version. Identify clients still on old versions. Reach out to high-usage clients before sunset. Implementation: separate route files per version. Shared validation schemas where possible. Version-specific transformations in response serializers. Testing: test all active versions in CI. Ensure backward compatibility tests pass. Documentation: maintain separate docs per version. Show version selector in docs UI. Highlight differences between versions.

instruction: Implement a multi-step data import wizard that validates CSV files, maps columns to database fields, previews data transformations, handles duplicates, and provides detailed error reports. The import must handle files with 100,000+ rows without timing out or running out of memory.
reasoning: Large file imports require streaming to avoid memory issues. Column mapping must handle varied CSV formats. Data transformation preview lets users verify before committing. Duplicate handling needs configurable strategies (skip, update, error). Error reporting must identify specific rows and columns. The wizard must guide users through a complex process without overwhelming them.
answer: Wizard steps: 1) Upload file, 2) Map columns, 3) Configure options, 4) Preview & validate, 5) Import. Step 1 - Upload: accept CSV/XLSX. Parse header row and first 10 data rows for preview. Store file temporarily (S3 or local). Show file info (rows detected, columns, encoding). Step 2 - Column mapping: show CSV columns and database fields side by side. Auto-detect mappings by column name similarity. Allow manual mapping via dropdowns. Mark required fields. Show data type and sample values for each column. Step 3 - Configure: duplicate handling strategy (skip, update existing, create new, error). Date format selection. Default values for unmapped fields. Step 4 - Preview: validate all rows against schema. Show summary (X valid, Y errors). List first 50 errors with row number, column, error message. Allow downloading full error report as CSV. Fix errors and re-upload or skip error rows. Step 5 - Import: process in background job. Stream file, process in batches of 1000. For each batch: validate, transform, insert in transaction. Update progress. Show progress bar with ETA. Backend: use streaming CSV parser (csv-parser for Node.js). Process rows in batches to limit memory. Insert with ON CONFLICT handling for duplicates. Return detailed results: imported count, updated count, skipped count, error count with details. Performance: set job timeout (30 minutes). Allow cancellation. Rate limit imports per user. Cleanup: delete temporary files after import. Delete import records after 30 days.

instruction: Add a real-time typing indicator and read receipts to a chat application. Requirements: show when other users are typing, debounce typing events to prevent spam, mark messages as read when scrolled into view, show read status per message, and handle these features efficiently at scale with thousands of concurrent users.
reasoning: Typing indicators generate high-frequency events that can overwhelm WebSocket servers if not throttled. Read receipts require tracking per-user per-message state which grows quadratically. Efficient implementation needs careful data structures and batching. The features must degrade gracefully under load. Privacy considerations: some users may want to disable read receipts.
answer: Typing indicators: client emits 'typing:start' event when user starts typing in a conversation. Debounce: only emit if not already in typing state. Auto-emit 'typing:stop' after 3 seconds of no typing. Server: maintain typing state in Redis (key: typing:{conversationId}, value: Set of userIds, TTL: 5 seconds). Broadcast typing state to other conversation participants. Client: show 'User is typing...' with animated dots. Show multiple users: 'Alice and Bob are typing...'. Read receipts: when user opens conversation, mark all messages as read. Use IntersectionObserver to detect when message scrolls into view. Batch read receipts: collect message IDs, send batch update every 2 seconds. Backend: message_reads table (message_id, user_id, read_at). For efficiency, store last_read_message_id per conversation per user instead of per-message reads. API: POST /api/conversations/:id/mark-read with {lastMessageId}. Show read status: single check (sent), double check (delivered), blue double check (read by all). For group chats: show read by count, expandable to list of readers. Privacy: allow users to disable read receipts in settings. When disabled: don't send read events, don't show others' read status. Performance: typing events: rate limit to 1 per 2 seconds per user per conversation. Read receipts: batch updates, use last_read_message_id instead of per-message tracking. WebSocket: use rooms per conversation. Only send events to relevant participants. Scale: for large group chats (1000+ members), disable typing indicators. Show read count instead of individual readers. Use Redis pub/sub for horizontal scaling.

instruction: Implement a permission-based navigation system that dynamically shows/hides menu items based on user roles, handles route guards for protected pages, and provides a seamless experience when permissions change during an active session. The system must prevent both unauthorized navigation and unauthorized API access.
reasoning: Permission-based navigation requires both frontend hiding (UX) and backend enforcement (security). Route guards must check permissions before rendering protected pages. Permission changes during a session need real-time updates to the UI. The system must handle complex permission hierarchies and resource-level permissions. Frontend-only protection is insufficient - backend must always validate.
answer: Permission model: define permissions as resource:action pairs (users:read, users:write, orders:delete). Roles map to permission sets. Users have one or more roles. Permission provider: React context that provides user's permissions on app load. usePermission hook: returns boolean for permission check. Components use it to conditionally render: {can('users:write') && <EditButton />}. Navigation config: define routes with required permissions. [{path: '/users', permission: 'users:read', children: [{path: '/users/new', permission: 'users:write'}]}]. Route guard component: checks permission before rendering route. If unauthorized: redirect to 403 page or show 'Access denied' message. Dynamic menu: filter navigation items by permissions. Only show items user can access. Recursively filter children. API protection: all API endpoints check permissions in middleware. Return 403 with {error: 'Insufficient permissions', required: 'users:write'}. Frontend handles 403 by showing error or redirecting. Session permission updates: when admin changes user's permissions, backend sends WebSocket event or includes updated permissions in next API response. Frontend updates permission context, re-renders affected components. If current page becomes unauthorized, redirect to dashboard. Permission caching: cache permissions in memory and localStorage. Refresh on login and periodically (every 15 minutes). Invalidate on permission change event. Resource-level permissions: some permissions depend on the specific resource (can edit own posts but not others'). Check in component: {can('posts:edit', post) && <EditButton />}. Backend: check ownership in middleware. Admin override: admin role bypasses all permission checks. Don't check individual permissions for admins.

instruction: Add a comprehensive error boundary system that catches React errors at different levels, shows appropriate fallback UIs, logs errors with component stack traces, and allows users to recover without full page reload. Requirements: different error UIs for page-level, component-level, and widget-level errors.
reasoning: Error boundaries prevent entire app crashes by catching errors at appropriate levels. Different scopes need different fallback UIs - a widget error shouldn't take down the whole page. Component stack traces help developers identify error sources. Recovery without reload improves UX. The system must handle both render errors and async errors that boundaries don't catch by default.
answer: Error boundary hierarchy: RootErrorBoundary wraps entire app (shows full-page error with reload button). PageErrorBoundary wraps each route (shows error with navigation to other pages). ComponentErrorBoundary wraps complex components (shows inline error with retry). WidgetErrorBoundary wraps dashboard widgets (shows error in widget area). Error boundary component: class component with static getDerivedStateFromError(error) and componentDidCatch(error, errorInfo). State: {hasError: true, error, errorInfo}. Render fallback UI based on level. Fallback UIs: Root level - 'Something went seriously wrong. [Reload page] [Go home]'. Include error ID for support. Page level - 'This page encountered an error. [Try again] [Go to dashboard]'. Component level - 'This component failed to load. [Retry]'. Widget level - 'Widget unavailable. [Retry]'. Error logging: send to Sentry with error message, stack trace, componentStack from errorInfo, user context, URL, breadcrumbs. Generate error ID, show to user for support reference. Async error handling: error boundaries don't catch errors in event handlers, async code, or SSR. Wrap async operations in try/catch. Use useErrorHandler hook to trigger nearest error boundary from async code. Recovery: 'Try again' button resets error state (setState({hasError: false})). Component re-renders. If error persists after 3 retries, show 'Contact support' option. Reset on navigation: clear error state when route changes (useEffect on location). Development mode: show full error details, stack trace, and component hierarchy. Production: show user-friendly message only. Testing: add error boundary stories in Storybook. Test with components that throw in render, useEffect, and event handlers.

instruction: Implement a database connection pool monitor that tracks connection usage, identifies slow queries, detects connection leaks, and provides alerts before pool exhaustion. The monitor must work with PostgreSQL connection pooling and provide actionable insights for performance optimization.
reasoning: Connection pool exhaustion causes application-wide outages. Monitoring pool usage helps identify issues before they become critical. Slow query detection points to optimization opportunities. Connection leak detection finds code that doesn't properly release connections. The monitor must not add significant overhead to database operations.
answer: Pool instrumentation: wrap pg-pool or similar with event listeners. Track: total connections, idle connections, waiting requests, connection checkout duration. Expose metrics via /api/health/db endpoint and Prometheus metrics. Slow query detection: intercept all queries, measure execution time. Log queries taking >1 second with query text, parameters, duration, stack trace. Store in slow_queries table for analysis. Connection leak detection: track connection checkout time. If connection held for >30 seconds, log warning with stack trace of checkout location. This identifies code paths that don't release connections. Dashboard: show real-time pool usage (gauge chart), connection checkout time (line chart), active queries table, slow query log. Alert thresholds: warn at 80% pool usage, critical at 95%. Alert on connection wait time >5 seconds. Query analysis: group slow queries by query pattern (parameterized). Show top 10 slowest query patterns with average duration and count. Suggest indexes based on EXPLAIN ANALYZE output. Connection pool tuning: recommend pool size based on usage patterns. Formula: pool_size = (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count for disk-bound workloads. Monitor queue wait times to identify undersized pools. Health check: ping database every 30 seconds. If ping fails, mark instance as unhealthy, remove from load balancer. Alerting: send alerts to PagerDuty/Slack when pool usage exceeds thresholds or slow query rate spikes. Include actionable information (which queries are slow, which code paths are leaking). Integration: expose metrics in Prometheus format. Create Grafana dashboards. Set up alerts in AlertManager.

instruction: Add a comprehensive dark mode implementation that respects system preferences, allows manual override, prevents flash of wrong theme on page load, and handles all UI components including third-party libraries and embedded content. The implementation must use CSS custom properties for runtime theme switching.
reasoning: Dark mode requires systematic replacement of all color values with theme-aware variables. System preference detection uses media queries but manual override must take precedence. Flash of wrong theme occurs when theme is applied after initial render - needs inline script before React loads. Third-party components may not support theming and need wrapper styles. CSS custom properties enable runtime switching without CSS-in-JS overhead.
answer: CSS custom properties: define all colors as CSS variables in :root (light theme) and [data-theme='dark'] (dark theme). Example: :root { --color-bg: #ffffff; --color-text: #1a1a1a; --color-primary: #0066cc; }. [data-theme='dark'] { --color-bg: #121212; --color-text: #e0e0e0; --color-primary: #4da6ff; }. All components use var(--color-bg) instead of hardcoded colors. Theme detection: check localStorage for manual preference first. If not set, use matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)'). Listen for system preference changes with media query listener. Flash prevention: add inline script in <head> before any CSS or JS loads: <script>const theme = localStorage.getItem('theme') || (matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches ? 'dark' : 'light'); document.documentElement.setAttribute('data-theme', theme);</script>. This sets theme before first paint. Theme toggle: component that cycles through light/dark/system. Update localStorage and data-theme attribute. Show current theme icon. Third-party libraries: for components that don't use CSS variables (e.g., date pickers, charts), add override styles targeting their class names. [data-theme='dark'] .react-datepicker { background: var(--color-bg); }. Embedded content: add dark mode styles for iframes where possible. For images: provide dark mode variants or apply CSS filters (brightness, invert) for decorative images. Color palette: design dark theme with proper contrast ratios (WCAG AA). Don't just invert colors - use dark gray backgrounds (#121212, not pure black) and reduced-contrast text. Elevation: use lighter shades for elevated surfaces in dark mode (card on dark background is slightly lighter). Transitions: add transition: background-color 0.2s, color 0.2s to body for smooth switching. Respect prefers-reduced-motion. Testing: audit all pages in both themes. Check contrast ratios with accessibility tools. Test with color blindness simulators.

instruction: Implement a webhook management UI where users can register webhook endpoints, view delivery history, test webhooks, and configure retry policies. Requirements: show real-time delivery status, provide request/response details for debugging, allow manual retry of failed deliveries, and validate endpoint URLs before saving.
reasoning: Webhook management UI must balance simplicity for basic users with depth for advanced debugging. Real-time delivery status requires WebSocket or polling. Request/response details help debug integration issues. URL validation prevents misconfigured webhooks. The UI must handle webhook secrets securely and provide clear documentation for signature verification.
answer: Webhook registration: form with URL input, event type checkboxes (order.created, user.updated, etc.), optional secret (auto-generate if not provided). URL validation: check format, verify HTTPS (production), send test request to verify endpoint responds with 2xx. Show validation status (checking, valid, invalid with reason). Secret management: show secret once on creation, allow regeneration. Provide code examples for signature verification in multiple languages (Node.js, Python, Ruby). Delivery history: table showing all deliveries for this webhook. Columns: timestamp, event type, status (delivered, failed, pending), response code, duration. Filter by status and date range.
