Delivery details: expand row or click to see full request (URL, headers, body) and response (status code, headers, body). Highlight errors in red. Show retry attempts. Manual retry: button on failed deliveries to retry immediately. Show confirmation. Bulk retry for multiple failed deliveries. Real-time status: WebSocket or polling (every 5 seconds) updates delivery status. Show spinner for pending deliveries. Webhook configuration: set retry policy (number of attempts, backoff strategy), timeout duration, active/paused toggle. Pause stops deliveries without deleting webhook. Testing: 'Send test event' button sends sample event to endpoint. Show full request/response for debugging. Allow selecting event type for test. Documentation: inline documentation explaining webhook format, signature verification, common error codes. Link to full API docs. Security: mask secret in UI (show only on reveal). Log all webhook management actions (created, updated, deleted, tested) for audit.

instruction: Add a comprehensive breadcrumb navigation system that handles deep nesting, truncates long paths, integrates with the router, and supports both click navigation and drag-and-drop for moving items between folders. The breadcrumbs must update dynamically with route changes.
reasoning: Breadcrumb navigation requires mapping URL paths to human-readable labels. Deep nesting needs truncation strategies to avoid horizontal overflow. Router integration ensures breadcrumbs stay in sync with navigation. Drag-and-drop to breadcrumbs enables quick file organization. Dynamic updates require reactive state tied to the current route. The system must handle async label loading for dynamic segments.
answer: Breadcrumb data: derive from router configuration. Each route can define a breadcrumb label or function. Example: /projects/:projectId/files/:folderId -> [{label: 'Projects', href: '/projects'}, {label: async (params) => getProject(params.projectId).name, href: '/projects/:projectId'}, ...]. Dynamic labels: for routes with params (e.g., :projectId), fetch entity name from API. Cache results. Show skeleton while loading. Truncation: if breadcrumb path exceeds container width, truncate middle items with ellipsis. Show first and last 2 items always. Expand on click or hover. Use CSS overflow with JavaScript measurement. Router integration: use router's useLocation hook. Rebuild breadcrumbs on route change. Handle query parameters (don't show in breadcrumbs). Click navigation: each breadcrumb item is a link. Clicking navigates to that level. Last item (current page) is not a link or has different styling. Drag-and-drop: when dragging a file, highlight breadcrumb items as drop targets. Dropping on breadcrumb moves file to that folder. Show folder name on hover. Accessibility: nav element with aria-label='Breadcrumb'. Ordered list with aria-current='page' on last item. Separator between items (aria-hidden). Keyboard navigation with Tab. Mobile: show only current page and parent with back arrow. Swipe right to go up one level. Schema.org: add BreadcrumbList structured data for SEO. JSON-LD with item list.

instruction: Implement a comprehensive data export system that supports CSV, Excel, PDF, and JSON formats with custom column selection, data filtering, scheduled exports, and email delivery. Large exports (100k+ rows) must be processed in the background without timing out.
reasoning: Data export of large datasets requires background processing to avoid HTTP timeouts. Different formats need different libraries and formatting logic. Custom column selection requires mapping UI selections to data fields. Scheduled exports need reliable job scheduling. Email delivery must handle large attachments (use download links instead). The system must handle concurrent exports without overwhelming server resources.
answer: Export request: POST /api/exports with {resource: 'orders', format: 'csv', filters: {status: 'completed', date_from: '2024-01-01'}, columns: ['id', 'customer_name', 'total', 'status'], schedule: null|{frequency: 'daily', time: '09:00', timezone: 'America/New_York'}}. Returns export ID immediately. Background processing: queue export job in Bull/BullMQ. Worker streams data from database using cursor (not loading all rows into memory). CSV: use csv-stringify streaming. Handle special characters, newlines in cells. Add BOM for Excel compatibility. Excel: use exceljs with streaming workbook. Format headers (bold, frozen row). Set column widths. Add auto-filter. PDF: generate HTML table, render with puppeteer. Include header with title, date, filters. Page numbers. JSON: stream JSON array with proper formatting. Progress tracking: update export record with progress percentage. Frontend polls or uses WebSocket. Show progress bar. Completion: upload file to S3 with signed URL (expires in 7 days). Update export record with download URL. Notify user via in-app notification and email with download link. Column selection: UI shows available columns with checkboxes, drag to reorder. Map column IDs to data fields and formatters (currency, date, enum labels). Scheduling: cron job at specified time runs export with saved configuration. Email results to specified addresses. Store schedule in export_schedules table. Allow pause/resume/cancel. Concurrent exports: limit to 5 concurrent export jobs per server. Queue additional requests. Rate limit per user (10 exports/hour). Large file handling: for exports >10MB, split into multiple files or use compression (zip). Email download link instead of attachment. Cleanup: delete export files after 7 days. Delete export records after 90 days. Cron job for cleanup.

instruction: Add a comprehensive state machine for a multi-step payment checkout flow. Requirements: manage states (cart, shipping, payment, processing, confirmation, error), handle browser back/forward buttons, prevent double submissions, recover from payment failures, and persist state across page refreshes.
reasoning: Payment flows are stateful and must handle many edge cases: users going back to edit shipping, network failures during payment processing, browser refresh during processing, and double-clicking the pay button. A state machine makes these transitions explicit and prevents invalid states. Persistence prevents losing checkout progress. The implementation must handle both happy path and error recovery.
answer: State machine: use XState or implement custom. States: cart, shipping, payment, processing, confirmation, error. Transitions: cart -> shipping (on continue), shipping -> payment (on valid address), payment -> processing (on submit), processing -> confirmation (on success), processing -> error (on failure), error -> payment (on retry). Each state has entry/exit actions. State persistence: store current state and form data in sessionStorage. On page load: restore state and data. Don't persist sensitive data (credit card). Browser navigation: use History API. Each state pushes to history. Back button goes to previous state (not previous page). Intercept popstate to handle state transitions. Double submission prevention: in 'processing' state, disable submit button and show spinner. State machine prevents transition from 'processing' to 'processing'. Payment recovery: on payment failure, transition to 'error' state with error details. Show retry button (transitions to 'payment' with preserved data). For specific errors (card declined), show message to use different card. For network errors, auto-retry once. Processing state: show processing screen with spinner. Don't allow navigation away (show confirmation dialog). If user refreshes during processing: check payment status from backend, redirect to confirmation or payment accordingly. Timeout: if processing takes >30 seconds, show 'Still processing' message. Check status periodically. Confirmation: show order summary, order number, estimated delivery. Send confirmation email. Clear cart and checkout state.

instruction: Implement a responsive email client interface with conversation threading, drag-and-drop label management, keyboard shortcuts, and offline support. The interface must handle mailboxes with 10,000+ emails while remaining responsive.
reasoning: Email threading requires grouping messages by subject and references headers. Large mailboxes need virtualization for the email list. Drag-and-drop labels need both visual feedback and optimistic updates. Keyboard shortcuts are essential for power users. Offline support requires local caching and sync on reconnect. The interface must handle complex state (selected emails, active filters, current folder) efficiently.
answer: Email list: virtualized list (react-window) rendering only visible emails. Each row shows sender, subject, preview, date, labels. Thread detection: group emails by thread_id (derived from References/In-Reply-To headers or subject similarity). Show thread count badge. Click to expand thread. Conversation view: show all messages in thread chronologically. Collapse quoted text. Show sender avatars. Reply/forward inline. Drag-and-drop labels: drag email to label in sidebar to apply. Drag label chip off email to remove. Optimistic update with rollback on error. Labels: color-coded chips. Create/edit/delete labels. Filter by label. Keyboard shortcuts: j/k navigate emails, enter opens, r replies, a replies all, f forwards, e archives, # deletes, / searches. Show shortcut help modal (?). Folder navigation: sidebar with Inbox, Sent, Drafts, Archive, Trash, custom folders. Show unread counts. Starred and important emails. Search: full-text search across all folders. Filter by from, to, subject, date, has:attachment. Compose: modal or split pane. Rich text editor. Attach files with drag-and-drop. Auto-save drafts every 30 seconds. Offline support: cache recent emails in IndexedDB. Queue sent emails and actions (archive, delete) for sync on reconnect. Show offline indicator. Performance: lazy load email content (fetch full body on open). Preload next/previous email. Use cursor-based pagination for email list. Accessibility: full keyboard navigation, ARIA labels, screen reader announcements for new emails.

instruction: Add a real-time collaborative spreadsheet with formula support, cell formatting, conditional formatting, and chart generation. Requirements: support basic formulas (SUM, AVERAGE, IF, VLOOKUP), handle circular reference detection, show formula errors, and sync all changes in real-time between multiple users.
reasoning: Collaborative spreadsheets combine the complexity of formula evaluation with real-time sync challenges. Formulas create dependency graphs that must be recalculated when cells change. Circular references need detection to prevent infinite loops. Cell formatting and conditional formatting add visual complexity. Real-time sync must handle concurrent edits to cells and formulas without conflicts. The system must scale to large spreadsheets without performance degradation.
answer: Data model: spreadsheet has cells map (key: 'A1', value: {value, formula, format}). Formulas: parse with formula parser (Hot-formula-parser or custom). Support: arithmetic, SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, IF, COUNTIF, VLOOKUP, CONCATENATE. Dependency graph: when formula references other cells (SUM(A1:A10)), add edges to dependency graph. On cell change, recalculate all dependent cells. Topological sort for evaluation order. Circular reference detection: before adding edge to dependency graph, check for cycles (DFS). If cycle detected: show #CIRCULAR! error in cell, don't evaluate. Cell formatting: bold, italic, underline, font size, text/background color, alignment, number format (currency, percentage, date). Store per cell. Conditional formatting: rules like 'if value > 100, background = green'. Evaluate on cell change. Chart generation: select cell range, choose chart type (bar, line, pie). Generate chart from cell values. Store chart config, render with chart library. Real-time sync: use Yjs with custom CRDT for spreadsheet. Each cell is independent CRDT. Concurrent edits to different cells merge automatically. Same cell: last writer wins (with visual indicator of conflict). Show other users' active cell (colored border with name). Performance: lazy evaluate formulas (only when displayed). Cache formula results. Recalculate in batches. Virtualize grid (render only visible cells). Limit spreadsheet size (1000x100 cells). Undo/redo: track operations per user. Undo only affects user's own changes. Keyboard: Excel-like navigation (Tab right, Enter down, arrow keys). F2 to edit cell. = to start formula.

instruction: Implement a comprehensive A/B testing system with user assignment, metric tracking, statistical analysis, and gradual rollout. Requirements: consistently assign users to variants, track conversion metrics, calculate statistical significance, support feature flag integration, and allow targeting specific user segments.
reasoning: A/B testing requires consistent user assignment so the same user always sees the same variant. Statistical significance calculation determines if results are meaningful or just noise. Feature flag integration allows testing without code deployments. Targeting enables testing on specific segments before full rollout. The system must handle the full experiment lifecycle from creation to analysis.
answer: Experiment definition: experiments table (id, name, status, start_date, end_date, variants: [{id, weight}], target_segments, metrics). Variants have traffic weights (e.g., control: 50%, variant_a: 25%, variant_b: 25%). User assignment: deterministic hash of (userId + experimentId) % 100. Map hash ranges to variants. Consistent: same user always gets same variant. Store assignment in user_experiments table and client-side cookie. Feature flag integration: useExperiment('button_color') returns variant ID. Conditionally render based on variant. Targeting: check user attributes against experiment segments before assignment. Non-matching users get control. Metric tracking: define primary metric (conversion rate) and guardrail metrics (revenue, latency). Track events with experiment and variant context. Example: {event: 'purchase', experiment: 'checkout_v2', variant: 'variant_a', value: 49.99}. Statistical analysis: calculate conversion rate per variant with confidence intervals. Use chi-squared test for proportions, t-test for continuous metrics. Require 95% confidence and minimum sample size before declaring winner. Show results dashboard with lift percentage, confidence level, sample size, and time series. Experiment lifecycle: draft (configure), running (collecting data), paused (stop assignment), completed (analyze results). Auto-stop if guardrail metric drops significantly. Gradual rollout: start with 10% traffic, increase to 50%, then 100% if results are positive. Each phase requires minimum sample size. Client performance: load experiment assignments in initial page load (don't make extra API call). Cache assignments. Fallback to control if experiment service unavailable. Analysis: calculate required sample size before starting. Show progress toward target. Account for multiple comparisons (Bonferroni correction). Segment analysis: break down results by user segments (device, geography, new vs returning).

instruction: Add a comprehensive file versioning system that tracks changes to uploaded documents, allows comparing versions side-by-side, restoring previous versions, and showing who made each change. The system must handle large binary files efficiently without duplicating storage for unchanged portions.
reasoning: File versioning requires storing multiple versions without excessive storage costs. Text files can use delta compression (store only changes). Binary files need content-addressable storage (deduplicate identical chunks). Version comparison differs by file type (text diff vs image diff). Restore must maintain the full version history. The system must handle concurrent edits and merge conflicts.
answer: Storage strategy: content-addressable storage. Split files into chunks (4KB-64KB), hash each chunk (SHA-256), store unique chunks in S3. File versions reference chunk lists. Identical chunks across versions share storage (deduplication). Text files: additionally store diffs between versions (using diff-match-patch) for efficient comparison. Data model: documents table (id, name, current_version_id, owner_id), document_versions table (id, document_id, version_number, chunks (JSON array of chunk hashes), size, checksum, user_id, comment, created_at). Version creation: on file upload/update, split into chunks, hash each, upload new chunks (skip existing), create version record with chunk list. Return version number. Version history: GET /api/documents/:id/versions returns list with version_number, user, timestamp, size, comment. Version comparison: text files - compute diff between versions, show side-by-side with additions/deletions highlighted. Images - show side-by-side or overlay with differences highlighted. Other files - show metadata comparison (size, checksum). Restore version: create new version record pointing to old version's chunks. Don't delete intermediate versions. Maintain full history. Large files: stream file content during upload/download. Use multipart upload for S3. Show upload progress. Chunking happens client-side for large files. Concurrent edits: if two users edit same document simultaneously, detect conflict (version number mismatch). Show conflict resolution UI: compare versions, choose which to keep or merge manually. Comments: prompt for version comment on save ('Fixed typo in section 3'). Show in version history. Permissions: only users with edit permission can create versions. Only owner can delete versions (soft delete). Cleanup: keep all versions for 30 days, then daily versions for 1 year, then weekly versions indefinitely. Configurable per plan.

instruction: Implement OAuth 2.0 social login with Google and GitHub. Requirements: handle the OAuth flow correctly with PKCE, store tokens securely, link social accounts to existing email accounts, handle token refresh, and provide account unlinking. The app currently only supports email/password authentication.
reasoning: OAuth flows require careful state management to prevent CSRF attacks. PKCE adds security for public clients. Account linking must handle the case where a user signs up with email first, then tries social login with same email. Token refresh needs to happen transparently. Unlinking must ensure the user still has a way to log in.
answer: OAuth flow: use Authorization Code flow with PKCE. Generate code_verifier (random string), compute code_challenge (SHA256 hash). Redirect to provider with code_challenge. On callback: exchange code + code_verifier for tokens. Store access_token and refresh_token in httpOnly cookies (not localStorage). Account linking: on social login, check if email matches existing account. If yes: link social provider to existing account (add google_id/github_id to user record). If no: create new account. Don't auto-merge without verification. Token refresh: middleware checks token expiry before API calls. If expired: use refresh_token to get new access_token. If refresh fails: redirect to login. Unlinking: allow unlinking social account only if user has another login method (password or other social). Prevent locking out. Security: validate state parameter to prevent CSRF. Use nonce for OpenID Connect. Verify id_token signature. Scopes: request minimum scopes needed. Google: 'openid email profile'. GitHub: 'user:email'. Error handling: handle user denying permission, expired codes, invalid states. Show user-friendly error messages.

instruction: Add JWT token rotation with refresh tokens stored in httpOnly cookies. The current implementation stores JWTs in localStorage which is vulnerable to XSS. Requirements: implement short-lived access tokens (15 min) with long-lived refresh tokens (7 days), rotate refresh tokens on each use, detect token reuse (theft), and handle concurrent requests during token refresh.
reasoning: Moving from localStorage to httpOnly cookies prevents XSS token theft but introduces CSRF concerns. Short-lived access tokens limit the window of compromise. Refresh token rotation means each use issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If a stolen refresh token is used after the legitimate user, both tokens are invalidated, detecting theft. Concurrent requests during refresh need queuing to avoid race conditions.
answer: Token architecture: access token (JWT, 15 min expiry, in memory only), refresh token (opaque, 7 days expiry, httpOnly Secure SameSite=Strict cookie). Login: POST /api/auth/login returns access token in response body (store in memory), sets refresh token cookie. API requests: include access token in Authorization header. Refresh flow: when access token expires, POST /api/auth/refresh (refresh token sent automatically via cookie). Server validates refresh token, issues new access token AND new refresh token (rotation), invalidates old refresh token. Token reuse detection: store refresh token family ID. If a refresh token is used that was already rotated, invalidate the entire family (all tokens for that user). This detects theft. Concurrent requests: if multiple requests fail with 401 simultaneously, only one triggers refresh. Others queue and retry after refresh completes. Use a promise that resolves when refresh is done. CSRF protection: SameSite=Strict cookie prevents cross-site requests. Add CSRF token for additional protection on state-changing requests. Logout: POST /api/auth/logout invalidates refresh token server-side, clears cookie, clears access token from memory. Remember me: extend refresh token expiry to 30 days. Token storage: refresh_tokens table (id, user_id, token_hash, family_id, expires_at, revoked_at). Hash refresh tokens before storing.

instruction: Implement a magic link (passwordless) authentication flow. Requirements: send login link via email, link expires in 15 minutes, link is single-use, handle multiple concurrent magic link requests, prevent enumeration attacks, and provide fallback to email/password for users who prefer it.
reasoning: Magic links replace passwords with email-based authentication. Single-use tokens prevent replay attacks. Expiration limits the attack window. Preventing enumeration means not revealing whether an email exists in the system. Concurrent requests need deduplication to prevent email spam. The flow must handle email delivery delays and users requesting multiple links.
answer: Flow: user enters email on login page. POST /api/auth/magic-link with {email}. Server: always return 200 (don't reveal if email exists). If email exists: generate token (crypto.randomBytes(32)), store hash in magic_links table (token_hash, email, expires_at, used), send email with link containing token. If email doesn't exist: silently do nothing (or send 'sign up' email). Email: include login URL with token as query parameter. Add expiration warning. Link: https://app.example.com/auth/verify?token=abc123. Verification: GET /auth/verify?token=abc123. Server validates: token exists, not expired, not used. If valid: mark as used, create session/JWT, redirect to app. If invalid: show 'Link expired or invalid, request a new one'. Security: hash tokens before storing (prevent database leak from compromising accounts). Rate limit magic link requests (3 per email per 15 minutes). Use constant-time comparison for token validation. Single-use: mark token as used immediately on verification. If used again, reject. Concurrent requests: if user requests multiple links, all are valid until used or expired. Each generates a new token. Don't invalidate previous tokens on new request (user might click older email). Fallback: allow users to set a password in addition to magic link. On login page, show 'Or sign in with password' option. Accessibility: email should include plain text URL for users who can't click links. UX: show 'Check your email' message after requesting link. Don't auto-redirect (email might be slow). Provide 'Resend' option after 60 seconds.

instruction: Implement a soft delete system with cascading soft deletes, restore functionality, and periodic cleanup. Requirements: mark records as deleted instead of removing them, soft delete related records when parent is deleted, allow restoring deleted records with their relations, and permanently delete records after retention period.
reasoning: Soft deletes prevent accidental data loss but add complexity to every query (must filter deleted records). Cascading soft deletes maintain referential integrity. Restore must handle conflicts (a record with the same unique constraint was created after deletion). Periodic cleanup prevents unbounded growth. The system must integrate with the ORM without requiring changes to every query.
answer: Implementation: add deleted_at (timestamp, nullable) column to all tables that support soft delete. NULL means not deleted. ORM integration: add global scope that filters WHERE deleted_at IS NULL on all queries. Override when explicitly querying deleted records. Soft delete: UPDATE table SET deleted_at = NOW() WHERE id = :id. Don't actually DELETE. Cascading: when parent is soft deleted, soft delete all children. Use database trigger or application logic. Store cascade_group_id to track which records were deleted together (for restore). Restore: UPDATE table SET deleted_at = NULL WHERE id = :id. For cascaded deletes: restore all records with same cascade_group_id. Conflict handling: if unique constraint violated on restore (e.g., email already taken), return error with options (restore with modified value, or permanently delete existing). Querying deleted records: provide withDeleted() scope to include deleted records. Provide onlyDeleted() to see only deleted records. Useful for admin views and trash. Permanent deletion: cron job permanently deletes records where deleted_at < NOW() - interval '90 days'. Use hard DELETE. Log permanently deleted records for audit. Performance: add index on deleted_at for filtered queries. Consider partitioning by deleted_at for large tables. Don't soft delete high-volume tables (use archival instead). Audit: log all soft deletes and restores with user ID and timestamp. UI: show 'Trash' section with deleted records. Allow restore and permanent delete. Show deleted timestamp and who deleted.

instruction: Add database read replicas with automatic failover and query routing. Requirements: route read queries to replicas and write queries to primary, handle replica lag, detect replica health, failover to primary when replicas are unhealthy, and distribute read load across multiple replicas.
reasoning: Read replicas improve read performance but introduce consistency challenges due to replication lag. Query routing must distinguish reads from writes. Some reads require strong consistency (must read from primary after a write). Health detection prevents routing to lagging or down replicas. Load distribution needs weighted round-robin or least-connections. The system must handle replica addition/removal without downtime.
answer: Setup: configure PostgreSQL streaming replication with one primary and 2+ replicas. Replication lag typically <1 second. Query routing: middleware or ORM plugin analyzes queries. SELECT -> replica, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE -> primary. Use separate connection pools for primary and replicas. Consistency: after a write, set a flag (session variable or context) to route subsequent reads to primary for 5 seconds. This handles read-after-write consistency. Alternatively, allow explicit .usePrimary() on queries that need strong consistency. Replica health: ping each replica every 5 seconds. Measure replication lag (pg_stat_replication). Mark replica as unhealthy if lag > 5 seconds or ping fails. Remove from rotation. Re-add when healthy. Load distribution: weighted round-robin. Assign weights based on replica capacity. Or use least-connections algorithm. Failover: if primary fails, promote healthiest replica to primary (automated with tools like Patroni or manually). Update connection strings. Application reconnects to new primary. Multi-region: place replicas in different regions. Route reads to nearest replica based on client geography. Reduces latency for global users. Monitoring: track query distribution (reads vs writes), replica lag, connection pool usage. Alert on high lag or replica failures. Connection pooling: use PgBouncer in front of primary and replicas. Reduces connection overhead. Configure pool sizes appropriately (primary: more connections for writes, replicas: optimized for reads).

instruction: Implement a full-text search with PostgreSQL tsvector that supports searching across multiple tables, ranking results by relevance, highlighting matches, and handling partial matches and typos. The current app uses LIKE queries which are slow and don't support relevance ranking.
reasoning: PostgreSQL full-text search is powerful but requires proper configuration of text search vectors and dictionaries. Multi-table search needs either a unified search index or federated queries. Relevance ranking uses ts_rank with configurable weights per field. Highlighting uses ts_headline. Typo tolerance requires trigram indexes or pg_trgm extension. The search must be fast enough for real-time use.
answer: Search index: create materialized view or separate search_index table combining searchable content from multiple tables. Example: search_index (id, type, title, body, searchable tsvector, metadata jsonb). Populate with triggers on source tables. tsvector creation: combine fields with weights. setweight(to_tsvector('english', title), 'A') || setweight(to_tsvector('english', body), 'B'). Title matches rank higher than body matches. Search query: SELECT *, ts_rank(searchable, query) as rank FROM search_index WHERE searchable @@ query ORDER BY rank DESC LIMIT 20. Parse user query with plainto_tsquery (handles natural language) or websearch_to_tsquery (supports operators). Highlighting: ts_headline('english', body, query, 'StartSel=<mark>, StopSel=</mark>, MaxWords=50, MinWords=20'). Returns text with matches wrapped in <mark> tags. Partial matches: add prefix matching with :* operator. 'run':* matches 'running', 'runner'. Typo tolerance: install pg_trgm extension. Create trigram index: CREATE INDEX idx_search_trgm ON search_index USING gin (title gin_trgm_ops). Use similarity() function or % operator for fuzzy matching. Combine with full-text search: WHERE searchable @@ query OR title % search_term. Performance: GIN index on tsvector column for fast @@ lookups. Limit result set. Use cursor for pagination. Cache common searches. Real-time updates: triggers on source tables update search_index. For high-write tables, update asynchronously via queue. API: GET /api/search?q=query&type=posts&page=1. Return results with highlighted snippets, type, and metadata. Autocomplete: use tsvector prefix matching with LIMIT 5. Debounce input.

instruction: Implement micro-frontends architecture where different teams own different parts of the UI. Requirements: independently deploy frontend modules, share authentication state across modules, handle CSS isolation between modules, provide a shell application that composes modules, and handle cross-module navigation.
reasoning: Micro-frontends enable team autonomy but introduce complexity in composition, state sharing, and styling isolation. Independent deployment requires a mechanism to discover and load modules at runtime. Authentication state must be shared without tight coupling. CSS isolation prevents style conflicts. Cross-module navigation needs to feel seamless despite being separate applications.
answer: Architecture: shell application (host) loads micro-frontends (remotes) at runtime. Use Module Federation (webpack 5) or import maps. Shell provides layout, navigation, authentication. Each micro-frontend is independently built and deployed. Module loading: shell dynamically imports remote entry points. Each micro-frontend exposes components and routes. Shell composes them based on URL routing. Example: /dashboard loads dashboard-mfe, /settings loads settings-mfe. Authentication: shell handles login and stores auth state. Expose auth context via shared module (Module Federation shared scope). Micro-frontends consume shared auth without implementing their own. CSS isolation: each micro-frontend uses CSS modules, CSS-in-JS with unique class names, or Shadow DOM. Avoid global styles. Use CSS custom properties for shared design tokens. Cross-module navigation: use shared router or custom event bus. When navigating between micro-frontends, shell unmounts current and mounts next. Preserve shared state (auth, theme). Shared dependencies: configure Module Federation to share React, React Router, etc. Avoid duplicate React instances. Specify version ranges for compatibility. Error handling: if a micro-frontend fails to load, show error boundary with retry. Don't crash the entire shell. Communication: use custom events or shared state store (Zustand/Redux in shared scope) for cross-module communication. Keep coupling minimal. Deployment: each micro-frontend deploys independently to its own CDN path. Shell fetches remote entry at runtime. Use semantic versioning for shared APIs. Testing: test each micro-frontend in isolation and integrated with shell. Use contract testing for shared interfaces.

instruction: Add a comprehensive design system with composable components, design tokens, and automated visual regression testing. Requirements: create a component library with primitives (Button, Input, Card) and patterns (Form, DataTable, Modal), use design tokens for consistency, generate documentation with live examples, and catch visual regressions in CI.
reasoning: Design systems require careful abstraction to create composable components that work together. Design tokens ensure consistency across components and themes. Documentation with live examples accelerates adoption. Visual regression testing catches unintended style changes. The system must be versioned and published as a package for consumption by multiple applications.
answer: Component architecture: primitives (Button, Input, Select, Checkbox) are building blocks. Patterns (Form, DataTable, Modal) compose primitives. Each component accepts variant, size, and style props. Use compound components for complex patterns (Select with Select.Option). Design tokens: define tokens for colors, spacing, typography, shadows, borders, breakpoints. Store in JSON. Generate CSS custom properties and TypeScript types. Tokens are the single source of truth for design decisions. Component styling: use CSS modules or CSS-in-JS (vanilla-extract, stitches) that reference tokens. Never hardcode colors or spacing. Support theming by swapping token values. Documentation: use Storybook with MDX for documentation pages. Show component API, variants, usage examples, accessibility notes. Auto-generate props table from TypeScript types. Publishing: publish as npm package with semantic versioning. Include TypeScript types, CSS, and ES modules. Use changesets for version management. Visual regression testing: use Chromatic or Percy. Capture screenshots of all Storybook stories on every PR. Compare with baseline. Flag differences for review. Component API: follow consistent patterns. All components accept className, style, and data-testid props. Use forwardRef for DOM access. Support controlled and uncontrolled modes for form components. Accessibility: all components meet WCAG AA. Document accessibility requirements. Test with screen readers and keyboard navigation. Include ARIA attributes. Responsive: components adapt to container size. Use CSS container queries where supported. Provide responsive variants where needed. Performance: tree-shakeable exports. Don't bundle unused components. Use React.memo for expensive components. Testing: unit test component behavior, not implementation. Test accessibility with jest-axe. Test keyboard interactions.

instruction: Implement a GraphQL API with DataLoader for N+1 query prevention, query complexity analysis to prevent abuse, and subscription support for real-time updates. The existing REST API has performance issues due to N+1 queries and doesn't support real-time features.
reasoning: GraphQL solves over-fetching but introduces N+1 query problems without DataLoader. Query complexity analysis prevents malicious or expensive queries from overwhelming the server. Subscriptions require WebSocket infrastructure. The migration from REST must maintain backward compatibility. DataLoader batches and caches database queries within a single request.
answer: GraphQL setup: use Apollo Server or graphql-yoga. Define schema with type definitions and resolvers. Start with core entities (User, Post, Comment) and expand. DataLoader: create loader per entity type per request. Example: userLoader = new DataLoader(async (ids) => { const users = await db.users.findByIds(ids); return ids.map(id => users.find(u => u.id === id)); }). In resolvers: use loader instead of direct DB query. DataLoader batches multiple load() calls in same tick into single query. Caches results within request. N+1 prevention: Post.comments resolver uses commentLoader.loadMany(post.id) instead of querying per post. All comments for all posts in the request are fetched in one query. Query complexity: assign cost to each field (scalar: 1, list: 10, nested: multiply). Calculate total cost before execution. Reject queries exceeding limit (e.g., 1000). Use graphql-query-complexity library. Subscriptions: use graphql-ws protocol over WebSocket. Implement PubSub with Redis adapter for horizontal scaling. Example: subscription onPostCreated publishes when new post is created. Clients subscribe to receive updates in real-time. Authentication: extract user from JWT in context. Pass to resolvers. Check permissions in resolvers or with directives (@auth(role: ADMIN)). Error handling: use Apollo error handling. Map database errors to GraphQL errors with appropriate codes. Don't expose internal errors. Performance: enable query plan caching. Use persisted queries to reduce payload size. Implement automatic persisted queries (APQ). Monitoring: track resolver execution times. Identify slow resolvers. Log query complexity for abuse detection. Migration: run GraphQL alongside REST. Gradually migrate clients. Share business logic between REST controllers and GraphQL resolvers.

instruction: Add API pagination with cursor-based pagination for large datasets and offset-based pagination for admin views. Requirements: support both pagination styles, return pagination metadata (total count, has more, cursor), handle concurrent inserts between page requests, and provide consistent results despite data changes.
reasoning: Cursor-based pagination provides stable results even when data changes between requests, making it ideal for feeds and real-time data. Offset-based pagination is simpler for admin views where users jump to specific pages. Concurrent inserts can cause items to appear on multiple pages or be skipped with offset pagination. The implementation must handle both patterns efficiently.
answer: Cursor-based pagination: use for feeds, search results, user-facing lists. Cursor is an opaque token encoding the last item's sort key (e.g., base64 of {id, created_at}). API: GET /api/posts?limit=20&cursor=eyJpZCI6MTIzfQ. Query: WHERE (created_at, id) < (:cursor_created_at, :cursor_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20. Stable: new posts don't shift existing results. Offset-based pagination: use for admin tables where users need to jump to page 5. API: GET /api/admin/users?page=3&limit=20. Query: OFFSET (page-1)*limit LIMIT 20. Include total count: SELECT COUNT(*) for total pages. Response format: cursor-based: {data: [...], pagination: {hasMore: true, nextCursor: 'abc', previousCursor: 'xyz'}}. Offset-based: {data: [...], pagination: {page: 3, totalPages: 15, totalItems: 295, hasMore: true}}. Concurrent inserts: cursor-based handles this naturally (cursor position is stable). Offset-based: document that results may shift. Use snapshot isolation for consistent reads within a page. Performance: cursor-based needs composite index on (sort_key, id). Offset-based becomes slow for large offsets (OFFSET 100000 scans and discards rows). For large admin tables, consider keyset pagination even for admin views. Edge cases: empty result set (return empty array, hasMore: false). Cursor for first page (omit cursor parameter). Last page (hasMore: false, nextCursor: null). Testing: test with concurrent inserts between page requests. Verify cursor stability.

instruction: Implement a global error handling system that catches errors from API calls, React components, async operations, and unhandled promise rejections. Requirements: categorize errors by severity, show appropriate user feedback, log errors with context, and provide recovery mechanisms without full page reloads.
reasoning: Errors come from many sources and need different handling strategies. API errors might be retryable. Component errors need error boundaries. Async errors in event handlers aren't caught by error boundaries. Unhandled rejections can silently fail. A unified system ensures no error goes unnoticed while providing appropriate user feedback for each type.
answer: Error categories: network errors (retryable), validation errors (user-fixable), authentication errors (redirect to login), authorization errors (show access denied), server errors (show generic message), client errors (log and show feedback). API error handler: axios/fetch interceptor catches all API errors. Categorize by status code. 401: redirect to login. 403: show 'Access denied'. 422: extract field errors, show inline. 500: show 'Something went wrong' with retry. Network error: show 'Connection lost' with retry. React error boundaries: catch render errors. Show fallback UI with retry. Log error with component stack. Async error handling: wrap async event handlers in try/catch. Use custom useAsync hook that catches errors and calls global error handler. Unhandled rejections: window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection'). Log and show generic error. Error UI: toast for transient errors (network, validation). Modal for critical errors (auth expired). Inline for field-level errors. Error boundary for component crashes. Error context: include user ID, URL, action being performed, request/response details. Send to error tracking service (Sentry). Recovery: retry button for network errors. Refresh token for auth errors. Reset component state for render errors. Navigate away for unrecoverable errors. Deduplication: don't show multiple toasts for the same error within 5 seconds. Group similar errors.

instruction: Add optimistic updates with automatic rollback for a task management application. Requirements: immediately update UI on user actions, sync with server in background, rollback on failure, handle conflicts when server state differs, and queue offline mutations for later sync.
reasoning: Optimistic updates improve perceived performance but require careful state management. Rollback must restore exact previous state. Conflicts arise when server state changed between the optimistic update and the server response. Offline queuing requires persistent storage and conflict resolution on sync. The system must handle rapid successive actions on the same entity.
answer: Optimistic update pattern: 1) Capture previous state. 2) Update local state immediately. 3) Send API request. 4) On success: confirm update, discard previous state. 5) On failure: rollback to previous state, show error. Implementation: create useOptimisticMutation hook wrapping React Query's useMutation. onMutate: snapshot current data, update cache optimistically. onError: restore snapshot. onSettled: invalidate queries to refetch. Conflict handling: include version number in update request. Server compares with current version. If mismatch (409): server returns current state. Client shows conflict dialog: 'This task was modified by another user. Keep your changes or use their version?' Rapid actions: if user toggles task status 3 times quickly, only the final state is sent to server. Debounce or use operation queue. Each action cancels previous pending action for same entity. Offline queue: when offline, store mutations in IndexedDB with timestamp and entity info. Show offline indicator. On reconnect: replay queued mutations in order. Handle conflicts during replay (entity may have changed while offline). UI feedback: show subtle animation on optimistic update. Show spinner on entity during sync. Show error state on failure with retry button. Undo: show 'Undo' toast for 5 seconds after action. Clicking undo sends reverse mutation. State reconciliation: periodically refetch data to catch any drift between optimistic state and server state.

instruction: Implement code splitting and lazy loading for a large React application. Requirements: split code by route, lazy load heavy components (charts, editors), prefetch routes on hover, show loading states during code fetch, and measure the impact on initial load time.
reasoning: Code splitting reduces initial bundle size by loading code on demand. Route-based splitting is the highest-impact split. Component-level splitting handles heavy components like chart libraries. Prefetching on hover makes lazy loading feel instant. Loading states prevent blank screens during fetch. The implementation must handle errors (chunk load failures) gracefully.
answer: Route splitting: use React.lazy with dynamic imports for each route. const Dashboard = lazy(() => import('./pages/Dashboard')). Wrap in Suspense with loading fallback. Router: {path: '/dashboard', element: <Suspense fallback={<PageSkeleton />}><Dashboard /></Suspense>}. Component splitting: lazy load heavy components. const Chart = lazy(() => import('./components/Chart')). Use for components not needed on initial render (modals, editors, charts). Prefetching: on link hover or focus, start loading the route. const prefetch = () => import('./pages/Settings'). Use onMouseEnter/onFocus on navigation links. Debounce to avoid rapid prefetches. Loading states: show skeleton matching the page layout during load. Don't show generic spinner (causes layout shift). Chunk load errors: when deployment happens, old chunk URLs return 404. Catch ChunkLoadError, show 'New version available, click to refresh' message. Auto-retry once before showing error. Bundle analysis: use webpack-bundle-analyzer to identify large dependencies. Split moment.js (use date-fns instead), lodash (use individual imports), chart libraries. Preloading: for critical routes (next likely navigation), use <link rel='prefetch'> in HTML head. Build-time analysis can predict common navigation paths. Named chunks: use webpack magic comments for meaningful chunk names. import(/* webpackChunkName: 'dashboard' */ './pages/Dashboard'). This helps with debugging and caching. Measurement: track Time to Interactive (TTI) before and after splitting. Use Lighthouse and real user monitoring (RUM). Target: initial JS < 200KB gzipped. Caching: content-hash in chunk filenames for long-term caching. Shared chunks: webpack extracts common dependencies into shared chunks.

instruction: Add image optimization pipeline that automatically converts uploads to modern formats (WebP/AVIF), generates responsive sizes, creates blur-up placeholders, and serves optimal format based on browser support. The current app serves original uploaded images which are often 5MB+ JPEGs.
reasoning: Image optimization dramatically improves page load times. Modern formats (WebP, AVIF) are 30-50% smaller than JPEG. Responsive images serve appropriate sizes for each device. Blur-up placeholders prevent layout shift and provide visual feedback. Content negotiation serves the best format the browser supports. The pipeline must handle uploads asynchronously without blocking the user.
answer: Upload flow: user uploads image, store original in S3. Queue processing job. Don't block response. Processing pipeline: 1) Generate responsive sizes (thumbnail: 200px, small: 640px, medium: 1024px, large: 1920px, original). 2) Convert each size to WebP and AVIF (with JPEG fallback). 3) Generate tiny blur-up placeholder (20px wide, heavily blurred). Use sharp library for processing. Storage: store all variants in S3 with predictable paths: /images/{id}/{size}.{format}. CDN: serve through CDN with content negotiation. Use Accept header to serve best format. Vary: Accept header for caching. HTML: use element with for each format. . Responsive: use srcset with sizes attribute. srcset='img-640.webp 640w, img-1024.webp 1024w' sizes='(max-width: 640px) 100vw, (max-width: 1024px) 50vw, 33vw'. Browser selects optimal size. Blur-up: load placeholder first (tiny base64 image with CSS blur), then load full image. Fade in when loaded. Lazy loading: use loading='lazy' for below-fold images. Use IntersectionObserver for more control. Don't lazy load above-fold images (hurts LCP). Performance: set explicit width/height to prevent layout shift. Use fetchpriority='high' for LCP image. Monitoring: track image sizes, format distribution, load times. Alert on large images (>1MB).

instruction: Implement Content Security Policy (CSP) headers that prevent XSS attacks while allowing necessary third-party scripts (analytics, payment processors). Requirements: start with report-only mode, gradually tighten policy, handle nonce-based script execution, and set up violation reporting.
reasoning: CSP is one of the most effective XSS defenses but is difficult to implement without breaking existing functionality. Report-only mode allows discovering violations before enforcing. Nonce-based CSP is more secure than hash-based for dynamic content. Third-party scripts need explicit allowlisting. Violation reporting helps identify and fix issues. The policy must be strict enough to be effective while not breaking the application.
answer: CSP implementation: set Content-Security-Policy header on all responses. Start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only to test without blocking. Policy directives: default-src 'self' (only same origin by default). script-src 'self' 'nonce-{random}' https://cdn.example.com (allow self, nonced scripts, specific CDN). style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' (inline styles often needed for CSS-in-JS). img-src 'self' data: https: (allow data URIs and HTTPS images). connect-src 'self' https://api.example.com (API endpoints). frame-src https://checkout.stripe.com (payment iframe). report-uri /api/csp-reports (violation reporting). Nonce generation: generate random nonce per request (crypto.randomBytes(16).toString('base64')). Set in CSP header: script-src 'nonce-{nonce}'. Add nonce attribute to all script tags: <script nonce='{nonce}'>. Server-side rendering must inject same nonce. Inline scripts: avoid inline scripts entirely. If unavoidable, use nonce or hash. 'unsafe-inline' defeats CSP purpose for scripts. Third-party scripts: explicitly allowlist each domain. Use subresource integrity (SRI) hashes for additional security. <script src='https://analytics.example.com/script.js' integrity='sha384-...' crossorigin='anonymous'>. Violation reporting: endpoint receives JSON reports with violated directive, blocked URI, source file, line number. Log and analyze reports. Set up alerts for new violation types. Gradual enforcement: 1) Deploy report-only, collect violations for 1 week. 2) Fix violations (add nonces, update policy). 3) Switch to enforcing mode. 4) Tighten policy over time (remove 'unsafe-inline' when possible).

instruction: Add SQL injection prevention across the application by implementing parameterized queries everywhere, adding input validation middleware, setting up automated SQL injection testing, and creating a query whitelist for dynamic queries. The codebase has a mix of ORM queries and raw SQL with some string concatenation.
reasoning: SQL injection remains one of the most dangerous vulnerabilities. Parameterized queries are the primary defense but raw SQL with string concatenation may exist in legacy code. Input validation provides defense in depth. Automated testing catches regressions. Query whitelisting handles cases where dynamic SQL is necessary (dynamic ORDER BY, column names). The audit must find all vulnerable code paths.
answer: Audit: search codebase for string concatenation in SQL queries. Look for patterns like `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}` or `query += ' AND ' + condition`. Flag all instances for remediation. Parameterized queries: replace all string concatenation with parameterized queries. ORM: use ORM methods (Prisma: prisma.user.findMany({where: {id}})). Raw SQL: use parameter placeholders (pg: db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1', [id])). Never interpolate user input. Input validation: validate all inputs before they reach queries. Type check (ensure ID is integer), range check, whitelist allowed values. Use Zod/Joi schemas. Dynamic queries: when column names or ORDER BY must be dynamic, use whitelist approach. const allowedSortColumns = ['name', 'created_at', 'email']. if (!allowedSortColumns.includes(sortColumn)) throw new Error('Invalid sort column'). Never use user input directly as SQL identifiers. LIKE queries: escape special characters in LIKE patterns. const escaped = searchTerm.replace(/[%_\\]/g, '\\$&'). Automated testing: add SQL injection test cases to CI. Try common payloads (' OR 1=1--, '; DROP TABLE users;--) on all endpoints. Use tools like sqlmap in test environment. ORM safety: even ORMs can be vulnerable if using raw query methods incorrectly. Audit ORM usage for .raw(), .$queryRaw(), or similar escape hatches. Least privilege: database user should have minimum permissions. Application user can't DROP TABLE. Separate users for migrations (DDL) and application (DML). Monitoring: log all database errors. Alert on SQL syntax errors (may indicate injection attempts). Use WAF (Web Application Firewall) as additional layer.

instruction: Implement a zero-downtime deployment strategy using blue-green deployments with database migrations. Requirements: deploy new version alongside old, run database migrations that work with both versions, switch traffic atomically, and rollback instantly if issues are detected.
reasoning: Zero-downtime deployments require both old and new versions to work simultaneously during the transition. Database migrations are the hardest part - they must be backward compatible with the old code still running. Traffic switching must be atomic to avoid partial updates. Rollback must be instant, not require another deployment. Health checks determine when the new version is ready.
answer: Blue-green setup: maintain two identical production environments (blue and green). One serves traffic, one is idle. Deploy new version to idle environment. Database migrations: use expand-contract pattern for breaking changes. Phase 1 (expand): add new column/ table while keeping old. Both old and new code work. Phase 2 (migrate): backfill data in new format. Phase 3 (contract): remove old column/table after new version is stable. Each phase is a separate deployment. Never make breaking changes in a single deployment. Deployment process: 1) Run expand migrations (additive only). 2) Deploy new version to green environment. 3) Run health checks on green (hit /health endpoint, verify database connectivity, check error rates). 4) If healthy: switch load balancer to green (atomic DNS or LB config change). 5) Monitor for 15 minutes. 6) If issues: switch back to blue instantly. 7) After stable: deploy contract migration in next cycle. Health checks: /health endpoint checks database connection, Redis connection, critical dependencies. Returns 200 if healthy, 503 if not. Load balancer only routes to healthy instances. Rollback: keep blue environment running for 1 hour after switch. If issues detected (error rate spike, latency increase), switch load balancer back to blue. Instant rollback, no redeployment needed. Monitoring: compare metrics before and after switch. Error rate, latency, throughput. Auto-rollback if error rate exceeds threshold. Database compatibility: new code must work with old schema (before migration) and new schema (after migration). Use feature flags to control new behavior. Test both scenarios. Connection draining: before switching away from old environment, stop sending new requests, wait for in-flight requests to complete (30 seconds), then shut down.

instruction: Add comprehensive health checks and graceful shutdown to a Node.js API server. Requirements: implement liveness and readiness probes, handle SIGTERM gracefully (finish in-flight requests, close database connections), implement circuit breakers for dependencies, and provide detailed health information for debugging.
reasoning: Health checks enable orchestrators (Kubernetes) to manage application lifecycle. Liveness probes detect deadlocks (restart needed). Readiness probes detect when app can't serve traffic (remove from load balancer). Graceful shutdown prevents dropped requests during deployments. Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures. The implementation must distinguish between different types of health issues.
answer: Liveness probe: GET /health/live. Returns 200 if process is running and not deadlocked. Check: event loop responsiveness (setImmediate callback within 5 seconds), memory usage (not exceeded limit). Don't check external dependencies (a down database shouldn't cause restart). Readiness probe: GET /health/ready. Returns 200 if app can serve traffic. Check: database connection (ping), Redis connection, critical dependencies. Return 503 if any check fails. Include details in response body for debugging. Detailed health: GET /health (internal only). Returns status of all dependencies with latency, last check time, error count. Useful for debugging. Graceful shutdown: listen for SIGTERM (Kubernetes) and SIGINT (manual). On signal: 1) Stop accepting new requests (close server). 2) Wait for in-flight requests to complete (timeout: 30 seconds). 3) Close database connections, Redis connections, message queue connections. 4) Flush pending logs and metrics. 5) Exit with code 0. Force kill after timeout. Implementation: server.close() stops accepting new connections but allows existing to complete. Track active connections. Force close after timeout. Circuit breakers: wrap external service calls with circuit breaker (opossum). States: closed (normal), open (failing, fail fast), half-open (testing recovery). Configure thresholds (5 failures in 1 minute = open, 30 seconds before half-open). When open: return cached response or degraded service. Startup: don't mark as ready until initialization complete (database migrations, cache warming). Use startup probe in Kubernetes for slow-starting apps. Kubernetes configuration: livenessProbe: httpGet /health/live, initialDelaySeconds: 10, periodSeconds: 10. readinessProbe: httpGet /health/ready, initialDelaySeconds: 5, periodSeconds: 5. terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60.

instruction: Implement a complex multi-section form with conditional visibility, cross-field validation, async validation, and auto-save. The form has 5 sections with fields that appear/disappear based on other field values, email uniqueness checking, and must not lose data if the user accidentally navigates away.
reasoning: Conditional visibility requires a dependency graph to determine which fields to show. Cross-field validation needs to consider multiple fields together. Async validation (email uniqueness) needs debouncing and cancellation. Auto-save prevents data loss but must handle conflicts with manual save. Unsaved changes detection prevents accidental navigation. The form state management must handle all these concerns without becoming a tangled mess.
answer: Form library: use react-hook-form with zod resolver. Schema: define with zod, including cross-field validation with .refine(). Conditional visibility: define field dependencies. {fieldId: 'companyName', visibleWhen: {employmentStatus: 'employed'}}. Evaluate on each render. Hide fields that don't meet conditions. Clear hidden field values to prevent submitting irrelevant data. Cross-field validation: zod .refine() for rules involving multiple fields. Example: .refine(data => data.endDate > data.startDate, {message: 'End date must be after start date', path: ['endDate']}). Show error on relevant field. Async validation: for email uniqueness, use zod .refine() with async function. Debounce with useDebounce hook (500ms). Show 'Checking...' state during validation. Cancel pending validation if field value changes (AbortController). Section navigation: show one section at a time with Next/Previous buttons. Validate current section before allowing Next. Show progress indicator. Allow clicking completed sections to edit. Auto-save: save to localStorage every 30 seconds and on field blur. Key by form ID and user session. On mount: check for saved data, prompt to restore. Unsaved changes: use beforeunload event to warn about unsaved changes. Track isDirty state. Custom hook useUnsavedChanges blocks navigation. Submission: on final submit, validate all sections. Send complete data to API. Show loading state. On success: clear auto-save, navigate to success page. On error: show error message, allow retry. Accessibility: associate labels with inputs. Show errors with aria-describedby. Announce section changes. Keyboard navigation between sections.

instruction: Add client-side file validation that checks file type (by magic bytes, not just extension), dimensions (for images), aspect ratio, and content (detect corrupted files). Requirements: validate before upload to save bandwidth, show specific error messages, and handle validation asynchronously without blocking the UI.
reasoning: File type validation by extension alone is insufficient (users can rename files). Magic bytes (file signatures) provide reliable type detection. Image dimension and aspect ratio validation requires loading the image, which is asynchronous. Corrupted file detection prevents server-side processing errors. All validation must happen without blocking the UI thread for large files.
answer: File type validation: read first 4-12 bytes of file (magic bytes). Compare against known signatures: JPEG (FF D8 FF), PNG (89 50 4E 47), PDF (25 50 44 46), GIF (47 49 46 38). Use file-type library for comprehensive detection. Compare detected type with extension. Reject mismatches. Dimension validation: for images, create Image object with URL.createObjectURL(file). On load: check width and height against constraints (min: 100x100, max: 5000x5000). Revoke object URL after. Aspect ratio: calculate width/height, compare with allowed ratios (e.g., 16:9 ± 0.1). Show preview with crop suggestion if aspect ratio is wrong. Size validation: check file.size against max (10MB). Show human-readable size in error message. Content validation: for images, check if image loads successfully (corrupted files fail to load). For PDFs, check if first page renders. For videos, check if metadata loads. Async validation: run validations in Web Worker to avoid blocking UI. Show progress indicator during validation. Return results via postMessage. Validation pipeline: run validations in sequence. Stop on first error (or collect all errors). Show specific error messages: 'File is not a valid JPEG', 'Image must be at least 100x100 pixels', 'File is corrupted and cannot be uploaded'. UI: show file preview after successful validation. Show validation status (checking, valid, invalid). Allow removing and re-selecting file. Batch validation: for multiple files, validate in parallel (up to 3 at a time). Show progress for each file. Security: validate on server too (client validation is UX, not security). Server re-checks magic bytes and dimensions.

instruction: Implement a mobile-first responsive navigation with bottom tab bar on mobile, side drawer on tablet, and top navigation bar on desktop. Requirements: share navigation state across layouts, handle orientation changes, support swipe gestures on mobile, and maintain scroll position when switching between layouts.
reasoning: Different screen sizes need fundamentally different navigation patterns, not just resized versions. Sharing navigation state across layouts prevents losing the user's place. Orientation changes can trigger layout switches. Swipe gestures provide native-like experience on mobile. Scroll position maintenance prevents jarring UX when resizing between breakpoints.
answer: Breakpoints: mobile (<768px): bottom tab bar. Tablet (768-1024px): side drawer. Desktop (>1024px): top navigation bar. Shared state: navigation context tracks current route, open/closed state for drawer, selected tab. All layouts read from and write to the same context. Bottom tab bar: fixed at bottom, 4-5 main sections with icons and labels. Highlight active tab. Safe area inset for notched phones (env(safe-area-inset-bottom)). Side drawer: hamburger menu opens drawer from left. Overlay backdrop. Swipe right from left edge to open (use react-swipeable). Swipe left to close. Top navigation: horizontal menu with dropdowns for nested items. Show user menu on right. Responsive switching: use CSS media queries for layout, but also use useMediaQuery hook for JavaScript logic (which layout to render). When switching layouts (e.g., resizing from mobile to desktop), maintain current route and scroll position. Scroll position: save scroll position per route in context. When layout changes, restore scroll position for current route. Swipe gestures: on mobile, swipe between tabs (swipe left for next tab, right for previous). Use framer-motion for gesture handling and animations. Accessibility: bottom tab bar: role='tablist', each tab role='tab', aria-selected. Side drawer: trap focus when open, close on Escape. Top nav: keyboard navigation with arrow keys. Performance: render only the active layout. Don't render hidden layouts. Use CSS for simple show/hide, conditional rendering for fundamentally different layouts. Testing: test on real devices, not just browser resize. Test with different viewport sizes and orientations.

instruction: Add pull-to-refresh, infinite scroll, and swipe actions to a mobile list view. Requirements: pull-to-refresh with visual feedback and momentum, infinite scroll with prefetching, swipe left for delete and swipe right for archive, and handle all gestures without conflicts.
reasoning: Mobile gestures require careful implementation to feel native. Pull-to-refresh needs to track touch movement and show progress. Infinite scroll needs IntersectionObserver with prefetch threshold. Swipe actions need to track horizontal movement while allowing vertical scroll. Gesture conflicts (swipe vs scroll) need threshold-based resolution. All features must work together without interfering with each other.
answer: Pull-to-refresh: track touchstart, touchmove, touchend. On touchstart at top of list: record start Y. On touchmove: calculate pull distance (currentY - startY). Show refresh indicator that grows with pull distance. Apply CSS transform: translateY(pullDistance * 0.5) to list (dampening factor). On touchend: if pull distance > 80px, trigger refresh. Otherwise, animate back. Refresh: show spinner, fetch new data, prepend to list, animate back to top. Infinite scroll: IntersectionObserver on sentinel element at end of list. When visible: fetch next page. Prefetch: trigger fetch when user is 5 items from end (not at end). Show loading indicator at bottom. Handle end of list (no more data). Swipe actions: use touch events or library (react-swipeable-list). Track horizontal movement. If horizontal movement > vertical movement and > 30px threshold: activate swipe mode. Show action buttons (delete on left, archive on right) as user swipes. On release: if swiped > 50% of item width, execute action with animation. Otherwise, snap back. Gesture conflict resolution: determine gesture direction within first 20px of movement. If vertical: scroll. If horizontal: swipe action. Lock direction until gesture ends. Visual feedback: rubber-band effect at list boundaries. Haptic feedback on action execution (navigator.vibrate). Accessibility: provide non-gesture alternatives. Long-press for action menu. Buttons for refresh. Performance: use CSS transforms for animations (GPU accelerated). Use will-change: transform. Debounce scroll events. Memoize list items.

instruction: Implement a live cursor tracking feature showing other users' mouse positions on a shared canvas. Requirements: broadcast cursor position at 60fps without overwhelming the WebSocket server, interpolate remote cursors for smooth movement, show user name labels, and handle 100+ concurrent cursors.
reasoning: High-frequency cursor updates can overwhelm WebSocket servers if sent naively. Throttling reduces bandwidth while interpolation maintains smooth visual experience on the receiving end. With many concurrent cursors, rendering performance becomes critical. The system must balance update frequency with server load.
answer: Throttling: send cursor position every 50ms (20fps) instead of every mousemove event (60fps+). Use requestAnimationFrame to batch updates. Interpolation: on receive, store target position and current position. Use requestAnimationFrame to lerp (linear interpolate) current toward target. This smooths out the 20fps updates to appear as 60fps. WebSocket: use binary protocol (ArrayBuffer) instead of JSON for cursor updates. Format: [userId(4bytes), x(4bytes float), y(4bytes float)]. 12 bytes per update vs 50+ bytes JSON. Server: broadcast cursor updates to all users in the same room. Use Redis pub/sub for multi-server. Don't persist cursor positions (ephemeral data). Rendering: use HTML5 Canvas for cursor rendering (not DOM elements). 100+ DOM elements with frequent updates causes layout thrashing. Canvas redraws are much faster. Draw colored cursor triangles with name labels. Culling: only render cursors within viewport. Skip off-screen cursors. User colors: assign deterministic color from user ID hash. Consistent color across sessions. Disconnect handling: remove cursor on WebSocket disconnect. Fade out animation before removal. Performance: limit to 50 visible cursors. Show '+50 more' indicator for larger groups.

instruction: Add a real-time presence system showing which users are online and what page they're viewing. Requirements: detect user online/offline status accurately, show last active time, handle multiple tabs/devices per user, and scale to 10,000 concurrent users.
reasoning: Presence detection is deceptively complex. Users may have multiple tabs or devices. A user is 'online' if any tab is active. Heartbeat-based detection must balance accuracy with server load. 'Last active' needs to distinguish between active interaction and idle tabs. The system must handle network blips without marking users as offline.
answer: Heartbeat: each active tab sends heartbeat every 30 seconds via WebSocket. Server maintains presence in Redis: HSET presence:{userId} tab:{tabId} {timestamp}. User is online if any tab heartbeat is within 60 seconds. Multi-tab: each tab has unique tabId (crypto.randomUUID()). On tab close: send goodbye message, remove tab from Redis. On browser close: all tabs send goodbye (use sendBeacon for reliability). Idle detection: use visibility API and user interaction events. If tab is hidden and no interaction for 5 minutes, stop heartbeat (mark as idle). Resume on interaction. Presence API: GET /api/presence?userIds=1,2,3 returns {1: {status: 'online', lastActive: '...', currentPage: '/dashboard'}, 2: {status: 'offline', lastActive: '2 hours ago'}}. Batch queries for efficiency. Page tracking: include current page path in heartbeat. Show 'Viewing /projects' in presence info. Rate limit page change updates. Scaling: Redis can handle millions of presence keys. Use Redis keyspace notifications for presence changes (subscribe to key expiry events). WebSocket broadcasts presence changes to subscribed clients. Offline detection: Redis key expiry (TTL 60 seconds on heartbeat key). When key expires, user is offline. Use keyspace notifications to detect expiry and broadcast. UI: green dot for online, yellow for idle, gray for offline. Show 'Active now', 'Active 5m ago', 'Active 2h ago'. Click to see all active devices.

instruction: Implement a webhook retry system with exponential backoff, dead letter queue, and delivery dashboard. Requirements: retry failed webhook deliveries with increasing delays, move permanently failed deliveries to a dead letter queue, provide a dashboard showing delivery status, and allow manual retry of failed deliveries.
reasoning: Webhook delivery must be reliable without blocking the main application. Exponential backoff prevents overwhelming failing endpoints. Dead letter queues capture permanently failed deliveries for manual inspection. The dashboard helps developers debug integration issues. The system must handle millions of deliveries without data loss.
answer: Delivery queue: use Bull (Redis-based job queue) for webhook delivery jobs. On event: create delivery job for each subscribed webhook. Job includes URL, payload, attempt number. Delivery: POST to webhook URL with JSON payload and X-Webhook-Signature header. Timeout: 10 seconds. Consider 2xx as success, anything else as failure. Retry: on failure, schedule retry with exponential backoff: 1min, 5min, 30min, 2hr, 24hr (5 attempts). Add jitter (±20%) to prevent thundering herd. Use Bull's built-in retry with backoff strategy. Dead letter queue: after 5 failed attempts, move to DLQ (separate Bull queue). Store full delivery record: URL, payload, all attempt results (status code, response body, error, timestamp). Dashboard: list webhook endpoints with delivery stats (success rate, avg latency). Drill into individual deliveries. Filter by status (delivered, failed, pending). Show timeline of attempts with request/response details. Manual retry: button to retry failed delivery immediately. Bulk retry for multiple failures. Webhook management: create/edit/delete webhooks. Test delivery button sends sample event. Show signing secret with copy button. Pause/resume webhooks. Monitoring: alert on high failure rates (>10% in last hour). Track delivery latency percentiles. Performance: process deliveries in background workers. Scale workers based on queue length. Don't block application. Security: validate URL is HTTPS in production. Prevent SSRF (don't allow internal IPs). Rate limit deliveries per endpoint.

instruction: Add a comprehensive request logging middleware that captures request/response details, masks sensitive data, calculates request duration, and sends logs to a centralized logging service. Requirements: log all API requests with method, path, status, duration, user ID, and IP. Mask passwords, tokens, and credit card numbers in request/response bodies.
reasoning: Request logging provides visibility into API usage and helps debug issues. Sensitive data masking is critical for security and compliance. Duration calculation helps identify slow endpoints. Centralized logging enables searching across all server instances. The middleware must add minimal latency to request processing.
answer: Middleware: add as first middleware in Express/Fastify chain. On request: record start time (process.hrtime.bigint()), generate request ID (UUID), attach to request object and response header (X-Request-ID). Log request: method, path, query params, user ID (from auth middleware), IP address (from X-Forwarded-For or req.ip). Mask sensitive fields in request body. On response: intercept res.end to capture status code and response body. Calculate duration. Log response: status, duration, response size. Mask sensitive fields. Sensitive data masking: define patterns to mask. Passwords: any field named password, passwd, secret, token, api_key, authorization. Replace value with '[MASKED]'. Credit cards: regex for card number patterns (\d{4}[- ]?\d{4}[- ]?\d{4}[- ]?\d{4}). Replace with '[CARD]'. Email/phone: optionally mask PII for privacy. Use recursive object walker to mask nested fields. Structured logging: output JSON logs with consistent schema. {level: 'info', timestamp, requestId, method, path, status, duration, userId, ip, requestBody (masked), responseBody (masked)}. Centralized logging: send logs to ELK stack (Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana) or Datadog. Use winston or pino logger with transport to logging service. Buffer logs and flush in batches for performance. Performance: logging must add <1ms to request latency. Use async logging (pino is fastest). Don't log response bodies for large responses (>10KB). Sampling: in production, log 100% of errors, 10% of successful requests. Reduces log volume and cost. Correlation: request ID flows through all services. Include in all logs for a request. Enables tracing request flow across microservices. Dashboard: Kibana/Datadog dashboards showing request rate, error rate, latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99), top endpoints by traffic, top errors.

instruction: Implement a database query caching layer that caches query results in Redis with automatic invalidation on writes. Requirements: cache SELECT query results, invalidate cache when related data is modified, support cache tags for bulk invalidation, and handle cache stampedes.
reasoning: Database query caching reduces load on the database and improves response times. Automatic invalidation ensures cached data stays consistent with the database. Cache tags enable efficient bulk invalidation (e.g., invalidate all post-related caches when a post is updated). Cache stampedes occur when many requests simultaneously miss an expired cache entry, overwhelming the database.
answer: Cache layer: wrap database query methods with caching logic. Before query: check Redis for cached result. On hit: return cached result. On miss: execute query, store result in Redis with TTL, return result. Cache key: generate from query parameters. Hash the SQL + parameters: cache:query:{hash}. TTL: 5 minutes for frequently changing data, 1 hour for rarely changing data. Cache tags: associate cache entries with tags. Example: post query tagged with ['posts', 'post:123']. Store tag->keys mapping in Redis sets. On invalidation: get all keys for tag, delete them. Use Redis SADD for tag sets, SMEMBERS to get keys. Automatic invalidation: on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, determine affected tables and entities. Invalidate related cache tags. Example: UPDATE posts SET title='...' WHERE id=123 invalidates tags ['posts', 'post:123']. Use ORM hooks (afterSave, afterUpdate) to trigger invalidation. Cache stampede prevention: use mutex (Redlock) so only one request executes the query while others wait. Or use stale-while-revalidate: return stale cached data while refreshing in background. Probabilistic early expiration: refresh cache before TTL with increasing probability as expiry approaches. Selective caching: don't cache everything. Cache: frequently accessed read queries, expensive aggregations, rarely changing data. Don't cache: personalized queries, real-time data, queries with high write frequency. Monitoring: track cache hit rate, miss rate, eviction rate. Alert on low hit rates (<50%). Log cache operations for debugging. Invalidation debugging: log what was invalidated and why. Performance: use Redis pipeline for batch operations. Compress large cached results (gzip). Use Redis connection pooling.
