instruction: Add a data table with server-side sorting, filtering, and pagination that preserves user selections across page changes. Requirements: sort by clicking column headers, filter with text search and dropdown filters, paginate with page size selection, and maintain row selections when navigating between pages.
reasoning: Server-side data operations are needed for large datasets that can't be loaded client-side. Sorting, filtering, and pagination must work together (filter first, then sort, then paginate). Row selections must persist across page changes, requiring tracking selected IDs separately from visible rows. The URL should reflect the current state for shareability.
answer: State management: track {sort: {column, direction}, filters: {search, status, dateRange}, pagination: {page, pageSize}, selectedIds: Set<string>}. Sync to URL params for shareability and browser back/forward support. API: GET /api/items?sort=name:asc&search=john&status=active&page=2&pageSize=20. Response: {data: [...], meta: {total, page, pageSize, totalPages}}. Sorting: click column header to sort. First click: ascending. Second click: descending. Third click: no sort. Show sort indicator (▲/▼) on header. Only one column sorted at a time. Send sort params to API. Filtering: text search input with debounce (300ms). Dropdown filters for enum fields (status, category). Date range picker for date fields. Apply filters: reset to page 1 when filters change. Pagination: page size selector (10, 20, 50, 100). Page navigation (first, prev, next, last, page numbers). Show 'Showing 21-40 of 1,234 results'. Row selection: checkbox column. Header checkbox selects/deselects all visible rows. Track selectedIds as Set (not array) for O(1) lookup. Persist across page changes: selectedIds maintained in state, not cleared on page change. Show 'X rows selected' with 'Select all 1,234' option. Bulk actions: show action bar when rows selected (delete, export, change status). Confirm before destructive actions. Performance: debounce search input. Cancel previous API request on new sort/filter/page (AbortController). Use React.memo for table rows. Virtualize for 1000+ visible rows. Accessibility: table with proper headers, scope attributes. Keyboard navigation between cells. Announce sort changes and page changes to screen readers.

instruction: Implement a color picker component that supports hex, RGB, and HSL input, shows a color palette with recent colors, provides contrast ratio checking against a background color, and integrates with the form's validation system.
reasoning: Color pickers require converting between color spaces (hex, RGB, HSL). The visual picker needs hue/saturation/brightness controls. Recent colors improve workflow. Contrast ratio checking ensures accessibility compliance. Form integration requires the component to work with form state management libraries. The component must handle invalid color inputs gracefully.
answer: Color model: store color internally as HSL for easy manipulation. Convert to/from hex and RGB for display. Use a color conversion library (colord) or implement conversion functions. Picker UI: saturation/brightness square (2D gradient) with hue slider. Click/drag to select. Show color preview swatch. Input modes: hex input (#FF5733), RGB inputs (R: 255, G: 87, B: 51), HSL inputs (H: 11°, S: 100%, L: 60%). Switch between modes with tabs. Validate inputs (hex: 6 chars, RGB: 0-255, HSL: H 0-360, S/L 0-100%). Color palette: show preset colors (brand colors, material design palette). Show recent colors (last 10 used, stored in localStorage). Click to select. Contrast checking: accept backgroundColor prop. Calculate contrast ratio using WCAG formula: (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05) where L is relative luminance. Show ratio and pass/fail for AA (4.5:1) and AAA (7:1). Show warning icon if contrast is insufficient. Form integration: implement as controlled component with value and onChange props. Support react-hook-form (register), formik (field), and native forms. Validation: integrate with form validation schema. Example: zod.string().refine(isValidHex, 'Invalid color'). Accessibility: keyboard controls for picker (arrow keys adjust hue/saturation/brightness). ARIA labels for all inputs. Screen reader announces color value changes. High contrast mode support. Performance: debounce color conversion calculations. Use requestAnimationFrame for smooth dragging. Memoize color conversions.

instruction: Add a toast notification system with stacking, auto-dismiss, pause on hover, action buttons, and different severity levels. Requirements: show multiple toasts stacked vertically, auto-dismiss after configurable duration, pause timer on hover, support undo actions, and handle screen reader announcements.
reasoning: Toast notifications need careful state management for stacking and timing. Auto-dismiss timers must pause on hover to prevent missed notifications. Action buttons (undo, retry) require maintaining references to callback functions. Different severity levels need distinct visual treatment and dismiss behavior. Screen reader support requires ARIA live regions.
answer: Toast state: array of {id, type: 'success'|'error'|'warning'|'info', message, action?: {label, onClick}, duration, createdAt}. Manage with context provider and useToast hook. Stacking: render toasts in fixed container (bottom-right). Each toast positioned with CSS (stack from bottom, newest on top). Animate entry (slide in from right) and exit (fade out). Auto-dismiss: setTimeout on mount. Duration: success 3s, info 4s, warning 5s, error manual dismiss. Clear timeout on unmount. Pause on hover: onMouseEnter clears timeout. onMouseLeave restarts with remaining duration (track elapsed time). Action buttons: toast can include action {label: 'Undo', onClick: undoFn}. Render button in toast. Click executes callback and dismisses toast. API: toast.success('Item saved'), toast.error('Failed to save', {action: {label: 'Retry', onClick: retry}}), toast.info('New version available', {duration: 10000}). Update existing: const id = toast.loading('Saving...'); toast.success('Saved!', {id}). Deduplication: don't show duplicate messages within 2 seconds. Group similar notifications. Limit: max 3 visible toasts. Queue additional toasts. Show when space available. Accessibility: container has role='region' aria-label='Notifications'. Each toast has role='status' (info/success) or role='alert' (error/warning). aria-live='polite' for non-urgent, 'assertive' for errors. Screen reader announces toast content. Keyboard: Escape dismisses focused toast. Tab navigates between toasts and action buttons. Swipe to dismiss on mobile.

instruction: Implement a brute force protection system that locks accounts after failed login attempts, implements progressive delays, sends security notifications, and provides account unlock mechanisms. Requirements: track failed attempts per account and per IP, lock after 5 failures, implement exponential delay between attempts, and send email alerts.
reasoning: Brute force protection requires tracking at both account and IP levels. Progressive delays slow down attackers without significantly impacting legitimate users. Security notifications alert users to potential attacks. Account unlock must balance security (not too easy) with usability (not too hard). The system must handle distributed attacks from many IPs.
answer: Tracking: failed_logins table (id, email, ip_address, attempted_at, user_agent). Track per-email and per-IP separately. Rate limiting: per-email: after 3 failures, add 5 second delay between attempts. After 5 failures, lock account for 15 minutes. After 10 failures, lock for 1 hour. Per-IP: after 20 failures from same IP in 1 hour, block IP for 24 hours. Progressive delay: calculate delay based on recent failure count. delay = min(base_delay * 2^(failures-3), max_delay). Sleep before responding to login attempt. Don't reveal whether delay is due to lockout or progressive delay (prevent username enumeration). Account lock: set locked_until timestamp on user record. On login attempt: if locked_until > NOW(), return generic 'Invalid credentials' (don't reveal lockout). Show 'Account locked, try again in X minutes' only after successful password reset. Security notifications: on account lock, send email to account owner: 'We detected multiple failed login attempts on your account. If this wasn't you, change your password immediately.' Include IP address, location, and timestamp. On IP block: log for security team review. Account unlock: user can unlock by verifying email (click link sent to registered email). Or admin can unlock from admin panel. CAPTCHA: after 3 failed attempts, require CAPTCHA on next attempt. Use reCAPTCHA v3 (invisible) or hCaptcha. Distributed attack detection: if same email has failures from 10+ different IPs in 1 hour, trigger additional protection (require email verification on next login). Monitoring: dashboard showing failed login attempts by email and IP. Alert on unusual patterns. Fail2ban integration for server-level IP blocking.

instruction: Add CSRF protection using the double-submit cookie pattern with SameSite attributes. Requirements: generate CSRF tokens, validate tokens on state-changing requests, handle token rotation, support both form submissions and AJAX requests, and provide clear error messages for CSRF failures.
reasoning: CSRF attacks trick authenticated users into making unintended requests. The double-submit cookie pattern sends a token in both a cookie and a request header/body, which an attacker can't do cross-origin. SameSite cookie attributes provide additional protection. Token rotation prevents token reuse. The implementation must work with both traditional forms and modern AJAX applications.
answer: Token generation: on session creation, generate CSRF token (crypto.randomBytes(32)). Set as cookie: _csrf=token; SameSite=Strict; Secure; HttpOnly=false (needs to be readable by JS). Also store hash in session server-side. AJAX requests: client reads _csrf cookie, includes token in X-CSRF-Token header. Server compares header token with cookie token. If match: request is legitimate (attacker can't read cookies cross-origin). Form submissions: include token as hidden field <input type='hidden' name='_csrf' value='token'>. Server validates field matches cookie. SameSite: set SameSite=Strict on session cookie and CSRF cookie. Prevents cross-site requests from including cookies. For cross-site use cases (e.g., embedded widgets), use SameSite=Lax with additional CSRF protection. Token rotation: generate new token after each successful state-changing request. Prevents token reuse if leaked. Update both cookie and session. Error handling: on CSRF validation failure, return 403 with clear message: 'Security validation failed. Please refresh the page and try again.' Log CSRF failures for security monitoring. Don't reveal whether it was CSRF or session issue. Exemptions: exempt safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) from CSRF check. Exempt webhook endpoints (use signature verification instead). Exempt API endpoints using token authentication (Bearer tokens are not sent cross-origin). Testing: test CSRF protection in integration tests. Verify state-changing requests without token are rejected. Verify cross-origin requests are blocked. Monitoring: track CSRF failure rate. Spike may indicate attack or implementation issue.

instruction: Implement a service worker that caches API responses, serves stale content while revalidating, and handles offline mode with a fallback page. Requirements: cache static assets with cache-first strategy, cache API responses with stale-while-revalidate, show offline page when network is unavailable, and handle service worker updates.
reasoning: Service workers intercept network requests and can serve cached responses. Different strategies suit different content types: cache-first for static assets (immutable), stale-while-revalidate for API responses (show cached while fetching fresh), network-first for dynamic content. Offline fallback improves UX when network is unavailable. Service worker updates must be handled carefully to avoid serving stale code.
answer: Service worker registration: in main.js, register service worker if supported. navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js'). Use Workbox library for common patterns. Static assets: use CacheFirst strategy. Cache JS, CSS, images, fonts on first request. Serve from cache on subsequent requests. Cache name includes content hash, so updates create new cache entries. Precache critical assets during service worker install event. API responses: use StaleWhileRevalidate strategy. On request: return cached response immediately (if exists), then fetch from network and update cache. This provides instant response while keeping data fresh. Set max cache age (1 hour) and max entries (50) per API endpoint. Network-first for auth endpoints (always need fresh tokens). Offline fallback: on network failure (fetch throws), check if request is for HTML page. If yes: return cached offline.html page. If API: return cached response or error JSON. Precache offline.html during install. Service worker updates: browser checks for updates on navigation. When new service worker is found: it installs but waits (doesn't activate until all tabs using old SW are closed). To force update: self.skipWaiting() in new SW, clients.claim() on activate. Show 'Update available' banner when new SW waiting. Click to reload and activate. Cache management: version caches (v1, v2). On activate: delete old cache versions. Monitor cache storage usage (navigator.storage.estimate). Request persistent storage. Debugging: use Chrome DevTools Application tab to inspect caches, service worker state, and network requests. Unregister SW for testing. Scope: service worker controls requests within its scope (usually /). Be specific about which URLs to intercept. Performance: service worker adds ~5ms overhead per request. Don't intercept requests that don't need caching.

instruction: Add bundle analysis and optimization to reduce JavaScript bundle size by 50%. Requirements: identify large dependencies, implement tree shaking, use dynamic imports for route-based code splitting, replace heavy libraries with lighter alternatives, and set up CI checks to prevent bundle size regression.
reasoning: Large JavaScript bundles slow down page load, especially on mobile networks. Bundle analysis identifies the biggest contributors. Tree shaking removes unused code but requires ES module syntax. Code splitting loads only what's needed for the current route. Library replacement can dramatically reduce size (moment.js 300KB -> date-fns 30KB). CI checks prevent future regressions.
answer: Analysis: use webpack-bundle-analyzer or source-map-explorer to visualize bundle contents. Identify largest modules. Common offenders: moment.js (300KB), lodash (500KB full), chart.js (200KB), material-ui icons (all icons). Tree shaking: ensure all imports use ES module syntax (import {x} from 'y', not import y from 'y'). Set sideEffects: false in package.json for tree-shakeable packages. Configure webpack/rollup for tree shaking (production mode). Code splitting: use React.lazy for route-based splitting. const Dashboard = lazy(() => import('./pages/Dashboard')). Each route becomes separate chunk. Use dynamic imports for heavy components: const Chart = lazy(() => import('./components/Chart')). Library replacements: moment.js -> date-fns (tree-shakeable, 30KB). lodash -> lodash-es or individual imports (import debounce from 'lodash/debounce'). Full icon library -> only import used icons. chart.js -> recharts or lightweight alternative. Polyfills: use @babel/preset-env with useBuiltIns: 'usage' to only include polyfills actually needed. Don't include polyfills for modern browsers. Serve modern bundle to modern browsers (module/nomodule pattern). Compression: enable Brotli compression on server (30% smaller than gzip). Pre-compress static assets at build time. CDN serves pre-compressed files. CI checks: use bundlesize or size-limit package. Define budget per chunk: {path: './dist/main.js', maxSize: '200KB gzipped'}. Fail CI if exceeded. Track bundle size over time in CI dashboard. Caching: use content-hash in filenames for long-term caching. Split vendor chunk (changes less frequently than app code). Lazy load: defer non-critical JavaScript. Load analytics, chat widgets, etc. after page is interactive. Use requestIdleCallback for non-urgent scripts.

instruction: Implement a database migration system that supports rolling deployments where old and new code versions run simultaneously. Requirements: migrations must be backward compatible, support expand-contract pattern for schema changes, provide rollback scripts, and handle concurrent migration execution.
reasoning: Rolling deployments mean old and new code versions run simultaneously during deployment. Database migrations must work with both versions. The expand-contract pattern adds new structures first (expand), migrates data, then removes old structures (contract) in separate deployments. Concurrent migration execution can cause conflicts if multiple instances try to migrate simultaneously. Rollback scripts must be tested and reliable.
answer: Migration tool: use Knex migrations, Prisma migrate, or custom solution. Migrations are versioned files with up() and down() functions. Tracking: migrations table records which migrations have been applied. Check before running to avoid duplicates. Locking: use database advisory locks (PostgreSQL) or distributed locks (Redis) to prevent concurrent migration execution. Only one instance runs migrations. Expand-contract pattern: for renaming a column: Deployment 1 (expand): add new column, copy data from old to new, update code to write to both columns and read from new. Deployment 2 (migrate): backfill any remaining old data. Deployment 3 (contract): remove old column, update code to only use new column. Each deployment is independently deployable and rollback-safe. Backward compatibility: every migration must work with both old and new code. Adding a column: make it nullable or provide default. Old code ignores it, new code uses it. Removing a column: stop using it in code first (deploy), then remove in migration (next deploy). Adding a NOT NULL column: add as nullable, backfill, then add constraint. Rollback: every migration has a down() function that reverses the change. Test rollbacks in staging. For data migrations, keep backup of original data. Execution: run migrations before deploying new code (in CI/CD pipeline). If migration fails, don't deploy new code. Alert team. Large table migrations: for tables with millions of rows, don't use ALTER TABLE (locks table). Use pt-online-schema-change or gh-ost for online schema changes. Backfill data in batches with sleep between batches. Monitoring: log all migrations with duration and affected rows. Alert on long-running migrations. Dashboard showing migration history.

instruction: Add a connection pool monitoring and auto-tuning system for PostgreSQL. Requirements: monitor pool utilization, detect connection leaks, auto-adjust pool size based on load, alert on pool exhaustion, and provide recommendations for query optimization.
reasoning: Connection pool exhaustion causes application-wide outages. Monitoring pool utilization helps identify issues before they become critical. Connection leaks (connections not returned to pool) gradually exhaust available connections. Auto-tuning adjusts pool size based on actual usage patterns. Query optimization recommendations help reduce connection hold time.
answer: Pool instrumentation: wrap pg-pool with event listeners. Track: total connections, idle connections, active connections, waiting requests, connection checkout duration, connection lifetime. Expose metrics via Prometheus endpoint (/metrics). Leak detection: track when each connection was checked out. If held for >30 seconds, log warning with stack trace of checkout location. This identifies code paths that don't release connections. Common causes: missing await, error paths that don't release, long-running queries. Auto-tuning: monitor pool utilization over time. If utilization consistently >80%, increase pool size. If consistently <20%, decrease. Adjust in steps (±2 connections). Min: 5, Max: 50. Apply changes without restart (pg-pool supports dynamic resizing). Alerting: alert when active connections >90% of pool size. Alert when wait queue >5 requests. Alert when connection checkout time >1 second. Send to PagerDuty/Slack with actionable information. Query optimization: track query duration per connection. Log queries taking >1 second with EXPLAIN plan. Identify top 10 slowest query patterns. Suggest indexes based on sequential scans in EXPLAIN output. Dashboard: real-time pool utilization gauge. Connection checkout time histogram. Active queries table (query text, duration, user). Slow query log with EXPLAIN plans. Recommendations. Configuration: provide recommended pool size based on formula: connections = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count). For SSD: connections = core_count * 2. Monitor actual usage and adjust. Health check: include pool status in /health endpoint. If pool exhausted, return 503 (unhealthy). Load balancer stops sending traffic. Integration: expose metrics in Prometheus format. Create Grafana dashboards. Set up alerts in AlertManager. Correlate pool metrics with application latency.

instruction: Implement a global state management solution using Zustand that handles server state, UI state, and form state separately. Requirements: use React Query for server state, Zustand for UI state, React Hook Form for form state, and provide clear guidelines for when to use each.
reasoning: Mixed state types in a single store leads to unnecessary re-renders and complex logic. Server state (API data) has different requirements (caching, invalidation) than UI state (theme, sidebar). Form state is transient and component-specific. Using the right tool for each state type improves performance and maintainability. Clear guidelines prevent confusion.
answer: State categorization: Server state: data from API (users, posts, settings). Use React Query (useQuery, useMutation). Provides caching, background refetching, optimistic updates, loading/error states. UI state: app-wide UI state (theme, sidebar open, active modal). Use Zustand. Persists across navigation, not tied to API. Form state: form field values, validation, submission. Use React Hook Form. Component-specific, cleared on unmount. Zustand store: create separate slices for different UI concerns. const useUIStore = create((set) => ({theme: 'light', toggleTheme: () => set(s => ({theme: s.theme === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light'})), sidebarOpen: true, toggleSidebar: () => set(s => ({sidebarOpen: !s.sidebarOpen})), activeModal: null, openModal: (id) => set({activeModal: id}), closeModal: () => set({activeModal: null})})). Selectors: use selectors to prevent unnecessary re-renders. const theme = useUIStore(s => s.theme). Only re-renders when theme changes, not when other state changes. React Query: configure QueryClient with defaults. staleTime: 5 minutes, cacheTime: 30 minutes. Use query keys consistently: ['users', {page: 1}]. Invalidate on mutations. React Hook Form: use per-form. Register fields, handle validation, manage submission. Clear on unmount. Guidelines: document when to use each. Server data -> React Query. UI preferences -> Zustand. Form inputs -> React Hook Form. Local component state -> useState. Performance: Zustand selectors prevent re-renders. React Query caches prevent refetches. React Hook Form uses uncontrolled inputs for performance. DevTools: Zustand devtools middleware for state inspection. React Query DevTools for cache inspection. Persist UI state: use Zustand persist middleware to save theme, sidebar state to localStorage.

instruction: Add a comprehensive data fetching layer with request deduplication, automatic retries, and offline support. Requirements: deduplicate identical concurrent requests, retry failed requests with exponential backoff, cache responses for offline access, and sync mutations when back online.
reasoning: Request deduplication prevents sending the same API call multiple times when components mount simultaneously. Automatic retries handle transient network failures. Offline caching ensures the app remains functional without network. Mutation sync queues changes made offline and replays them when connectivity returns. The layer must handle all these concerns transparently.
answer: Request deduplication: maintain a Map of in-flight requests keyed by method+URL+params. If a request with the same key is already in flight, return the existing promise instead of making a new request. Clear from map when request completes. Automatic retries: on network error or 503 response, retry with exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s (max 3 retries). Add jitter (random 0-500ms) to prevent thundering herd. Don't retry 4xx errors (client errors). Don't retry non-idempotent requests (POST) without idempotency key. Response caching: cache GET responses in IndexedDB with TTL. Key: method+URL+params. Value: {data, timestamp, ttl}. On network failure: return cached response with 'stale data' indicator. Show 'Last updated: 5 minutes ago'. Offline detection: listen to navigator.onLine and online/offline events. Show offline banner when offline. Disable features requiring network. Mutation queue: when offline, store mutations in IndexedDB outbox. {id, method, url, body, timestamp, retryCount}. When back online: process queue in order. Send each mutation. On success: remove from queue. On failure: increment retryCount, retry later. Conflict resolution: include version number in mutations. If server returns 409 (conflict), show conflict dialog to user. Don't silently overwrite. UI feedback: show loading spinner during fetch. Show error message with retry button on failure. Show offline indicator with queued mutation count. Show sync progress when coming back online. Implementation: wrap fetch/axios with custom client that handles all these concerns. Provide useQuery and useMutation hooks that use the client. Libraries: React Query handles deduplication, retries, and caching out of the box. Add offline support with react-query-offline or custom IndexedDB persistence.

instruction: Implement a visual regression testing system that catches unintended UI changes. Requirements: capture screenshots of all pages and components, compare with baseline screenshots, flag differences for review, integrate with CI/CD pipeline, and handle dynamic content (timestamps, random data).
reasoning: Visual regression testing catches CSS changes that break layouts or styling. Pixel-by-pixel comparison identifies even subtle changes. Dynamic content (timestamps, random IDs) must be masked to avoid false positives. CI integration ensures every PR is checked. The system must handle different viewport sizes and browsers.
answer: Tool: use Percy, Chromatic, or Playwright screenshots. Percy/Chromatic: cloud services that handle screenshot capture, comparison, and review. Playwright: self-hosted, more control but more setup. Capture: in CI, run test suite that navigates to all pages and captures screenshots. Also capture Storybook stories for component-level testing. Use consistent viewport sizes (mobile: 375px, tablet: 768px, desktop: 1280px). Baseline: first run creates baseline screenshots. Subsequent runs compare against baseline. When intentional changes are made, approve new screenshots as new baseline. Comparison: pixel-by-pixel diff with configurable threshold (ignore anti-aliasing differences). Highlight changed pixels in red. Show side-by-side comparison. Dynamic content: mask dynamic elements before comparison. Replace timestamps with fixed text. Hide random avatars. Use data-test-id attributes to identify elements to mask. Percy/Chromatic support DOM manipulation before screenshot. Review workflow: when differences are detected, create review in Percy/Chromatic dashboard. Developer reviews: approve (intentional change) or reject (bug). Approved changes update baseline. CI integration: PR checks include visual regression test. Block merge if unreviewed visual changes exist. Show diff summary in PR comments. Flaky tests: handle flaky visual tests by retrying screenshots. Ignore sub-pixel rendering differences. Set appropriate diff threshold. Browser testing: capture screenshots in Chrome, Firefox, Safari. Identify browser-specific rendering differences. Performance: parallelize screenshot capture across multiple machines. Cache screenshots to avoid re-capturing unchanged pages. Only capture pages affected by changed files (use code coverage data).

instruction: Add end-to-end testing with Playwright that covers critical user flows, handles flaky tests, and integrates with CI/CD. Requirements: test signup, login, create item, checkout flows. Handle async operations reliably. Run tests in parallel. Provide clear failure reports with screenshots and videos.
reasoning: E2E tests verify critical user flows work end-to-end. They're slower and more flaky than unit tests but catch integration issues. Flakiness often comes from improper async handling (waiting for elements). Parallel execution speeds up test runs. Failure reports with screenshots and videos help debug failures quickly. The test suite must be reliable enough to run on every PR.
answer: Setup: install Playwright, configure with multiple browsers (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit). Set base URL, timeouts, retry count. Test organization: group by feature (auth.spec.ts, checkout.spec.ts). Use page objects for reusable page interactions. Critical flows: signup (fill form, submit, verify redirect to dashboard, check welcome email). Login (enter credentials, submit, verify authenticated state). Create item (navigate to create page, fill form, submit, verify item appears in list). Checkout (add to cart, go to checkout, enter payment, submit, verify confirmation). Async handling: use Playwright's auto-waiting (waits for elements to be actionable). For custom waits: use expect().toPass() with timeout. Never use arbitrary waits (page.waitForTimeout). Use web-first assertions (expect(page.locator('.success')).toBeVisible()). Flaky test prevention: use data-testid attributes for selectors (not CSS classes that change). Reset database state before each test. Use test fixtures for setup/teardown. Retry flaky tests once (test.describe.configure({retries: 1})). Parallel execution: configure workers: 4 in playwright.config.ts. Tests run in parallel across workers. Ensure tests are independent (no shared state). Use separate database per worker or transactions. CI integration: run E2E tests in GitHub Actions. Use Playwright's GitHub reporter for annotations on PR. Upload test artifacts (screenshots, videos, traces) on failure. Show failure summary in PR comment. Failure reports: on failure, capture screenshot, video recording, and trace file. Trace shows every action and network request. Upload to CI artifacts. Use Playwright's HTML reporter for detailed report. Test data: use factories to create test data (faker.js). Clean up after tests. Use database transactions that rollback after each test. Performance: run E2E tests only on changed areas (use code coverage to determine affected tests). Cache Playwright browsers in CI. Use headed mode only for debugging.

instruction: Implement a user avatar upload feature across the application. The current app has user profiles but no avatar support. Add avatar upload with cropping, display avatars in the navigation bar, comments, and user cards, and handle default avatars gracefully.
reasoning: Avatar upload requires changes across multiple layers: file upload endpoint, image processing, storage, user model, and multiple UI components. Default avatars need a deterministic generation strategy. Image cropping adds client-side complexity. The avatar must display consistently across all views without breaking existing layouts.
answer: Backend: add avatar_url column to users table. Create POST /api/users/avatar endpoint accepting multipart form data. Validate file type (JPEG, PNG, WebP), size (max 5MB). Process with sharp: resize to 200x200, crop to square. Upload to S3 with content-hash filename. Update user's avatar_url. Frontend upload: create AvatarUpload component with react-easy-crop for cropping. Show circular crop area. Upload on crop confirm. Display: create Avatar component accepting user object. Shows avatar image if avatar_url exists, otherwise generates default avatar (initials on colored background, color from name hash). Use Avatar in NavBar (top-right), Comment component (next to username), UserCard (profile picture). Default avatar: generate SVG with initials and background color. Color = hash(name) % 360 for HSL hue. Consistent across all views. Cache busting: append ?v=timestamp to avatar URL when updated. Prevents browser caching old avatar. Performance: lazy load avatar images. Use loading='lazy'. Generate multiple sizes (50px, 100px, 200px) for different contexts. Serve appropriate size with srcset.

instruction: Add email notification preferences to the settings page. Users should be able to choose which email notifications they receive (marketing, product updates, security alerts, weekly digest). Update the email sending service to respect these preferences. Security alerts must always be sent regardless of preferences.
reasoning: Notification preferences require changes across multiple layers: database schema, settings UI, API endpoints, and email sending logic. Some notifications (security) must bypass preferences. The email service needs to check preferences before sending without adding significant latency. Default preferences for existing users must be sensible.
answer: Database: add email_preferences JSON column to users table. Default: {marketing: false, product_updates: true, security: true, weekly_digest: true}. For existing users, use default values (don't require migration to populate all rows). Settings UI: add 'Email Preferences' section to settings page. Checkboxes for each notification type. Security alerts shown as always-on (disabled checkbox with explanation). Save button calls PUT /api/users/preferences. API: GET /api/users/preferences returns current preferences. PUT /api/users/preferences validates and saves. Email service: before sending, check user's preferences. getPreference(user, type) returns boolean. Security type always returns true. Cache preferences in Redis (key: prefs:{userId}, TTL: 1 hour) to avoid database query on every email. Invalidate cache on preference update. Batch checking: when sending to many users (e.g., marketing blast), batch load preferences. Filter out users who opted out before sending. Unsubscribe link: include one-click unsubscribe in marketing emails. Links to preference page with specific type pre-selected. Compliance: honor unsubscribe within 10 days (CAN-SPAM). Immediate for GDPR users. Analytics: track preference distribution. Show in admin dashboard. Identify underperforming notification types with high opt-out rates.

instruction: Refactor the authentication system from session-based cookies to JWT tokens while maintaining backward compatibility during migration. Existing users with active sessions must not be logged out. The API must support both authentication methods during the transition period.
reasoning: Migrating authentication methods is risky because getting it wrong locks out all users. Backward compatibility means supporting both old and new methods simultaneously. Existing sessions must continue working while new logins use JWT. The transition period needs monitoring to ensure no authentication failures. Eventually, old sessions need to be phased out.
answer: Phase 1 (dual support): Add JWT authentication alongside existing session cookies. Login endpoint returns both session cookie AND JWT token. Auth middleware checks JWT first (Authorization header), falls back to session cookie. New frontend code uses JWT. Old frontend code continues using cookies. Phase 2 (frontend migration): Update frontend to use JWT for all API calls. Store JWT in memory (not localStorage for XSS protection). Send in Authorization header. Keep session cookie for backward compatibility. Phase 3 (monitoring): Track authentication method usage. Log which requests use JWT vs session. Identify any remaining session-based clients. Phase 4 (deprecation): Set session expiry to 7 days (no new sessions). After 7 days, remove session support. All clients must use JWT. Implementation details: Auth middleware: extract token from Authorization header. If present: verify JWT, attach user to request. If not: check session cookie (legacy). If neither: return 401. JWT structure: {sub: userId, iat, exp: 15min}. Short expiry for security. Refresh token: separate long-lived token (7 days) in httpOnly cookie. Use for getting new access tokens. Token refresh: POST /api/auth/refresh. Validates refresh token, issues new access token. Rotate refresh token on each use. Migration monitoring: add metric auth_method: 'jwt'|'session'. Dashboard shows migration progress. Alert if session usage doesn't decrease. Rollback plan: if JWT causes issues, revert frontend to use sessions. Backend still supports both. No user impact. Testing: test both auth methods in CI. Verify existing session tests still pass. Add JWT-specific tests.

instruction: Implement a GraphQL subscription system for real-time updates on a project management board. Requirements: subscribe to board changes (new tasks, status changes, comments), handle connection management, support filtering subscriptions by project, and handle reconnection gracefully.
reasoning: GraphQL subscriptions require WebSocket infrastructure and PubSub for event distribution. Connection management handles authentication and cleanup. Filtering allows clients to subscribe only to relevant events. Reconnection must restore subscriptions without missing events. The system must scale to many concurrent subscribers without performance degradation.
answer: Setup: use graphql-ws protocol with WebSocket server. Apollo Server or graphql-yoga with subscriptions. PubSub: use Redis PubSub for horizontal scaling across multiple server instances. Events: TASK_CREATED, TASK_UPDATED, TASK_DELETED, COMMENT_ADDED, BOARD_UPDATED. Subscription resolver: Subscription.taskUpdated: {subscribe: (_, {projectId}, {user}) => { if (!hasAccess(user, projectId)) throw new AuthenticationError('No access'); return pubsub.asyncIterator(`TASK_UPDATED_${projectId}`); }}. Publishing: when task is updated, publish event: pubsub.publish(`TASK_UPDATED_${projectId}`, {taskUpdated: task}). Include relevant data in payload. Connection management: on WebSocket connect: authenticate with JWT. Attach user to connection context. On disconnect: clean up subscriptions. Track active connections per user (limit to 5 per user). Filtering: subscriptions accept projectId parameter. Only receive events for specified project. Support multiple subscriptions per connection (subscribe to multiple projects). Reconnection: client library (graphql-ws) handles reconnection with exponential backoff. On reconnect: re-subscribe to all active subscriptions. Server doesn't need to track missed events (client can fetch current state). Performance: batch PubSub publishes for bulk operations. Use Redis streams instead of PubSub for persistence (optional). Limit subscription payload size. Don't send entire task object, send changed fields only. Monitoring: track active subscriptions, connection count, event throughput. Alert on connection spikes. Dashboard shows real-time metrics. Security: validate user has access to subscribed project on each event (not just on subscribe). Permissions may change during subscription lifetime.

instruction: Add a comprehensive API rate limiting system with different tiers for free, pro, and enterprise users. Requirements: implement sliding window rate limiting, show rate limit status in response headers, provide a dashboard for users to view their usage, and allow enterprise customers to configure custom limits.
reasoning: Rate limiting with user tiers requires looking up the user's tier on each request. Sliding window is more accurate than fixed windows. Response headers inform clients of their remaining quota. Usage dashboards help users understand their consumption. Enterprise custom limits need admin configuration. The system must be performant (rate check on every request) and distributed (work across multiple servers).
answer: Tier configuration: define limits per tier. Free: 100 requests/minute, 1000/day. Pro: 1000/minute, 50000/day. Enterprise: custom (default 10000/minute, unlimited/day). Store in tiers table with per-endpoint overrides. Sliding window: use Redis sorted set. Key: ratelimit:{userId}:{endpoint}:{window}. Add request timestamp as score. Remove entries older than window. Count remaining entries. If count > limit: reject with 429. Middleware: on each request: 1) Authenticate user (get tier). 2) Look up limit for endpoint + tier. 3) Check Redis sliding window. 4) If under limit: allow, increment counter. 5) If over limit: reject with 429. Headers: add to all responses: X-RateLimit-Limit: 1000, X-RateLimit-Remaining: 847, X-RateLimit-Reset: 1705312800 (Unix timestamp). On 429: add Retry-After: 30 (seconds). Usage dashboard: GET /api/usage returns {minute: {used: 153, limit: 1000}, day: {used: 12453, limit: 50000}, endpoints: [{path: '/api/search', count: 523}, ...]}. Show usage charts over time. Enterprise configuration: admin portal for enterprise customers. Set custom limits per endpoint. Set monthly quotas. Configure overage behavior (hard limit vs soft limit with overage charges). Performance: cache tier lookup in Redis (TTL: 5 min). Use Lua scripts for atomic rate limit operations in Redis. Pipeline Redis commands. Monitoring: track rate limit hits by tier, endpoint, user. Alert on unusual patterns. Dashboard for admin to view top API consumers. Graceful degradation: if Redis is down, fall back to in-memory rate limiting (less accurate but prevents total bypass). Log fallback events.

instruction: Implement a comprehensive error handling strategy for a React application that handles API errors, render errors, async errors, and network errors differently. Requirements: show appropriate UI for each error type, log errors with context, provide retry mechanisms, and prevent error cascades.
reasoning: Different error types need different handling strategies. API errors might be retryable or require user action. Render errors need error boundaries to prevent app crashes. Async errors in event handlers aren't caught by error boundaries. Network errors need offline detection. A unified strategy ensures consistent UX while handling each type appropriately. Error cascades (one error triggering another) must be prevented.
answer: API errors: create error interceptor in API client. Categorize by status code. 401: redirect to login. 403: show 'Access denied' modal. 404: show 'Not found' page. 422: extract field errors, show inline in form. 429: show 'Too many requests, please wait'. 500: show 'Server error' with retry button. Network errors: show 'Connection lost' banner. Retry automatically when back online. Render errors: use React error boundaries at multiple levels. Root boundary: full-page error with reload. Page boundary: page-level error with navigation. Component boundary: inline error with retry. Each boundary logs error to Sentry with component stack. Async errors: wrap async event handlers in try/catch. Create useAsyncCallback hook that catches errors and routes to global error handler. For promises without handlers: add global unhandledrejection listener. Error UI: toast for transient errors (auto-dismiss after 5s). Modal for blocking errors (requires user action). Inline for field-level errors. Banner for persistent issues (connection lost). Error context: include user ID, URL, action, request/response details, component stack (for render errors). Send to error tracking service. Generate error ID for support reference. Retry mechanisms: exponential backoff for network errors (1s, 2s, 4s). Single retry for server errors. Manual retry button for user-triggered actions. Prevent cascades: debounce error handlers. Don't show multiple error toasts for the same issue. Suppress secondary errors caused by primary error. Recovery: after error is resolved, dismiss error UI automatically. Clear error state on navigation.

instruction: Add a comprehensive caching strategy for a React application using React Query. Requirements: cache API responses with appropriate stale times, implement optimistic updates for mutations, prefetch data on route hover, handle background refetching, and provide cache invalidation on mutations.
reasoning: React Query provides powerful caching but requires careful configuration. Different data types need different stale times (user profile: 5 min, notifications: 30 sec, static content: 1 hour). Optimistic updates improve perceived performance but need rollback on failure. Prefetching makes navigation feel instant. Background refetching keeps data fresh. Cache invalidation must be precise to avoid unnecessary refetches.
answer: QueryClient configuration: staleTime: 5 * 60 * 1000 (5 min default), cacheTime: 30 * 60 * 1000 (30 min), retry: 3, refetchOnWindowFocus: true, refetchOnReconnect: true. Override per query as needed. Query keys: use consistent, hierarchical keys. ['users'] for all users, ['users', userId] for specific user, ['users', {page: 1, sort: 'name'}] for filtered list. Hierarchical keys enable targeted invalidation. Stale times by data type: user profile: 5 min (changes rarely). Notifications: 30 sec (changes frequently). Product catalog: 1 hour (changes rarely). Real-time data: 0 (always stale, always refetch). Static content: Infinity (never stale). Optimistic updates: useMutation with onMutate. Example: updateTodo. onMutate: cancel queries, snapshot previous data, update cache optimistically. onError: rollback to snapshot. onSettled: invalidate queries. Prefetching: on navigation link hover, prefetch the route's data. useQueryClient().prefetchQuery(['project', projectId], fetchProject). Data ready when user navigates. Background refetching: refetchInterval: 30000 for real-time data (poll every 30s). refetchOnWindowFocus: true for data that might change while user is away. Cache invalidation: after mutation, invalidate related queries. createTodo -> invalidateQueries(['todos']). updateTodo -> invalidateQueries(['todos', todoId]). Use query filters for precise invalidation. DevTools: use React Query DevTools in development. Inspect cache, queries, mutations. Identify stale data and unnecessary refetches. Performance: use select to transform data and reduce re-renders. Use keepPreviousData for pagination (show old data while fetching new page).

instruction: Implement a soft delete system with cascading deletes, restore functionality, and audit logging. Requirements: mark records as deleted instead of removing them, cascade soft deletes to related records, allow restoring deleted records, and maintain an audit log of all delete and restore operations.
reasoning: Soft deletes prevent accidental data loss but add complexity to every query (must filter deleted records). Cascading soft deletes maintain referential integrity (deleting a project should soft delete its tasks). Restore must handle conflicts (unique constraints). Audit logging tracks who deleted/restored what and when. The system must integrate with the ORM to automatically filter deleted records.
answer: Schema: add deleted_at (timestamp, nullable) and deleted_by (user_id, nullable) to all soft-deletable tables. NULL means not deleted. Add index on deleted_at for filtered queries. ORM integration: create SoftDelete model mixin. Override find methods to add WHERE deleted_at IS NULL by default. Provide withDeleted() scope to include deleted records. Soft delete: UPDATE table SET deleted_at = NOW(), deleted_by = :userId WHERE id = :id. Don't actually DELETE. Cascading: define cascade relationships in model. When project is soft deleted, cascade to tasks, comments, files. Use cascade_group_id to track which records were deleted together (for restore). Restore: UPDATE table SET deleted_at = NULL, deleted_by = NULL WHERE id = :id. For cascaded deletes: restore all records with same cascade_group_id. Conflict handling: if unique constraint violated on restore (e.g., email already taken by new record), return error with options. Audit log: audit_logs table (id, action: 'soft_delete'|'restore', table_name, record_id, user_id, cascade_group_id, timestamp). Log every soft delete and restore. Include cascade information. Querying deleted records: admin UI shows 'Trash' with deleted records. Filter by table, date range, user. Allow restore and permanent delete. Permanent delete: actually DELETE from database. Require confirmation. Log permanent deletes. Cleanup: cron job permanently deletes records older than 90 days. Configurable per table. Performance: add composite indexes including deleted_at. Use partial indexes where supported (PostgreSQL: CREATE INDEX ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL).

instruction: Add a full-text search implementation using PostgreSQL tsvector with support for searching across multiple entity types, ranking results by relevance, and providing search suggestions. The current app uses LIKE queries which are slow and don't support relevance ranking.
reasoning: PostgreSQL full-text search is powerful but requires proper configuration. Multi-entity search needs either a unified search index or federated queries. Relevance ranking uses ts_rank with configurable weights per field. Search suggestions need fast prefix matching. The search must be fast enough for real-time use and handle partial matches and typos.
answer: Search index: create search_documents materialized view combining searchable content. SELECT 'user' as type, id, name as title, bio as body, to_tsvector('english', coalesce(name, '') || ' ' || coalesce(bio, '')) as searchable FROM users UNION ALL SELECT 'post', id, title, body, to_tsvector('english', coalesce(title, '') || ' ' || coalesce(body, '')) FROM posts. Weights: setweight(to_tsvector('english', title), 'A') || setweight(to_tsvector('english', body), 'B'). Title matches rank higher. Refresh materialized view periodically (every 5 minutes) or use triggers for real-time updates. Search query: SELECT type, id, title, ts_headline('english', body, query) as snippet, ts_rank(searchable, query) as rank FROM search_documents, plainto_tsquery('english', :searchTerm) query WHERE searchable @@ query ORDER BY rank DESC LIMIT 20. Highlighting: ts_headline wraps matches in <b> tags. Configure: MaxWords=50, MinWords=20, StartSel=<mark>, StopSel=</mark>. Search suggestions: use tsvector prefix matching with :* operator. SELECT DISTINCT title FROM search_documents WHERE searchable @@ to_tsquery('english', :prefix || ':*') LIMIT 5. Typo tolerance: install pg_trgm extension. Create trigram index. Use similarity() function for fuzzy matching. Combine with full-text search. Performance: GIN index on searchable column. Limit result set. Use cursor for pagination. Cache common searches (5 min TTL). API: GET /api/search?q=query&type=user,post&page=1. Return results with type, id, title, snippet, rank. Autocomplete endpoint: GET /api/search/suggest?q=prefix. Return top 5 suggestions.

instruction: Implement a comprehensive input sanitization system that prevents XSS, SQL injection, and command injection across the application. Requirements: sanitize HTML content, validate and sanitize file names, prevent path traversal, and handle Unicode normalization.
reasoning: Input sanitization is defense in depth against injection attacks. XSS prevention requires HTML sanitization with a whitelist approach. SQL injection prevention requires parameterized queries (not sanitization). Command injection prevention requires escaping shell arguments. File name sanitization prevents path traversal and special character issues. Unicode normalization prevents homograph attacks. Each input type needs appropriate sanitization.
answer: HTML sanitization: use DOMPurify for user-generated HTML content. Configure allowed tags and attributes. const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(dirty, {ALLOWED_TAGS: ['p', 'b', 'i', 'em', 'strong', 'a', 'ul', 'ol', 'li'], ALLOWED_ATTR: ['href', 'target']}). Never use dangerouslySetInnerHTML with unsanitized content. SQL injection: always use parameterized queries or ORM methods. Never concatenate user input into SQL. This is not sanitization - it's proper query construction. Command injection: never pass user input to shell commands. If unavoidable, use child_process.execFile (not exec) with arguments array. Validate input against whitelist. File names: sanitize uploaded file names. Remove path separators (/ \), null bytes, control characters. Replace special characters with safe alternatives. Limit length (255 chars). Use UUID or content-hash for stored filename to prevent conflicts. Path traversal: never use user input directly in file paths. Validate against base directory: const resolved = path.resolve(baseDir, userInput); if (!resolved.startsWith(baseDir)) throw new Error('Invalid path'). Unicode normalization: normalize all text input to NFC form before processing. 'café' can be represented multiple ways in Unicode. Normalization ensures consistent comparison and storage. Use String.prototype.normalize('NFC'). Validation layers: 1) Client-side validation (UX, can be bypassed). 2) Server-side validation (security boundary). 3) Parameterized queries (SQL injection prevention). 4) Output encoding (XSS prevention). Each layer serves a different purpose. Content Security Policy: set CSP headers as additional XSS defense. Restrict script sources, disable inline scripts. Security headers: set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Strict-Transport-Security. Use helmet.js middleware.

instruction: Add two-factor authentication (2FA) with TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) to the application. Requirements: generate QR codes for authenticator app setup, verify TOTP codes with clock drift tolerance, provide backup codes for account recovery, and allow disabling 2FA with proper verification.
reasoning: 2FA significantly improves account security. TOTP is the standard for authenticator apps (Google Authenticator, Authy). QR codes simplify setup. Clock drift tolerance handles time synchronization issues between server and user's device. Backup codes provide recovery if the authenticator device is lost. Disabling 2FA must require strong verification to prevent attackers from removing it.
answer: Setup flow: 1) User clicks 'Enable 2FA' in security settings. 2) Server generates TOTP secret (speakeasy library: speakeasy.generateSecret({name: 'MyApp', issuer: 'MyApp'})). 3) Generate QR code from secret URL (qrcode library). 4) Show QR code and manual entry key. 5) User scans QR with authenticator app. 6) User enters 6-digit code to verify setup. 7) Server verifies code, enables 2FA, generates backup codes. TOTP verification: use speakeasy.totp.verify({secret, encoding: 'base32', token: userCode, window: 1}). Window: 1 allows ±30 seconds clock drift. Backup codes: generate 10 random codes (crypto.randomBytes(8).toString('hex')). Hash with bcrypt before storing. Show codes once, require user to save them. Each code is single-use. Mark as used when redeemed. Login flow: 1) User enters email and password. 2) If 2FA enabled: show 2FA code input. 3) User enters TOTP code or backup code. 4) Verify: try TOTP first, then check backup codes. 5) On success: create session, mark backup code as used if used. Disabling 2FA: require current password + 2FA code (or backup code) to disable. Prevents attackers who gained session access from removing 2FA. Show warning about security implications. Storage: users table: two_factor_secret (encrypted), two_factor_enabled (boolean), backup_codes (JSON array of hashed codes). Encrypt secret at rest using application encryption key. Remember device: option to 'Remember this device for 30 days'. Generate device token, store in trusted_devices table. Skip 2FA on trusted devices. Security: rate limit 2FA verification attempts (5 per minute). Lock account after 10 failed attempts. Log all 2FA events (enable, disable, successful/failed verification).

instruction: Implement a feature flag system that allows enabling/disabling features without deployment. Requirements: support boolean flags and multi-variant flags, target flags to specific user segments, provide a management dashboard, and ensure flag evaluation is fast and doesn't impact page load.
reasoning: Feature flags enable continuous deployment and gradual rollouts. Boolean flags are simple on/off. Multi-variant flags support A/B testing. Targeting allows enabling features for specific users or segments (beta testers, premium users). The management dashboard allows non-developers to control flags. Flag evaluation must be fast (cached) and work even if the flag service is down.
answer: Data model: feature_flags table (id, key, name, description, type: 'boolean'|'multivariate', enabled, variants: JSON, targeting_rules: JSON, created_at, updated_at). Targeting rules: [{attribute: 'plan', operator: 'in', values: ['pro', 'enterprise']}, {attribute: 'email', operator: 'ends_with', values: ['@company.com']}]. Rules are evaluated in order, first match wins. Flag evaluation: create FlagService with evaluate(flagKey, userContext) method. Check targeting rules against user attributes. Return variant ID or boolean. Cache flag definitions in memory (refresh every 30 seconds). Fallback to last known state if flag service is down. Client-side: fetch all flags on app load, store in context. useFeatureFlag('new_dashboard') returns boolean. Conditionally render: {flags.new_dashboard && <NewDashboard />}. Server-side: evaluate flags in middleware, attach to request context. Use in route handlers. Management dashboard: list all flags with status (enabled/disabled). Create/edit flags with targeting rules. Preview flag evaluation for specific users. Rollout percentage: gradually increase from 0% to 100%. Analytics: track flag evaluations and user assignments. Measure feature adoption. Audit log: track who changed flags and when. Performance: cache flag definitions in Redis (shared across servers). Client-side: include flags in initial page load (don't make separate API call). Fallback: if flag service is down, use default values (all flags disabled). Cleanup: process to remove old flags after full rollout. Search codebase for flag usage, remove conditional code. Testing: test with flags enabled and disabled. Use flag overrides in tests. Provide test mode in dashboard to preview flags as different users.

instruction: Add comprehensive logging with structured logs, log levels, request tracing, and centralized log aggregation. Requirements: log all API requests with correlation IDs, log errors with full context, support log levels (debug, info, warn, error), and send logs to Elasticsearch for searching and alerting.
reasoning: Structured logs (JSON) are easier to parse and search than plain text. Log levels allow filtering noise. Request tracing with correlation IDs enables following a request across multiple services. Centralized aggregation (ELK stack) enables searching logs from all servers in one place. The logging system must be fast (async) and not impact request latency.
answer: Logger setup: use pino (fastest Node.js logger) or winston. Configure with transports: console (development), file (local), Elasticsearch (production). Structured format: JSON with consistent fields. Log levels: debug (detailed info for development), info (normal operations), warn (potential issues), error (failures). Configure minimum level per environment (debug in dev, info in prod). Request logging: middleware logs all API requests. On request: generate correlation ID (UUID), attach to request and response header (X-Correlation-ID). Log: {level: 'info', type: 'request', correlationId, method, path, userId, ip, userAgent}. On response: log: {level: 'info', type: 'response', correlationId, status, duration, responseSize}. Error logging: log errors with full context. {level: 'error', type: 'error', correlationId, error: {message, stack, code}, request: {method, path, body (sanitized)}, user: {id, email}}. Send to error tracking service (Sentry) in addition to logs. Application logs: use logger throughout application. logger.info('User created', {userId, plan}). logger.warn('Rate limit approaching', {userId, usage}). logger.error('Payment failed', {error, orderId}). Context: create child loggers with context. const reqLogger = logger.child({correlationId, userId}). All logs from this logger include context. Performance: use async logging (pino is async by default). Buffer logs and flush in batches. Don't block request processing. Sensitive data: never log passwords, tokens, credit card numbers. Mask sensitive fields in request/response bodies. Use allowlist approach (log only known-safe fields). Log rotation: rotate log files daily or by size (100MB). Keep 30 days locally. Compress old logs. Centralized logging: send to Elasticsearch via Logstash or directly. Create index pattern in Kibana. Set up dashboards for request rate, error rate, latency. Alerting: create alerts in Kibana/ElastAlert for error rate spikes, specific error patterns, slow requests. Send to Slack/PagerDuty.

instruction: Implement a responsive data table that transforms into a card layout on mobile. Requirements: show full table on desktop, transform to stacked cards on mobile, maintain sorting and filtering on mobile, support horizontal scrolling for wide tables on tablet, and ensure accessibility on all screen sizes.
reasoning: Data tables are challenging on mobile due to limited screen width. Simply making tables scrollable horizontally provides poor UX. Card layouts on mobile show one row at a time with all columns stacked. Sorting and filtering must remain accessible on mobile. The transformation must be seamless and maintain all functionality. Accessibility requires different approaches for table vs card layouts.
answer:
Desktop (>1024px): standard HTML table with sortable headers, filter inputs, pagination. Use proper table semantics (, , , becomes card container, . CSS: @media (max-width: 768px) { td::before { content: attr(data-label); font-weight: bold; } }. Sorting on mobile: show sort button that opens sort options modal. Select column and direction. Apply sort to underlying data (same as desktop). Filtering on mobile: show filter button that opens filter panel (slide-up sheet). Apply filters to data. Pagination on mobile: show 'Load more' button or infinite scroll instead of page numbers. Accessibility: desktop: proper table semantics with scope attributes. Mobile: card layout with proper heading hierarchy. Each card has heading (primary field). Use ARIA labels for sort and filter buttons. Announce sort/filter changes. Performance: virtualize table rows for large datasets (1000+ rows). Use react-window. Only render visible rows. Render card layout for mobile with same virtualization.
, ). Tablet (768-1024px): horizontal scrolling table with sticky first column. Add scroll indicators (gradient fade on edges). Show column count indicator. Mobile (<768px): card layout. Each row becomes a card showing all columns as label-value pairs. Card header shows primary field (e.g., name). Expandable details for secondary fields. Implementation: use CSS media queries to switch layouts. Desktop: display: table. Mobile: display: block, each row is a card.
becomes label-value pair. Use data-label attribute on to show column name: john@example.com

instruction: Add pull-to-refresh functionality to a mobile web app that works across different browsers and doesn't conflict with browser gestures. Requirements: show visual feedback during pull, trigger refresh when pulled past threshold, handle refresh completion, and prevent conflicts with browser back navigation gestures.
reasoning: Pull-to-refresh is a native mobile pattern that improves mobile web UX. Implementation requires tracking touch events and showing visual feedback. The refresh threshold must feel natural. Completion animation provides feedback. Browser gesture conflicts (swipe back, overscroll) must be handled carefully. The implementation must work across iOS Safari, Chrome, and Samsung Internet.
answer: Touch tracking: listen for touchstart, touchmove, touchend on the scroll container. On touchstart: record start Y position. Only activate if scrolled to top (scrollTop === 0). On touchmove: calculate pull distance (currentY - startY). If pulling down (positive distance): apply visual feedback. Show refresh indicator that grows with pull distance. Apply CSS transform: translateY(pullDistance * 0.5) to content (dampening factor makes it feel natural). On touchend: if pull distance > 80px (threshold): trigger refresh. Otherwise: animate back to original position. Refresh: show spinner in indicator. Call refresh function (refetch data). On completion: animate indicator away, update content. Browser conflict prevention: use overscroll-behavior: contain on scroll container to prevent browser's native pull-to-refresh. Use touch-action: pan-x to allow horizontal gestures (back navigation) while handling vertical pull. Don't call preventDefault on touchstart (blocks scrolling). Only preventDefault on touchmove when actively pulling. Visual feedback: circular progress indicator that fills as user pulls. At threshold: indicator shows checkmark or arrow. During refresh: spinner animation. On completion: success checkmark, then fade out. Use CSS animations and transitions for smooth movement. Implementation: create usePullToRefresh hook. Accepts onRefresh callback and options (threshold, maxPullDistance). Returns ref to attach to scroll container. Accessibility: provide alternative refresh mechanism (refresh button) for users who can't perform pull gesture. Announce refresh state to screen readers. Performance: use requestAnimationFrame for smooth animations. Use CSS transforms (GPU accelerated) instead of top/margin. Debounce refresh trigger to prevent multiple refreshes.

instruction: Implement a comprehensive performance monitoring system that tracks Core Web Vitals, custom metrics, and JavaScript errors. Requirements: measure LCP, FID, CLS, and INP. Track custom business metrics (time to interactive, search result time). Report to analytics dashboard. Alert on performance regressions.
reasoning: Core Web Vitals are Google's metrics for user experience and affect SEO. LCP measures loading performance, FID/INP measures interactivity, CLS measures visual stability. Custom metrics track business-specific performance. Real User Monitoring (RUM) captures actual user experience, not just lab measurements. Performance regressions must be caught before they affect many users.
answer: Core Web Vitals: use web-vitals library to measure LCP (Largest Contentful Paint, target <2.5s), FID (First Input Delay, target <100ms) / INP (Interaction to Next Paint, target <200ms), CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift, target <0.1). Import {onLCP, onFID, onCLS, onINP} from 'web-vitals'. Register callbacks that send metrics to analytics. Custom metrics: use Performance API. performance.mark('search-start'), performance.mark('search-end'), performance.measure('search-duration', 'search-start', 'search-end'). Track: time to interactive, search result time, form submission time, page load time. Reporting: send metrics to analytics endpoint. POST /api/metrics with {name: 'LCP', value: 2300, page: '/dashboard', connectionType: '4g', deviceType: 'mobile'}. Include context: page URL, user agent, connection type, device memory. Batch metrics and send with navigator.sendBeacon for reliability (works even if page unloads). Analytics dashboard: show Core Web Vitals distribution (p75 is the metric Google uses). Show percentage of users experiencing 'good', 'needs improvement', 'poor' performance. Break down by page, device, connection type. Show trends over time. Alerting: set up alerts when p75 of any metric crosses threshold. LCP p75 > 2.5s -> alert. Compare with previous week to detect regressions. Send to Slack/PagerDuty. LCP optimization: optimize largest element (usually hero image). Preload critical images. Use responsive images (srcset). Lazy load below-fold images. Use server-side rendering for above-fold content. CLS optimization: reserve space for images/videos (width/height attributes). Avoid inserting content above existing content. Use transform for animations instead of layout properties. FID/INP optimization: reduce JavaScript execution time. Code split, defer non-critical JS. Use web workers for heavy computation. Break up long tasks. Performance budgets: set limits in CI. Fail build if bundle size exceeds budget. Use Lighthouse CI to catch regressions before deployment.

instruction: Add image lazy loading with blur-up placeholder technique across the application. Requirements: lazy load all below-fold images, show low-quality blur-up placeholder while loading, fade in full image when loaded, handle images with unknown dimensions, and measure impact on page load performance.
reasoning: Lazy loading defers loading of off-screen images, reducing initial page weight. Blur-up placeholders provide visual feedback and prevent layout shift. The technique loads a tiny version of the image first (20px wide), applies CSS blur, then loads the full image and fades it in. Unknown dimensions cause layout shift unless handled. The implementation must work with responsive images and different image formats.
answer: Lazy loading: use native loading='lazy' attribute for simple cases. For more control (blur-up, fade-in), use IntersectionObserver. Create LazyImage component that observes when image enters viewport, then loads full image. Blur-up placeholder: generate tiny placeholder (20px wide) server-side during image upload. Encode as base64 and include in HTML. Apply CSS filter: blur(20px) and transform: scale(1.1) (hides blur edges). When full image loads: fade out placeholder, fade in full image. Use CSS transitions (opacity 0.3s). Unknown dimensions: require width and height props for all images. Use aspect-ratio CSS property as fallback. Reserve space with padding-bottom trick: padding-bottom: (height/width * 100)%. This prevents layout shift. Responsive images: use srcset and sizes attributes. . Browser selects optimal size. Format: serve WebP with JPEG fallback using element. . Above-fold images: don't lazy load images above the fold (hurts LCP). Use fetchpriority='high' for LCP image. Preload critical images with . Implementation: create Image component that wraps all image logic. Accept src, alt, width, height, priority props. Handle lazy loading, placeholder, responsive images, and format selection. Performance measurement: track image load times with Performance API. Measure LCP before and after implementation. Target: LCP < 2.5s. Monitor image sizes, alert on large images (>500KB).

instruction: Implement a multi-step form wizard with progress tracking, conditional steps, validation per step, and data persistence. Requirements: show progress indicator, allow navigation between completed steps, validate each step before proceeding, conditionally show/hide steps based on answers, and persist form data across page refreshes.
reasoning: Multi-step forms break complex forms into manageable chunks. Progress tracking shows users how far they've come. Conditional steps require a dependency graph to determine which steps to show. Per-step validation prevents advancing with invalid data. Data persistence prevents losing progress on accidental navigation. The wizard must handle going back to edit previous steps without invalidating later steps.
answer: Step configuration: define steps as array with conditions. [{id: 'personal', title: 'Personal Info', fields: ['name', 'email', 'phone']}, {id: 'employment', title: 'Employment', fields: ['status', 'company'], condition: (data) => data.age >= 18}, {id: 'company', title: 'Company Details', fields: ['companyName', 'role'], condition: (data) => data.status === 'employed'}, {id: 'review', title: 'Review'}]. Step evaluation: on mount and when data changes, evaluate conditions to determine visible steps. Build visibleSteps array. Current step must be in visible steps. Progress indicator: show step numbers relative to visible steps (Step 2 of 4). Show completed checkmarks for finished steps. Click completed steps to navigate back. Validation: each step has validation schema (yup/zod). On 'Next': validate current step. If valid: save data, advance to next step. If invalid: show errors, stay on step. Don't validate hidden steps. Data persistence: save form data to sessionStorage on each step change. Key by form ID. On mount: check for saved data, prompt 'Continue where you left off?' Clear on successful submission. Conditional step handling: if user changes answer in step 2 that affects step 4's visibility, clear step 4's data when navigating back. Show warning: 'Changing this will reset later steps'. Review step: show summary of all entered data organized by step. Allow clicking section to edit that step. Submission: validate all visible steps, send complete data to API. Show loading state, handle errors. Accessibility: announce step changes to screen readers. Use aria-current='step' on current step. Keyboard navigation between steps. Focus management: focus first field when entering step.

instruction: Add comprehensive form validation with real-time feedback, async validation, cross-field validation, and accessible error messages. Requirements: validate on blur and on submit, show inline error messages, support async validation (e.g., username availability), validate dependent fields, and ensure errors are announced to screen readers.
reasoning: Form validation requires multiple triggers (blur for immediate feedback, submit for final check). Async validation needs debouncing to avoid excessive API calls. Cross-field validation considers multiple fields together. Accessible error messages require proper ARIA attributes. The validation system must be performant and not cause unnecessary re-renders.
answer: Validation library: use Zod for schema definition with TypeScript inference. Example schema: const schema = z.object({username: z.string().min(3).refine(checkUsernameAvailability, 'Username taken'), email: z.string().email(), password: z.string().min(8).regex(/^(?=.*[A-Z])(?=.*[0-9])/, 'Must contain uppercase and number'), confirmPassword: z.string()}).refine(data => data.password === data.confirmPassword, {message: 'Passwords must match', path: ['confirmPassword']}). Form library: use react-hook-form with zodResolver. Register fields with validation. Trigger validation on blur (mode: 'onBlur') and on submit. Inline errors: show error message below field in red. Use aria-invalid='true' on invalid field, aria-describedby pointing to error message ID. Don't show errors until field is touched (to avoid overwhelming on load). Async validation: debounce async validators (500ms). Show 'Checking...' state during validation. Cancel pending validation if field value changes (AbortController). Cross-field validation: use zod .refine() for rules involving multiple fields. Trigger revalidation of dependent fields when source field changes. useWatch to track dependencies. Accessible errors: error message has id, field has aria-describedby pointing to it. Use aria-live='polite' on error container for screen reader announcements. Focus first invalid field on submit. Form-level errors: show summary of all errors at top of form on submit failure. Link to each field. Performance: validate only changed fields, not entire form. Use React.memo for field components. Debounce validation on change (if validating on change). Submit handling: disable submit button during submission. Show loading state. On success: clear form, show success message. On error: show error message, allow retry.

instruction: Implement a real-time notification system using WebSockets with fallback to Server-Sent Events (SSE) and polling. Requirements: deliver notifications instantly when connected, handle connection drops gracefully, queue notifications during disconnection, and provide a consistent API regardless of transport.
reasoning: Real-time notifications improve user engagement but require reliable delivery. WebSockets provide bidirectional communication but can be blocked by firewalls. SSE is unidirectional but more reliable. Polling is the universal fallback. The system must try the best transport available and fall back gracefully. Notifications sent during disconnection must be delivered when reconnected.
answer: Transport selection: try WebSocket first. If connection fails or is blocked, fall back to SSE. If SSE fails, fall back to polling (every 30 seconds). Detect transport capability on app load. WebSocket: connect to wss://api.example.com/ws. Authenticate with JWT on connection. Subscribe to user's notification channel. Receive notifications as JSON messages. SSE: connect to /api/notifications/stream. Server pushes notifications as text/event-stream. Unidirectional (server to client). Polling: GET /api/notifications?since=lastTimestamp every 30 seconds. Return new notifications since last check. Reconnection: exponential backoff on connection loss (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, max 30s). On reconnect: fetch missed notifications since last received timestamp. Server stores undelivered notifications for 24 hours. Notification queue: server maintains queue of undelivered notifications per user. On connection: deliver queued notifications in order. Clear queue after delivery confirmation. API: create NotificationService with consistent interface regardless of transport. onNotification(callback), markAsRead(id), getUnreadCount(). Components use this API without knowing transport. Server-side: when notification is created, try to deliver via WebSocket. If user not connected, add to queue. On next connection, deliver queue. Fallback detection: if WebSocket connection fails 3 times, switch to SSE. If SSE fails 3 times, switch to polling. Remember preference in sessionStorage for session duration. Monitoring: track transport usage (WebSocket vs SSE vs polling). Monitor connection stability. Alert on high fallback rates (indicates WebSocket issues). Performance: use binary protocol for WebSocket (smaller payloads). Batch notifications if multiple arrive simultaneously. Debounce UI updates.

instruction: Add a collaborative editing feature with conflict resolution for a document editor. Requirements: allow multiple users to edit simultaneously, show other users' cursors, handle concurrent edits without data loss, support offline editing with sync on reconnect, and provide version history.
reasoning: Collaborative editing requires a conflict resolution strategy. Operational Transformation (OT) and Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDT) are the two main approaches. CRDT is simpler to implement and reason about. Cursor sharing requires low-latency updates. Offline editing needs local persistence and merge on reconnect. Version history allows reverting to previous states.
